conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is microbiology, and what three clinical questions does it underpin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The study of microorganisms and their interaction with the host. It underpins diagnosis (what's the bug?), treatment (what kills it?) and prevention (infection control + vaccines).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the six major groups of microbes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria (prokaryote), viruses (acellular), fungi (eukaryote), parasites (eukaryote — protozoa/helminths), and prions (misfolded protein, no nucleic acid).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast bacteria and viruses by cell type and genome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria are prokaryotes (no nucleus, peptidoglycan wall, binary fission) with circular DNA; viruses are acellular obligate intracellular particles (protein capsid ± envelope) with either DNA or RNA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What defines fungi and parasites structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Both are eukaryotes. Fungi have a chitin cell wall and exist as yeasts (single-celled) or moulds (hyphae); parasites are protozoa (single-celled) or helminths (worms).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a prion?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A misfolded protein — not a true organism, containing NO nucleic acid — that causes disease by templating misfolding of normal proteins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the prokaryote vs eukaryote divide central to antimicrobial therapy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria (prokaryotes) have 70S ribosomes and a peptidoglycan wall that human (eukaryotic, 80S-ribosome) cells lack; antibiotics target these to achieve selective toxicity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Put the microbes in order of size.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Prions < viruses (nm) < bacteria (~1–10 µm) < fungi/protozoa < helminths (mm–cm, macroscopic). Viruses need electron microscopy and pass through filters that trap bacteria.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define commensal, pathogen, colonisation and infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Commensal = lives on/in us without harm (normal flora); pathogen = capable of causing disease; colonisation = present and multiplying but NOT causing disease; infection = tissue damage with a host response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an opportunistic pathogen?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A commensal or low-virulence organism that causes disease only when host defences are down (e.g. immunosuppression, breached barriers).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does a positive culture not always mean infection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It may represent colonisation or contamination rather than true infection — it must be interpreted in context (symptoms, host response, inflammatory markers).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give an example of how the same organism can be commensal or pathogen depending on site.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: E. coli is a harmless gut commensal but causes disease in the urinary tract/bloodstream; Staph aureus is a nasal commensal but pathogenic in a wound or on a heart valve — site matters as much as the organism.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is virulence, and what are the main categories of virulence factor?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Virulence is the degree of pathogenicity. Factors: adhesins (pili/fimbriae — attachment), capsule (resists phagocytosis), toxins, spreading enzymes (coagulase, hyaluronidase), immune evasion (antigenic variation, intracellular survival) and biofilms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast exotoxins and endotoxin.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Exotoxins = secreted proteins (mainly Gram-positive), specific and potent, can be made into toxoid vaccines (tetanus/diphtheria). Endotoxin = lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released on lysis, non-specific → fever, sepsis, DIC, shock; no toxoid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a biofilm and why does it matter clinically?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A protective community of organisms on surfaces such as prostheses and catheters; it causes chronic, antibiotic-resistant infection and often requires device removal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the chain of infection, and how does infection control use it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Pathogen → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host. Breaking any link prevents infection (e.g. hand hygiene breaks contact spread; isolation breaks droplet/airborne).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State Koch's postulates and their key caveat.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The organism is found in all cases, isolated and grown in pure culture, reproduces the disease in a healthy host, and is re-isolated from that host. Caveat: they fail for uncultureable organisms, asymptomatic carriers and viruses, but remain the conceptual basis of causation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are bacteria structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Single-celled prokaryotes — no nucleus, a circular DNA chromosome, 70S ribosomes and (usually) a peptidoglycan cell wall — reproducing by binary fission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the four axes used to classify bacteria?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The Gram stain (cell-wall structure), shape (cocci vs bacilli), arrangement (clusters/chains/pairs) and oxygen requirement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Gram-positive = purple, THICK peptidoglycan, no endotoxin. Gram-negative = pink, THIN peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane containing LPS (endotoxin → sepsis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the steps of the Gram stain in order.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Crystal violet → iodine (mordant) → alcohol (decolouriser) → safranin (counterstain). Gram-positives retain the crystal violet (purple); Gram-negatives are decolourised and take the pink safranin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give the shape/arrangement rule for the main bacteria.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staphylococci = cocci in clusters; streptococci = cocci in chains; diplococci = pairs (Neisseria, pneumococcus); bacilli = rods; spirochaetes = spiral.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Populate the four-quadrant Gram/shape grid.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Gram-positive cocci = Staph/Strep/Enterococcus; Gram-negative cocci = Neisseria/Moraxella; Gram-positive rods = Clostridium/Listeria/Corynebacterium/Bacillus; Gram-negative rods = Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella), Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Campylobacter.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify bacteria by oxygen requirement with examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Obligate aerobe (Pseudomonas, M. tuberculosis); obligate anaerobe (Clostridium, Bacteroides); facultative anaerobe (most Enterobacterales, Staph, Strep); microaerophilic (Campylobacter, Helicobacter).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Where do anaerobes dominate, and which drug is the classic anti-anaerobe?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Abscesses, deep/necrotic tissue, and the gut/oral cavity (low-oxygen sites); metronidazole is the classic anti-anaerobe.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the catalase test distinguish?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staphylococci (catalase POSITIVE) from streptococci/enterococci (catalase NEGATIVE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the coagulase test distinguish?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staph aureus (coagulase POSITIVE) from other staphylococci such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus (coagulase negative).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the haemolysis patterns of streptococci.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Alpha = partial/green (S. pneumoniae, viridans); beta = complete/clear (Group A S. pyogenes, Group B S. agalactiae); gamma = none (Enterococcus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the lab pathway for identifying Gram-positive cocci.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Catalase (Staph positive / Strep negative) → coagulase (S. aureus positive) → then haemolysis pattern and Lancefield grouping for streptococci.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which tests identify Gram-negative rods?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Oxidase (Pseudomonas and Neisseria positive; Enterobacterales negative) and lactose fermentation on MacConkey (fermenters pink — E. coli, Klebsiella; non-fermenters — Salmonella, Shigella, Pseudomonas).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which organisms don't fit the Gram stain, and how are they detected?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mycobacteria (waxy mycolic-acid wall — acid-fast/Ziehl-Neelsen); atypicals (Mycoplasma no wall, Chlamydia, Legionella — serology/PCR); spirochaetes (too thin — dark-field microscopy/serology).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do β-lactams fail against atypical organisms?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) lack a standard peptidoglycan wall or are intracellular, so wall-targeting β-lactams don't work — treat with macrolides, tetracyclines or quinolones.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which bacteria form endospores, and why does it matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Some Gram-positive rods — Clostridium (tetani, botulinum, difficile, perfringens) and Bacillus (anthracis, cereus) — form dormant spores that resist heat/chemicals/desiccation and standard disinfection, needing autoclaving (e.g. C. difficile needs soap-and-water, not just alcohol gel).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which bacteria are encapsulated, and who is at particular risk?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae and Klebsiella; the anti-phagocytic capsule makes them dangerous in asplenic/hyposplenic patients, who should be vaccinated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a virus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An acellular, obligate intracellular parasite — a nucleic-acid genome (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope — with no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of its own.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Viruses lack the bacterial targets antibiotics exploit (no cell wall, no 70S ribosome, no metabolism); antivirals must instead target virus-specific steps (entry, genome replication, integration, processing, release).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the master axes of viral classification?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genome (DNA vs RNA — the key divide), envelope (enveloped vs non-enveloped) and replication strategy (e.g. retroviruses, hepadnaviruses).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast enveloped and non-enveloped viruses.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Enveloped = fragile lipid envelope, spread by close contact/blood/respiratory/sexual routes, easily killed by alcohol/soap (HIV, HBV/HCV, influenza, herpesviruses, SARS-CoV-2, measles). Non-enveloped ('naked') = tough protein capsid, faecal-oral/environmental spread, resistant (norovirus, rotavirus, hepatitis A, HPV, adenovirus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does alcohol gel work well against influenza but poorly against norovirus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Influenza is enveloped (fragile → inactivated by alcohol); norovirus is non-enveloped (tough → resistant), so soap-and-water or chlorine is needed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast DNA and RNA viruses.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: DNA viruses are more stable, usually replicate in the nucleus and proofread (less drift). RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, mutate rapidly (no proofreading) → antigenic drift/shift.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is a new influenza vaccine needed yearly, with no HIV/HCV vaccine yet?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Their RNA genomes mutate rapidly (antigenic drift/shift for flu; continual variation for HIV/HCV), so immunity and vaccines are quickly evaded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the DNA virus families (mnemonic 'HHAPPPy').
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Herpesviridae, Hepadnaviridae, Adenoviridae, Papillomaviridae, Polyomaviridae, Parvoviridae, Poxviridae.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the defining behaviour of herpesviruses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lifelong latency after primary infection, with reactivation when immunity falls (e.g. VZV → shingles; CMV/EBV disease in transplant/HIV).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Where do the main herpesviruses establish latency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HSV-1/2 in sensory ganglia, VZV in dorsal root ganglia, EBV in B cells, CMV in many cell types.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the retrovirus replication strategy (e.g. HIV).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase, converting their RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome → lifelong infection; this provides drug targets (reverse-transcriptase, integrase and protease inhibitors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify the hepatitis viruses by transmission and chronicity.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vowels A and E = faecal-oral, acute only; consonants B, C, D = blood-borne, can be chronic (B and C → cirrhosis/HCC; D requires HBV co/super-infection). Hep E is severe in pregnancy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is unusual about the hepatitis B genome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a DNA virus (hepadnavirus) that replicates via an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is aciclovir selective for herpesviruses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is only activated (phosphorylated) by the viral thymidine kinase, so it is concentrated in infected cells — an example of selective toxicity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the key oncogenic viruses and their cancers.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HPV (cervical/anogenital/oropharyngeal), hepatitis B and C (hepatocellular carcinoma), EBV (Burkitt/other lymphomas, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma), HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which viral replication step does oseltamivir target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Release — it is a neuraminidase inhibitor used against influenza, preventing release of new virions from infected cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are fungi structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Eukaryotes (nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes) with a cell wall of chitin and β-glucans and a membrane containing ergosterol (not cholesterol); they exist as yeasts, moulds or dimorphic forms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is selective toxicity harder with antifungals than antibiotics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fungi are eukaryotes and share much cell machinery with us, so antifungals must exploit the few fungus-specific structures (ergosterol, chitin/β-glucan) and tend to be more toxic and narrower than antibiotics.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Distinguish yeasts, moulds and dimorphic fungi.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Yeasts = single budding cells (Candida, Cryptococcus); moulds = filamentous hyphae (Aspergillus, dermatophytes, Mucor); dimorphic = 'mould in the cold (environment), yeast in the heat (host)' (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast superficial and systemic/invasive fungal disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Superficial = skin/hair/nails/mucosa, often immunocompetent, mild (tinea, thrush, pityriasis versicolor). Systemic/invasive = deep organs/blood/lung/CNS, usually immunocompromised, life-threatening (invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PCP, mucormycosis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Candida infections.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A commensal yeast (mouth, gut, vagina, skin) that turns opportunistic: oral thrush (infants, inhaled steroids, HIV, antibiotics), vaginal thrush, intertrigo, and invasive candidiasis/candidaemia (ICU, central lines, neutropenia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the spectrum of Aspergillus disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ABPA (hypersensitivity in asthma/CF), aspergilloma (fungus ball in an old cavity such as prior TB), and invasive aspergillosis (in the neutropenic — high mortality).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Cryptococcus neoformans infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An encapsulated yeast (bird droppings) causing cryptococcal meningitis in HIV/AIDS with low CD4; diagnosed with India ink (capsule halo), cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) and CSF culture.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: P. jirovecii causes an AIDS-defining pneumonia when CD4 <200: dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, hypoxia and bilateral perihilar infiltrates; treated with co-trimoxazole, with prophylaxis when CD4 <200.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the HIV/CD4 fungal triad.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Oral/oesophageal Candida (early), Pneumocystis (PCP) below ~200, Cryptococcus below ~100.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe dermatophyte infections.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Moulds of keratin causing 'tinea'/ringworm (pedis, corporis, capitis, cruris, unguium); diagnosed on skin scrapings with KOH; treated with terbinafine or azoles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is mucormycosis and who gets it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aggressive angioinvasive infection by Mucor/Rhizopus (rhino-orbito-cerebral) in diabetic ketoacidosis or the immunocompromised — a medical/surgical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the predisposing factors for fungal disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HIV/low CD4, neutropenia/chemotherapy/transplant, diabetes (especially ketoacidosis), broad-spectrum antibiotics, indwelling lines/ICU/TPN, and corticosteroids/immunosuppressants — always ask 'why?'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How are fungal infections diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Microscopy (KOH for skin/nails, India ink for Cryptococcus), culture (Sabouraud agar, slower than bacteria), histology (tissue invasion), and antigen tests (cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan, β-D-glucan).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the antifungal classes and their targets.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Azoles (inhibit ergosterol synthesis — 14α-demethylase); polyenes/amphotericin B (bind ergosterol → membrane pores, nephrotoxic); echinocandins (inhibit β-glucan wall synthesis); terbinafine (squalene epoxidase, for dermatophytes); flucytosine (fungal DNA/RNA synthesis, with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why are antifungals generally more toxic than antibiotics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because fungi are eukaryotes like human cells, there are fewer unique targets — so agents such as amphotericin (nephrotoxicity) and azoles (hepatotoxicity, drug interactions) have a narrower therapeutic window.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are parasites, and how are they grouped medically?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Eukaryotic organisms that live on/in a host at its expense: protozoa (single-celled) and helminths (worms), plus ectoparasites (arthropods — lice, scabies, ticks).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What two clinical reflexes dominate parasitology?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 'Fever in a returning traveller → think malaria' and 'eosinophilia → think helminths (worms)'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast protozoa and helminths.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Protozoa are single cells that multiply in the host → acute fever/diarrhoea/systemic illness (malaria, giardia, amoeba). Helminths are worms that usually don't multiply in the host → chronic disease with eosinophilia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the malaria species.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Plasmodium falciparum (most dangerous — severe/cerebral malaria), vivax and ovale (relapse via dormant liver hypnozoites → need primaquine), malariae and knowlesi; transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria diagnosed and treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Thick and thin blood films (thick to detect, thin for species/parasitaemia) plus rapid antigen — send three films before excluding; treat with artemisinin combination therapy (uncomplicated) or IV artesunate (severe).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Giardia lamblia infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Faecal-oral/waterborne giardiasis causing chronic, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea with bloating and malabsorption ('backpacker's diarrhoea'); treated with metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Entamoeba histolytica infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Amoebiasis causing bloody dysentery and a liver abscess ('anchovy sauce' pus); treated with metronidazole plus a luminal agent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Cryptosporidium infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Watery diarrhoea that is severe and chronic in HIV/AIDS; an opportunistic protozoan.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Toxoplasma gondii infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acquired from cat faeces or undercooked meat; causes congenital toxoplasmosis and cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV (ring-enhancing brain lesions).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is leishmaniasis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A sandfly-borne protozoal infection causing either a cutaneous ulcer or visceral disease (kala-azar: fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the three helminth groups with examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Nematodes (roundworms — Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides, Enterobius/threadworm, filaria); cestodes (tapeworms — Taenia, Echinococcus/hydatid); trematodes (flukes — Schistosoma, liver/lung flukes).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Enterobius (threadworm) infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Common in UK children; causes perianal itch at night; diagnosed with the 'sellotape test'; treated with mebendazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does hookworm classically cause, and how is it acquired?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Iron-deficiency anaemia; acquired by walking barefoot on contaminated soil (larvae penetrate skin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is Strongyloides important before immunosuppression?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It can persist for years by autoinfection and cause life-threatening hyperinfection when immunosuppressed (e.g. before steroids), so at-risk patients are screened/treated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe schistosomiasis.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Freshwater snail-derived larvae penetrate skin; S. haematobium causes haematuria and predisposes to bladder cancer (others cause GI/liver disease); treated with praziquantel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise antiparasitic treatments.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Malaria → artemisinin combinations/IV artesunate; protozoal diarrhoea and trichomonas → metronidazole/tinidazole; roundworms → -bendazoles (albendazole/mebendazole); flukes and tapeworms → praziquantel; Strongyloides/scabies → ivermectin; scabies/lice → topical permethrin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe scabies.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infestation with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei causing intense itch (worse at night) and burrows in the finger webs/wrists; treated with topical permethrin (treat close contacts).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a prion?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An infectious protein that uniquely contains NO nucleic acid — a misfolded form of a normal host protein (PrP) that propagates by converting normal protein into the abnormal form (a self-templating chain reaction).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the molecular mechanism of prion propagation.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Normal PrP^C (α-helix-rich) is converted by contact with misfolded PrP^Sc (β-sheet-rich) into more PrP^Sc — an exponential chain reaction; aggregates accumulate in neurons causing spongiform (vacuolated) change.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do prions 'replicate' differently from all other pathogens?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: By conformational conversion — changing the shape of an existing protein — not by copying a genetic code; the 'information' is in the misfolded shape itself.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do prions resist standard sterilisation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They have no nucleic acid to damage, so they resist heat/autoclaving, formaldehyde, alcohol and radiation — requiring special decontamination (extended high-temperature autoclaving, sodium hydroxide/hypochlorite) or single-use instruments for CNS/eye/tonsil procedures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do prion diseases trigger no immune response?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The prion is a form of 'self' protein, so there is no fever, no raised inflammatory markers and typically normal routine CSF — distinguishing them from infective/inflammatory encephalopathies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify the prion diseases (transmissible spongiform encephalopathies).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sporadic (sporadic CJD, ~85% — spontaneous misfolding, elderly); inherited (familial CJD, GSS, fatal familial insomnia — PRNP gene mutations, autosomal dominant); acquired (variant CJD from BSE beef, iatrogenic CJD, kuru).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast sporadic and variant CJD.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sporadic CJD = commonest, elderly (~60s), rapid dementia with myoclonus, death in months. Variant CJD = younger (20s–30s), from BSE-contaminated beef, psychiatric/behavioural and sensory onset first, longer course (~1–2 years).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the clinical signature of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A rapidly progressive dementia (weeks–months, far faster than Alzheimer's) with myoclonus (classic), ataxia, visual/cerebellar signs, behavioural/psychiatric change and late akinetic mutism — relentless and uniformly fatal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the MRI findings in CJD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging; the pulvinar sign is characteristic of variant CJD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic EEG finding in sporadic CJD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Periodic sharp-wave complexes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What CSF tests support a diagnosis of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Routine analysis is normal, but 14-3-3 protein is elevated and RT-QuIC (a prion-seeding assay) is increasingly the key test.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the definitive diagnosis of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Spongiform change with PrP^Sc on brain histology (biopsy/autopsy) — rarely done ante-mortem; PRNP gene analysis identifies inherited forms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: There is no cure — it is uniformly fatal; management is supportive/palliative (symptom control, MDT, end-of-life care).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key public-health/infection-control measures for prions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Special decontamination or single-use instruments for high-risk (CNS/eye/tonsil) procedures; quarantine/destruction of contaminated equipment; BSE controls (removing cattle from the food chain, feed bans) that reduced variant CJD; and blood/tissue donation restrictions for at-risk individuals.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How are the clinically important viral infections grouped in this topic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: By family: the herpesviruses (sharing lifelong latency → reactivation) and the respiratory viruses (influenza, COVID-19).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the unifying herpesvirus principle?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops — which is why they dominate in immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two antiviral mechanisms mentioned?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aciclovir → inhibits viral DNA polymerase; neuraminidase inhibitors → block viral release.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How many human herpesviruses are there, and which form the alpha group?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 8 human herpesviruses, all establishing latency: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV (the alpha group — neurotropic, treated with aciclovir), EBV, CMV, HHV-6/7, HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the shared treatment principle for herpesviruses, and how does resistance arise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The '-ciclovirs' (aciclovir, valaciclovir, ganciclovir) inhibit viral DNA polymerase; resistance arises via mutation of viral thymidine kinase or DNA polymerase.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the side effects/toxicity of aciclovir?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Psychiatric (Cotard syndrome); toxicity → lethargy + myoclonus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What do HSV-1 and HSV-2 typically cause, and what are the reactivation triggers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HSV-1 → cold sores around the mouth; HSV-2 → genital herpes (overlap exists — either can cause either). Reactivation triggers: stress, infection, immunocompromise, UV light.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the serious presentations of HSV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe — the can't-miss; urgent IV aciclovir), neonatal herpes (HSV-2, peripartum), eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment of HSV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aciclovir (topical for mild cold sores; oral/IV for significant or systemic disease).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: VZV: how does primary infection (chickenpox) present, and when is it most infectious?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary = chickenpox: fever + vesicular rash (lesions at different stages); most infectious 1–2 days before the rash appears.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: VZV: how does reactivation (shingles) present?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Painful rash in a dermatomal distribution (doesn't cross the midline).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications of VZV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Post-herpetic neuralgia, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial nerve → facial palsy + ear vesicles), ophthalmic zoster (V1 — Hutchinson's sign, sight-threatening); severe in pregnancy and immunocompromise.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment for VZV, and when is the shingles vaccine offered?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aciclovir / valaciclovir; the shingles vaccine (Shingrix — recombinant, 2 doses) is offered routinely from age 65.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does EBV infectious mononucleosis present?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 'Kissing disease' / glandular fever: fever, malaise, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, transient macular rash.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the amoxicillin trap in EBV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Giving amoxicillin/ampicillin to someone with EBV → florid maculopapular rash (a classic SBA clue).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the investigations and management of EBV mononucleosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Investigations: raised lymphocytes (atypical lymphocytes), Monospot/heterophile antibody test (positive in the 2nd week). Management: conservative (resolves in 2–4 weeks); avoid contact sport ~4–6 weeks (splenic rupture risk).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What malignancies are associated with EBV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does CMV present in the immunocompetent, and what discriminates it from EBV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Typically a mononucleosis-like illness, but Monospot-negative — the discriminator from EBV; dormant in monocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the importance of CMV in the immunocompromised?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The real importance: retinitis (HIV/AIDS), colitis, oesophagitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is congenital CMV, and what are its features?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The commonest congenital infection → sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, growth restriction.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment of CMV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Adenovirus: what is the CSP 'ACE' trio, and what happens in immunocompromise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Normally self-limiting: keratoConjunctivitis, respiratory tract infection (respiratory), and gastroEnteritis. In immunocompromise: encephalitis, pneumonitis, enterocolitis, hepatitis, haemorrhagic cystitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does influenza present, and who are the at-risk groups?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Presentation: abrupt fever, coryzal symptoms, lethargy, anorexia, arthralgia, headache, dry cough, sore throat (more systemic/abrupt than a common cold). At-risk groups: elderly, pregnant, chronic disease, immunocompromised.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications and diagnosis of influenza?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Complications: pneumonia — primary viral or secondary bacterial (Staph aureus, pneumococcus). Diagnosis: viral nasal/throat swab PCR.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of influenza?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most supportive; if at risk + within 48h: oral oseltamivir or inhaled zanamivir (neuraminidase inhibitors — block sialic acid cleavage → prevent viral release); annual vaccination for prevention.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the causative virus, type, and incubation of COVID-19?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: SARS-CoV-2 — a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; incubation up to 14 days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does COVID-19 present, and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Presentation: anosmia, cough, fever, myalgia, headache, fatigue; respiratory failure if severe. Diagnosis: RT-PCR of upper respiratory swab; CXR = bilateral lower-zone ground-glass infiltrates.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of COVID-19, and what is long COVID?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mild–moderate → supportive; hospitalised/severe → dexamethasone + remdesivir (nucleotide analogue) + CPAP/respiratory support, escalating to ventilation. Long COVID: persistent fatigue, breathlessness, cognitive symptoms weeks–months after infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: how do you distinguish EBV from CMV mononucleosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Both cause mononucleosis, but EBV is Monospot-positive and CMV is Monospot-negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 2 months?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) + rotavirus (oral, live) + MenB. (PCV is NOT given at 2 months under the 1+1 schedule since 2020.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 3 months?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) + pneumococcal (PCV, the single primary dose) + rotavirus (2nd, oral).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 4 months?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) + MenB (2nd). (No PCV at 4 months under the 1+1 schedule — primary PCV is at 3 months, booster at 12 months.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 12 months (12–13 months)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hib/MenC + MMR + pneumococcal booster + MenB booster.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 3 years 4 months (3–4y)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 4-in-1 preschool booster (DTaP/IPV) + MMR 2nd dose.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 12–13 years, and what does it protect against?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HPV vaccine (girls + boys), given as a single dose (since 2023). Protects against HPV 16/18 (cervical/anal cancer) + 6/11 (genital warts).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 14 years?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 3-in-1 teenage booster (Td/IPV — tetanus, low-dose diphtheria, polio; no pertussis) + MenACWY.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which vaccines are given in pregnancy, and with what timing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Only these: pertussis (Tdap) at 16–32 weeks (ideally 20 weeks) — to protect the newborn from whooping cough; influenza — any trimester (inactivated only); COVID-19 booster (if eligible).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy — MMR, varicella, yellow fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccines for the elderly/specific adults: what is given at 65 years, 65+, and 70 years?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 65 years: pneumococcal (single dose) + shingles (Shingrix — recombinant, 2 doses; routine from 65 since 2023, catch-up at 70); 65+: influenza (annually).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which vaccines are recommended in asplenia/splenic dysfunction?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Live attenuated vaccines: give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: MMR, varicella (chickenpox), rotavirus (oral), yellow fever, BCG, nasal flu, oral typhoid. (The UK shingles vaccine is now Shingrix — recombinant/non-live — not a live vaccine.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Live attenuated vaccines: dosing, antibody response, adjuvant need, and key contraindication.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A single dose is often sufficient (produces strong cell-mediated immunity); produces IgG + IgA antibodies; no adjuvant needed. May cause mild disease — DON'T give to immunocompromised or pregnant patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines: give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IPV, DTaP, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, HPV, injectable influenza, meningococcal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines: dosing, antibody response, adjuvant need, and safety.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Multiple doses needed + booster; produces IgG only (not IgA); safe in pregnancy + immunocompromise; adjuvant required to boost immunogenicity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how do the diphtheria + tetanus vaccines work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant (inactivated toxin → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the pertussis vaccine work, and why was it changed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 5 purified protein components (acellular — replaced whole-cell due to side effects).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how do the meningococcus + Hib vaccines work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Capsular polysaccharide conjugated to a carrier protein (T-cell-dependent response → memory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the pneumococcus (PCV13) vaccine work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A conjugate containing polysaccharide from 13 common capsular types.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the hepatitis B vaccine work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recombinant viral surface antigen (HBsAg).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the MMR vaccine work, and why is it given from 12 months?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated strains — given from 12 months because maternal IgG would neutralise it earlier.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the rotavirus vaccine work, and why is it important?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated, oral — rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea/hospitalisation in infants.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: why is MMR given at 12 months and not earlier?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given before this; maternal IgG wanes by ~6 months.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what is the rule for live vaccines in immunocompromise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live vaccines + immunocompromise = absolute contraindication. Live vaccines in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <200, on biologics, post-stem cell transplant) → risk of vaccine-strain disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: how do conjugated vs unconjugated polysaccharide vaccines differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Conjugated (PCV, Hib, MenACWY) elicit a T-cell-dependent response → memory formation. Unconjugated are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: why is pertussis vaccination given in pregnancy, and when is it most important?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Maternal vaccination at 16–32 weeks → antibodies passively transferred to the neonate → protects the newborn for the first few weeks before their own vaccines. Particularly important as pertussis is most dangerous in <3 month infants.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what proportion of cervical cancers and genital warts do the key HPV types cause, and what does Gardasil 9 cover?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers; HPV 6 + 11 cause 90% of genital warts. Gardasil 9 (9-valent) now covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the central problem in transplant immunology?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) → mounts a rejection response → graft damage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is HLA, and how does the degree of mismatch relate to rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HLA (human leukocyte antigen) = the human MHC — cell-surface molecules distinguishing self from non-self; the more mismatched, the stronger the rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which T-cells recognise MHC Class I versus Class II?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: MHC Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) — on all nucleated cells, recognised by CD8+ T-cells. MHC Class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) — on APCs/B-cells, recognised by CD4+ T-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which HLA loci are most important to match, and which is most significant?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HLA-A, -B, and -DR (the '6-antigen match'); DR is the most significant.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must ABO blood group be compatible in transplantation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ABO incompatibility → hyperacute rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the pre-transplant crossmatch, and what does a positive result mean?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recipient serum is tested against donor lymphocytes to detect pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies — a positive crossmatch → hyperacute rejection → contraindication.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Allorecognition: describe the direct pathway and what it drives.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recipient T-cells recognise intact donor HLA on donor APCs → drives acute rejection (early, vigorous).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Allorecognition: describe the indirect pathway and what it drives.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recipient APCs process donor HLA and present it → drives chronic rejection (later).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the engine of rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: T-cell recognition of donor HLA is the engine of rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Hyperacute rejection: timing, mechanism, hypersensitivity type, and outcome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Timing: minutes–hours. Mechanism: pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis. Hypersensitivity Type II. Outcome: irreversible → remove graft; prevented by crossmatch.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Acute rejection: timing, mechanism, hypersensitivity type, and outcome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Timing: days–6 months. Mechanism: T-cell-mediated (cellular) ± antibody; HLA mismatch. Hypersensitivity Type IV. Outcome: often reversible with ↑immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chronic rejection: timing, mechanism, hypersensitivity type, and outcome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Timing: months–years. Mechanism: antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy). Hypersensitivity: mixed. Outcome: largely irreversible → graft failure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the memory hook linking the three rejection types to their mechanisms and treatability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hyperacute = preformed antibodies (Type II, prevented by crossmatch); acute = T-cells/HLA mismatch (Type IV, treatable); chronic = fibrosis (untreatable).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), and in what setting does it occur?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The opposite of rejection: in bone marrow/stem cell transplants, the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues (graft attacks host, not host attacks graft).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic triad of GVHD targets?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Skin (rash), gut (diarrhoea), and liver (deranged LFTs/jaundice).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is GVHD classified, managed, and prevented?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acute (<100 days) vs chronic; managed with immunosuppression; prevented by HLA matching + T-cell depletion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key contrast between solid-organ transplant and marrow transplant?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Solid-organ transplant → host rejects graft; marrow transplant → graft rejects host (GVHD).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the overall immunosuppression strategy for preventing rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Induction (intense, peri-transplant) then maintenance (lifelong, lower-dose); usually triple therapy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Calcineurin inhibitors: examples, mechanism, and key cautions.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Examples: tacrolimus, ciclosporin. Mechanism: block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation (the backbone). Cautions: nephrotoxic, narrow therapeutic index → need TDM.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Antiproliferatives: examples and mechanism.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Examples: mycophenolate, azathioprine. Mechanism: inhibit purine synthesis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Corticosteroids and mTOR inhibitors in transplant: examples and mechanism.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Corticosteroids: prednisolone — broad anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive. mTOR inhibitors: sirolimus — block T-cell proliferation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Biologics (induction) in transplant: examples and mechanism.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Basiliximab (anti-IL-2R), ATG — deplete/block T-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is standard maintenance immunosuppression, and how is acute rejection treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Standard maintenance: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone. Treating acute rejection: high-dose steroids first-line ± antibody therapy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complications of immunosuppression — infection: which opportunistic infections occur and what prophylaxis is used?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Opportunistic: CMV, PCP (prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole), fungal, BK virus, reactivation of TB/hepatitis. These patients have iatrogenic T-cell deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complications of immunosuppression — malignancy: which cancers are increased?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Skin cancers (esp. SCC — regular skin surveillance), post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD — EBV-driven), and others.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the drug-specific complications of the transplant immunosuppressants?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, new-onset diabetes, hypertension, tremor (tacrolimus); marrow suppression (azathioprine — check TPMT first); gum hypertrophy/hirsutism (ciclosporin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which general complications arise from corticosteroids in transplant patients?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cardiovascular risk and osteoporosis (from steroids).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must TPMT be checked before starting azathioprine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Azathioprine can cause marrow suppression, so TPMT is checked first.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is inflammation, and what does it achieve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection — bringing immune cells and mediators to the site to destroy the cause, clear debris, and begin repair.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of acute inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acute inflammation has a vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils to the site), driven by chemical mediators — producing the cardinal signs. It either resolves or, if unresolved, becomes chronic. It's protective, but excessive/chronic inflammation causes disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the five cardinal signs of inflammation and their causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Redness (rubor) — ↑blood flow (vasodilation); heat (calor) — ↑blood flow; swelling (tumor) — ↑vascular permeability → fluid leaks into tissue (exudate); pain (dolor) — mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandins) sensitise nerves; loss of function — pain + swelling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: From which two core processes do all five cardinal signs derive?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vasodilation (redness/heat) + increased permeability (swelling) + mediators (pain) — all five fall out of these.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The vascular response: what are the effects of vasodilation and increased vascular permeability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vasodilation → ↑blood flow to the area → redness + heat (mediated by histamine, prostaglandins, NO). ↑Vascular permeability → endothelial cells contract → gaps form → fluid + proteins leak out (exudate) → swelling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The vascular response: what is stasis and why does it matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Stasis is slowed flow (from fluid loss + haemoconcentration) → it lets leucocytes marginate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the exudate point — how does inflammatory exudate differ from a transudate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The fluid that leaks out is protein-rich (exudate) — carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen (which forms fibrin to wall off the area) → this distinguishes inflammatory exudate from a simple transudate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the five steps of the cellular response (neutrophil recruitment).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Margination (slowed flow → neutrophils move to the vessel edge); rolling + adhesion (bind endothelium via selectins → integrins); diapedesis/transmigration (squeeze through the vessel wall into the tissue); chemotaxis (migrate toward the pathogen following chemical gradients — chemokines, complement C5a); phagocytosis (engulf + destroy the pathogen, aided by opsonisation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the high-yield neutrophil-first point?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Neutrophils arrive first (acute inflammation), then macrophages later (clean-up + chronic); this is why the FBC shows neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is opsonisation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Coating the pathogen with antibody/complement → makes phagocytosis far more efficient ('opsonins' = 'to prepare for eating').

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Histamine: source and action (and what blocks it)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: mast cells. Action: vasodilation + ↑permeability (early) — antihistamines block it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Prostaglandins: source and action (and what blocks them)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: from arachidonic acid (COX). Action: vasodilation, pain, fever — NSAIDs block COX.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Leukotrienes: source and action (and what blocks them)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: from arachidonic acid (lipoxygenase). Action: bronchoconstriction, ↑permeability — leukotriene antagonists (in asthma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6): source and action?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: macrophages. Action: the systemic response — fever, acute-phase proteins; TNF/IL-6 = biologic drug targets.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Bradykinin and complement (C3a, C5a): source and action?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bradykinin (source: plasma) → pain + vasodilation. Complement C3a, C5a (source: plasma) → chemotaxis + mast cell activation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Drug-target payoff: how do NSAIDs and steroids act on inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: NSAIDs block COX → ↓prostaglandins → anti-inflammatory + analgesic + antipyretic. Steroids broadly suppress inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway) — the most powerful anti-inflammatories.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Drug-target payoff: how do biologics act, and give examples of their use.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) block specific cytokines — used in rheumatoid arthritis and IBD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The systemic response: how does fever arise, and what are the acute-phase proteins?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever: cytokines → hypothalamus → ↑temperature set point. Acute-phase proteins: the liver produces CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin (IL-6-driven) → CRP is the clinical inflammatory marker.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The systemic response: what are leucocytosis and malaise/anorexia due to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Leucocytosis: ↑white cell production (neutrophilia in bacterial infection). Malaise/anorexia: cytokine effects.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare CRP and ESR as inflammatory markers.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven) and ESR is slower (fibrinogen-related); both are clinical markers of inflammation used to detect + monitor inflammatory/infective disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the SIRS/sepsis extreme of the systemic response?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An overwhelming systemic inflammatory response → SIRS → sepsis (a dysregulated response to infection → organ dysfunction).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the possible outcomes of acute inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Resolution (the cause is cleared → tissue returns to normal — the ideal); chronic inflammation (if unresolved → shifts to macrophages + lymphocytes → ongoing tissue damage + repair); fibrosis/scarring (repair with fibrous tissue if tissue can't regenerate); abscess (a localised collection of pus — dead neutrophils + debris).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the high-yield picture of chronic inflammation, and what does it underlie?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chronic inflammation is macrophage + lymphocyte-driven (not neutrophils), with simultaneous tissue destruction + repair (fibrosis) → it underlies TB, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, atherosclerosis, and chronic infection → often with granuloma formation (organised macrophages — TB, sarcoid, Crohn's).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the acute-vs-chronic cell distinction?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acute = neutrophils; chronic = macrophages + lymphocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three phases of wound healing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inflammation → proliferation → remodelling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Clinically, what does neutrophilia indicate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acute bacterial infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two linked ideas of this topic — define HCAIs and infection control.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HCAIs (healthcare-associated/nosocomial infections) are acquired ≥48h after admission (not incubating on arrival); infection control is the measures that prevent them.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of infection control, and the single most effective intervention?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The organising principle is the chain of infection: every infection follows a predictable chain, and breaking any single link prevents transmission. The single most effective intervention is hand hygiene.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the definition threshold for a healthcare-associated infection (HCAI)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An HCAI is acquired ≥48h after admission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the six links in the chain of infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1. Infectious agent (the pathogen); 2. Reservoir (where it lives); 3. Portal of exit (how it leaves); 4. Mode of transmission (contact/droplet/airborne/vehicle); 5. Portal of entry (how it enters); 6. Susceptible host (the patient at risk).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chain of infection: how do you break the infectious agent and reservoir links?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infectious agent (the pathogen) → antimicrobials, sterilisation. Reservoir (people, equipment, water) → cleaning, decontamination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chain of infection: how do you break the portal of exit and mode of transmission links?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Portal of exit (secretions, blood, faeces) → respiratory hygiene, cover wounds. Mode of transmission (contact/droplet/airborne/vehicle) → hand hygiene, PPE, isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chain of infection: how do you break the portal of entry and susceptible host links?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Portal of entry (wounds, lines, mucosa) → aseptic technique, catheter care. Susceptible host (the patient at risk) → vaccination, treating comorbidity, nutrition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the four transmission routes and give examples of each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Contact (direct/indirect — MRSA, C. diff); droplet (large particles, settle quickly — influenza, COVID, pertussis, meningococcus); airborne (small particles, stay suspended — TB, measles, varicella); vehicle/vector (food, water, blood).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the standard precautions applied to every patient, always?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hand hygiene (the foundation); PPE (gloves, apron/gown, mask, eye protection as risk dictates); sharps safety (no re-sheathing; sharps bins); respiratory hygiene ('catch it, bin it, kill it'); safe waste + linen disposal; cleaning + decontamination of equipment/environment; aseptic technique for invasive procedures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the WHO '5 Moments for Hand Hygiene'?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1. Before touching a patient; 2. Before a clean/aseptic procedure; 3. After body-fluid exposure risk; 4. After touching a patient; 5. After touching patient surroundings.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Soap and water vs alcohol gel: what is the key distinction (the classic exam point)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Alcohol gel for most situations, BUT soap and water (not alcohol gel) for spore-forming organisms — C. difficile and norovirus (alcohol doesn't kill spores).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does 'bare below the elbows' refer to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a standard hand-hygiene requirement — being bare below the elbows to allow effective hand and forearm cleaning.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Transmission-based precautions: what organisms require CONTACT precautions and what measures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: For MRSA, C. diff, VRE, RSV. Measures: gloves + gown, single room, dedicated equipment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Transmission-based precautions: what organisms require DROPLET precautions and what measures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: For influenza, COVID-19, pertussis, meningococcus. Measures: surgical mask, single room.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Transmission-based precautions: what organisms require AIRBORNE precautions and what measures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: For TB, measles, varicella. Measures: N95/FFP3 respirator, negative-pressure room.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which combinations of precautions apply to TB and to C. diff?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: TB needs airborne + contact + standard; C. diff needs contact + standard.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: C. difficile as an HCAI: cause/association and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotic-associated (clindamycin/cephalosporins/fluoroquinolones), spore-forming. Prevention: stewardship, isolation, soap & water, oral vancomycin to treat.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: MRSA as an HCAI: cause/association and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Colonisation → infection; lines/wounds. Prevention: contact precautions, screening + decolonisation (chlorhexidine wash, nasal mupirocin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: CAUTI and CLABSI: their associations and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI): urinary catheters → avoid/remove catheters early, aseptic insertion. Central line-associated BSI (CLABSI): central venous catheters → insertion care bundles, aseptic technique, remove early.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: SSI and HAP/VAP: their associations and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Surgical site infection (SSI): surgery → prophylactic antibiotics, skin prep, normothermia. HAP/VAP: ventilation, aspiration → head elevation, oral care (cross-ref respiratory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Norovirus as an HCAI: cause/association and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Faecal-oral, causes outbreaks (wards/cruise). Prevention: soap & water, ward closure, isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: MRSA in focus: mechanism, screening, decolonisation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams (altered PBP2a); screen on admission (nasal/groin swab) → decolonise (mupirocin + chlorhexidine); contact precautions; treat infection with vancomycin/teicoplanin/linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: C. difficile in focus: pathogenesis and the '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotic use → loss of gut flora → toxin-producing C. diff overgrowth → pseudomembranous colitis. The '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics: clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: C. difficile in focus: management.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin (not metronidazole first-line now); stop the offending antibiotic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the system-level (organisational) prevention measures for HCAIs?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Care bundles (CLABSI, CAUTI, ventilator bundles); surveillance + audit (mandatory MRSA bacteraemia + C. diff reporting); antimicrobial stewardship, environmental cleaning; isolation facilities (side rooms, negative pressure); staff vaccination (flu, hepatitis B), education + hand-hygiene audits; outbreak management (identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, involve IPC team); Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT) for invasive procedures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is antimicrobial stewardship described as core infection control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antimicrobial stewardship is core infection control because it prevents C. diff and resistance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What steps does outbreak management involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, and involve the IPC (infection prevention and control) team.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is immunodeficiency, and what does it lead to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A missing or defective component of the immune system → recurrent, severe, unusual, or persistent infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the single organising principle of immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The deficient component predicts the infection pattern — work out which arm has failed, and you predict the bug.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the top-level fork of immunodeficiency, and which is commoner?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary (genetic/intrinsic) vs secondary (acquired) — secondary is far commoner.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the four functional arms that can fail in immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Humoral (B-cell/antibody), cell-mediated (T-cell), phagocyte, and complement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Humoral (B-cell/antibody) deficiency: characteristic infections and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Encapsulated bacteria — H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis ('SHiN'). Clue: recurrent sinopulmonary infections, after 6 months of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: T-cell (cell-mediated) deficiency: characteristic infections and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 'HIV-type' opportunists — viruses, fungi (PCP/candida), intracellular bacteria (TB), protozoa. Clue: severe/atypical viral + fungal infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Phagocyte deficiency: characteristic infections and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Catalase-positive bacteria (Staph aureus) + fungi (Aspergillus). Clue: abscesses, osteomyelitis, in childhood.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complement deficiency: characteristic infection and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Neisseria (recurrent meningococcal). Clue: recurrent meningococcaemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of primary vs secondary immunodeficiency.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary (intrinsic/genetic): named syndromes — XLA, DiGeorge, CGD, SCID. Secondary (acquired, commoner): HIV (the big one), drugs (steroids, rituximab, cytotoxics, natalizumab), malignancy (myeloma, leukaemia/lymphoma, CLL), protein loss (nephrotic, PLE), malnutrition, asplenia/hyposplenism, diabetes, extremes of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the MHC 'Rule of 8'.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Class I (HLA-A/B/C, all nucleated cells) → CD8 + NK; CD8 × MHC I = 8. Class II (HLA-DQ/DR/DP, APCs + B-cells only) → CD4; CD4 × MHC II = 8.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare the TH1 and TH2 pathways.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: TH1 (cell-mediated): IL-12 → TH1 → IFNγ → macrophage activation → IL-1/6/8, TNFα. TH2 (humoral): IL-4 → TH2; IL-4 → IgE + B-cell proliferation, IL-5 → IgA + eosinophils, IL-10 → inhibits TH1.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise complement function (C3/4/5a, C3b, C5a, C5–9).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: C3/4/5a = anaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation); C3b = opsonisation (splenic phagocytosis); C5a = neutrophil chemotaxis; C5–9 = membrane attack complex (kills Neisseria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: X-Linked Agammaglobulinaemia (XLA/Bruton's): defect, presentation, and infection pattern.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: BTK mutation → absent B-cells + absent antibodies; presents after 6 months (as maternal IgG wanes); recurrent URTI/LRTI with encapsulated organisms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Common Variable Immune Deficiency (CVID): how does it differ from XLA, and what are its risks?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Like XLA but less severe (low rather than absent antibodies); affects adults; increased risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Selective IgA Deficiency: how common is it, what infections, and what transfusion caution applies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The most common primary immunodeficiency; GI/respiratory infections (esp. Giardia, Cryptosporidium); often asymptomatic; risk of anaphylaxis to blood products → give washed/IgA-deficient products if transfusing.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Infection risk by antibody type: what do IgG and IgA deficiency predispose to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IgG deficiency → encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis); IgA deficiency → GI/respiratory (Giardia, Cryptosporidium).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion): mechanism, features, and mnemonic.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Loss of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal arch → thymic aplasia (↓T-cells) + hypoparathyroidism (↓PTH → hypocalcaemia); also cleft palate, conotruncal cardiac defects. CATCH-22: Cardiac, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia, 22q11.2. Tetany/hypocalcaemia at birth + cardiac defect → think DiGeorge.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the secondary causes of T-cell deficiency, and the infections to think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Secondary: HIV/AIDS (destroys CD4+ — the commonest acquired T-cell deficiency), natalizumab (blocks T-cell extravasation), cytotoxics. Infections (think HIV): bacteria (Mycoplasma, TB, Salmonella, Listeria); viruses (herpesviruses — VZV, HSV, CMV, HHV8, EBV; HPV); fungi (Candida, Pneumocystis jirovecii/PCP, Histoplasma); protozoa (Cryptosporidium, Toxoplasma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD): defect, organisms, presentation, and diagnosis.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: X-linked; loss of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst → can't kill catalase-positive organisms (esp. Staph aureus, Aspergillus); presents before age 5 with osteomyelitis, abscesses, sepsis. Diagnosis: NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test fails to turn blue, or DHR flow cytometry.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chédiak-Higashi and Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency: defects and features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chédiak-Higashi: lysosomal defect → dysfunctional phagocytosis + NK/CD8 → partial albinism + peripheral neuropathy + pancytopenia. Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency: CD18 mutation → impaired phagocyte migration → delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent bacterial infections without pus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complement deficits: what results from a terminal (C5–C9/MAC) defect and from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Terminal (C5–C9/MAC): recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal/gonococcal) — MAC is the only thing that kills Neisseria. C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency: hereditary angioedema (recurrent non-itchy angioedema, no urticaria; C4 low).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complement deficits: what results from early complement (C1/C2/C4) deficiency and C3 deficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Early complement (C1/C2/C4): SLE-like autoimmunity + encapsulated bacteria. C3 deficiency: severe recurrent bacterial infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency): defect, causes, presentation, and management.
