conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Failure of both B and T cells — the 'bubble baby'. Causes: X-linked common gamma chain mutation (commonest), adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Presents in infancy — FTT, persistent diarrhoea, chronic candidiasis, severe infections, disseminated infection from live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus). A paediatric emergency → stem cell transplant; avoid live vaccines (now on newborn screening).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Ataxia Telangiectasia: inheritance, gene, mnemonic, and features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Autosomal recessive, ATM gene; mnemonic 'AAA' — Ataxia + Angiomas (telangiectasia) + Antibodies low (IgG/A/E); lymphopenia; increased leukaemia/lymphoma; high radiation sensitivity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: inheritance, mnemonic, and features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: X-linked; 'WATER' — Wiskott (thrombocytopenia) + Atopy (eczema) + T-cell dysfunction + Elevated IgE/A + Recurrent pyogenic infections (IgM/G low). Eczema + thrombocytopenia + infections in a male = WAS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Hyper-IgM Syndrome: defect and consequences.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: CD40L mutation → no class switching → IgM only (absent IgG/A/E); susceptible to PCP and Cryptosporidium.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job's): features and mnemonic.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Raised IgE + eosinophilia → atopy, weak bones (pathological fractures), cold Staph abscesses (no inflammatory signs). Mnemonic FATED — coarse Facies, cold Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, raised IgE, Dermatological/eczema.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Asplenia/hyposplenism: what does the spleen clear, what are the causes, and what is the key risk?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The spleen clears encapsulated organisms → asplenia (post-splenectomy, sickle cell autosplenectomy, coeliac) → risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Asplenia/hyposplenism: blood film clue and management.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Blood film clue: Howell-Jolly bodies. Management: vaccination (pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY + MenB, annual influenza), lifelong prophylactic penicillin, patient alert card + education, prompt treatment of febrile illness.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When should immunodeficiency be suspected (the 'SPUR' mnemonic plus extras)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: SPUR: Severe, Persistent, Unusual (opportunistic organisms/sites), Recurrent; plus failure to thrive, family history, and infection from live vaccines.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which tests assess humoral immunity in an immunodeficiency workup?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Immunoglobulins (IgG/A/M) + electrophoresis assess humoral immunity; specific antibody responses to vaccines assess humoral function.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which tests assess T-cell/combined, complement, and phagocyte function?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lymphocyte subsets (CD4/CD8/B/NK) → T-cell/combined; complement (CH50, C3, C4) → complement; neutrophil function (NBT/DHR) → phagocyte (CGD).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the management principles for immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Prompt treatment + prophylactic antibiotics; immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG) for antibody deficiencies; vaccination (but avoid live vaccines in T-cell/combined defects); stem cell transplant (SCID); specialist immunology referral.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do hypersensitivity and autoimmunity both represent the immune system attacking the wrong target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hypersensitivity = an excessive/inappropriate immune response; autoimmunity = loss of self-tolerance so the immune system attacks the host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the examinable classification for hypersensitivity, and how many types does this course use?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The Gell & Coombs classification — this course uses a five-type version (Types I–IV + Type V for receptor antibodies).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type I hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Immediate/allergic. Mechanism: IgE cross-links → mast cell/basophil degranulation → histamine/leukotriene. Examples: anaphylaxis, atopy, asthma, allergic rhinitis, urticaria, angioedema.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type II hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibody-mediated (cytotoxic). Mechanism: IgG/IgM vs cell-surface/matrix antigen → destruction. Examples: AIHA, Goodpasture's (collagen IV), pemphigus (desmosomes), pemphigoid (hemidesmosomes).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type III hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Immune complex. Mechanism: antigen-antibody complexes deposit → inflammation. Examples: SLE, post-strep GN, serum sickness, extrinsic allergic alveolitis, membranous nephropathy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type IV hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Delayed (cell-mediated). Mechanism: T-cells (no antibody) + granuloma formation. Examples: contact dermatitis, coeliac, MS, sarcoidosis, Crohn's, TB/Mantoux.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type V hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Receptor stimulation (a subset of II). Mechanism: antibody stimulates/blocks a receptor. Examples: Graves' (TSH receptor), myasthenia gravis (ACh receptor).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the ABCD(E) mnemonic for hypersensitivity, and the core split?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ABCD(E): Allergic (I), antibody/B cytotoxic (II), immune Complex (III), Delayed (IV), receptor (V). Core split: I–III + V = antibody-mediated; IV = T-cell-mediated/delayed (no antibody).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: This course's classification choices: which type are Graves'/MG, coeliac/Crohn's/MS/sarcoid, and post-strep GN?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Graves'/MG = Type V (not lumped into II); coeliac/Crohn's/MS/sarcoid = Type IV; post-strep GN = Type III.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism of Type I reactions in depth, and its examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IgE cross-linking → mast cell/basophil degranulation → histamine + leukotriene release (also via complement C3/4/5a, substance P, axon reflex). Examples: allergy (aspirin sensitivity, allergic rhinitis, atopy), anaphylaxis, angioedema, asthma, urticaria.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Distinguish anaphylaxis from anaphylactoid reactions, and how does treatment differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anaphylaxis = IgE-mediated mast cell cross-linking; anaphylactoid = non-IgE degranulation — the treatment is the same.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does anaphylaxis present, and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Presentation: angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm/wheeze, urticaria (the ABC + skin picture). Diagnosis: clinical + mast cell tryptase (serial levels confirm retrospectively).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of anaphylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IM adrenaline 500 mcg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) — the key intervention, repeat every 5 min as needed; high-flow oxygen + IV fluids; adjuncts IV hydrocortisone 200 mg + chlorphenamine 10 mg (newer Resus Council guidance de-emphasises routine steroids/antihistamines acutely). Refractory → ICU; on discharge: observe + adrenaline auto-injector + allergy referral.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is angioedema, what deficiency can cause it, and how is it treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Subcutaneous/submucosal swelling ± urticaria; can be C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency (hereditary or acquired — autoimmune, haematological cancers, HepB/C). Acute (allergic) → treat as anaphylaxis; C1-INH-related → icatibant (bradykinin inhibitor); prevention → danazol, tranexamic acid, C1-esterase inhibitor.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is urticaria managed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Red, itchy dermal rash; non-sedating antihistamines first-line; add montelukast; omalizumab (anti-IgE) if persistent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the core defect in autoimmunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Loss of self-tolerance (central thymic deletion + peripheral tolerance failing) → immune attack on self.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the contributors to autoimmunity (genetic, infection, cancer, and demographic)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetic — strong HLA associations; non-HLA (CTLA4, IL-6R in RA; NOD2 in Crohn's). Infection (molecular mimicry) — AIHA (mycoplasma, syphilis), reactive arthritis (chlamydia), membranous nephropathy (HepB/C). Cancer (paraneoplastic) — MG ↔ thymoma, Lambert-Eaton ↔ small cell lung cancer, dermatomyositis; lymphoma → AIHA/ITP/pemphigus. Female preponderance (most systemic autoimmunity).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising fork for autoimmune diseases (organ-specific vs systemic)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Organ-specific (Hashimoto's, T1DM, MG, Graves') vs systemic/multisystem (SLE, RA, systemic sclerosis, vasculitis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autoantibodies by function: what are receptor antibodies (Type V) and their diseases?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Receptor antibodies (Type V): Graves' (anti-TSH receptor), MG (anti-ACh receptor), Lambert-Eaton (anti-VGCC).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autoantibodies by function: what are destructive antibodies and 'marker' antibodies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Destructive antibodies: AIHA, ITP (also CLL/SLE), SLE, Goodpasture's, pemphigus/pemphigoid. 'Marker' antibodies (less directly pathogenic): pernicious anaemia, PBC, PSC, autoimmune hepatitis; ANCA vasculitis — GPA (cANCA), microscopic polyangiitis & eGPA (pANCA). Note: polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is characteristically ANCA-NEGATIVE.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibodies are associated with SLE (screening and specific)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ANA — SLE (screening), other connective tissue disease. Anti-dsDNA / anti-Smith — SLE (specific).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-CCP/rheumatoid factor, anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin, and anti-TSH receptor?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anti-CCP / rheumatoid factor — rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-TPO / anti-thyroglobulin — Hashimoto's (+ Graves'). Anti-TSH receptor — Graves'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-ACh receptor and anti-GBM (collagen IV)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anti-ACh receptor — myasthenia gravis. Anti-GBM (collagen IV) — Goodpasture's.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with cANCA (anti-PR3) and pANCA (anti-MPO)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: cANCA (anti-PR3) — GPA (Wegener's). pANCA (anti-MPO) — microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic GPA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-TTG/anti-endomysial, anti-mitochondrial (AMA), and anti-smooth muscle?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anti-TTG / anti-endomysial — coeliac. Anti-mitochondrial (AMA) — PBC. Anti-smooth muscle — autoimmune hepatitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anti-centromere / anti-Scl-70 — limited / diffuse systemic sclerosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: HLA associations: what diseases are linked to HLA-B27 and HLA-DR3?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: B27 — ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, seronegative arthritis, IBD-associated. DR3 — T1DM, Hashimoto's, Graves', myasthenia gravis, SLE.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: HLA associations: what diseases are linked to HLA-DR4 and HLA-DQ2/DQ8?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: DR4 — T1DM, rheumatoid arthritis. DQ2/DQ8 — coeliac disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: HLA associations: what diseases are linked to HLA-Cw6 and HLA-DQ6?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cw6 — psoriasis. DQ6 — multiple sclerosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: which paraneoplastic autoimmune associations should you know?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: MG ↔ thymoma; Lambert-Eaton ↔ small cell lung cancer.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mandatory first step in every febrile traveller from an endemic area?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Malaria must be excluded in EVERY febrile traveller from an endemic area — it's the one that kills fast.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three questions that drive the differential in a febrile returning traveller?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: WHERE did they travel (geography → which diseases are endemic); WHEN (incubation period); WHAT exposures (water, food, sexual, insect bites, animals, healthcare).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exposure mapping: what should a mosquito bite and fresh water make you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mosquito bite → malaria, dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever. Fresh water → schistosomiasis, leptospirosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exposure mapping: what do unpasteurised dairy/animals and contaminated food/water suggest?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Unpasteurised dairy / animals → brucellosis. Contaminated food/water → typhoid, hepatitis A/E, travellers' diarrhoea.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exposure mapping: what do a tick bite, sexual contact, and caves/birds/farms suggest?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tick bite → Rickettsia, Lyme. Sexual contact → HIV, hepatitis B, gonorrhoea. Caves/birds/farms → histoplasmosis, Q fever, avian flu.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Geography: what diseases should Sub-Saharan Africa and South/SE Asia make you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sub-Saharan Africa → malaria (falciparum), HIV, schistosomiasis, rickettsia. South / SE Asia → typhoid, dengue, malaria (vivax), hepatitis A/E.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Geography: what diseases should South America and the Middle East make you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: South America → dengue, yellow fever, leptospirosis. Middle East → brucellosis, MERS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which traveller fevers are notifiable?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many traveller fevers are notifiable — malaria, typhoid, VHF, measles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the critical 'stop and isolate' step for VHF risk assessment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever + travel to a VHF area (e.g. Ebola, Lassa) within 21 days → isolate + urgent specialist/public-health involvement BEFORE routine bloods.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever >38.3°C on ≥3 occasions over ≥3 weeks, not diagnosed after 1 week of investigation (hospital) or 3 outpatient visits.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the categories of PUO causes and their approximate proportions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infective (30–40%): TB, endocarditis, abscess, EBV, CMV, HIV, typhoid. Malignant (20–30%): HCC, RCC, lymphoma, leukaemia. Inflammatory (20%): SLE, RA, Still's disease, temporal arteritis. Drug-induced: antibiotics (esp. beta-lactams), NSAIDs, antihypertensives, antihistamines. Undiagnosed (10–15%).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the investigation approach to PUO.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: History (travel, sexual contacts, animal exposure, occupation, medications); blood cultures (×3, different sites) + thick/thin blood films; FBC, CRP, LFTs, U&E, LDH, ferritin; serology (HIV, EBV, CMV, hepatitis, syphilis, Brucella, Leishmania); CXR, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; echocardiogram (endocarditis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Incubation <1 week: which diseases should you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningococcus, diphtheria, influenza, scarlet fever, dengue (4–7 days).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Incubation 1–2 weeks: which diseases should you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Malaria, dengue, typhoid, measles, rickettsia, leptospirosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Incubation 2–3 weeks and >3 weeks: which diseases should you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 2–3 weeks: mumps, rubella, chickenpox, brucellosis (5–30 days). >3 weeks: infectious mononucleosis, CMV, viral hepatitis, HIV seroconversion, TB, rabies (weeks–months, can be very long).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Malaria: which species is most common and severe, the vector, and typical symptoms?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Plasmodium falciparum is most common and severe; the vector is the Anopheles mosquito. Symptoms: fever + sweating + headache + vomiting + pallor + jaundice + hepatosplenomegaly.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Malaria: investigations and treatment for severe and uncomplicated disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Investigation: thick/thin blood films (×3). Severe malaria: IV artesunate (1st line) or IV quinine + doxycycline. Uncomplicated: artemether/lumefantrine.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Malaria: how do vivax/ovale differ from falciparum regarding relapse, and how is this managed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vivax/ovale have dormant liver hypnozoites → relapse → add primaquine (check G6PD first); falciparum has no hypnozoite stage (no relapse).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Dengue fever: vector, classic triad, symptom range, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aedes mosquito, tropical infection. Classic triad: fever + rash + bone pain ('breakbone fever'). Symptom range from fever/rash to haemorrhagic fever/shock (DHF/DSS). Treatment: supportive (careful with NSAIDs in dengue — bleeding risk); no antivirals.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chikungunya: vector, incubation, defining feature, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aedes mosquito; incubation 1–12 days. Defining feature: severe polyarthralgia (can persist months). Fever + rash. Treatment: supportive (NSAIDs, physiotherapy).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Rickettsia (African tick typhus): features, hallmark sign, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Non-specific: fever + headache + rash (petechial/maculopapular) + myalgia. Hallmark: black eschar at the bite site. Treatment: doxycycline (azithromycin if pregnant).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid): organism, symptoms, investigation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Salmonella typhi/paratyphi, after South/SE Asia travel. Symptoms: fever, headache, relative bradycardia, constipation then diarrhoea, dry cough, rose spots on the abdomen. Investigation: blood cultures (positive in week 1). Treatment: ceftriaxone (IV) or azithromycin (oral) first-line — fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) resistance is now high (including XDR strains), so cipro only for confirmed-sensitive isolates. Vaccine not 100% effective.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Schistosomiasis: source, features, malignancy association, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tropical parasitic flukes from fresh water. Eosinophilia + swimmer's itch. Katayama fever (acute); chronic: hepatic fibrosis, bladder cancer (squamous cell). Urine/stool microscopy shows eggs (if <2 months: serology). Treatment: praziquantel (repeat in 2 months — only kills adults).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease): exposure, phases, features of severe disease, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fresh water exposure. Biphasic illness: initial septicaemic phase (fever, headache, myalgia) then immune phase. Severe (Weil's): jaundice + conjunctival suffusion + renal failure + haemorrhage. Treatment: doxycycline/amoxicillin (mild) or IV penicillin (severe).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Brucellosis: setting, incubation, features, investigation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: High prevalence in farming/animal-human contact areas or eating unpasteurised food. Incubation 5–30 days. Fever + weight loss + night sweats + lymphadenopathy. Important cause of PUO. Investigation: blood cultures (gold standard) + serology. Treatment: doxycycline + rifampicin or gentamicin (6 weeks total).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Amoebic liver abscess: organism, route, features, investigation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Entamoeba histolytica (faeco-oral). Single mass usually in the right lobe — 'anchovy sauce' contents. Fever + RUQ pain + hepatomegaly. Amoebic dysentery: profuse bloody diarrhoea. Investigation: USS + serology (95% positive). Treatment: oral metronidazole + diloxanide furoate (luminal agent to clear the gut).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Tetanus: setting, risk factors, progression, diagnosis, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mostly developing world (no vaccine). Risk factors: wounds contaminated with soil, manure, rusty metals. Prodromal malaise + fever → trismus (lockjaw) + muscle spasms + abdominal rigidity + dysphagia → respiratory failure + aspiration pneumonia. Diagnosis: clinical. Treatment: ITU admission + tetanus IG + wound debridement + supportive care.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Viral haemorrhagic fever (Ebola, Lassa, Marburg): features, incubation, and the isolation imperative.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever + bleeding + organ failure after travel to West/Central Africa (incubation up to 21 days). The isolation imperative: isolate + urgent specialist/public-health involvement BEFORE routine bloods — don't delay. Notifiable. (Yellow fever is a related mosquito-borne VHF — vaccine-preventable.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which infections cause chronic disease via HPV, EBV, and HTLV-1?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HPV (16, 18) → cervical + anal + oropharyngeal cancer; HPV (6, 11) → genital warts. EBV → nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt's lymphoma (Africa), Hodgkin's lymphoma. HTLV-1 → adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which infections cause chronic disease via H. pylori, schistosomiasis, and hepatitis B + C?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: H. pylori → gastric cancer + MALT lymphoma. Schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Hepatitis B + C → hepatocellular carcinoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what are the severe features of malaria, and how quickly can falciparum be fatal?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Always suspect malaria in any febrile returning traveller. Falciparum can be fatal within 24–48 hours; do not wait for the thick blood film — treat empirically if suspicious. Severe features: cerebral malaria, respiratory failure, hypoglycaemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what are the distinctive analgesia and features points for dengue and typhoid?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Dengue: NSAIDs are traditionally avoided due to bleeding risk in haemorrhagic dengue — paracetamol is the preferred analgesia. Typhoid: rose spots on the abdomen in week 2 + relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation); blood cultures most sensitive in week 1, stool/urine cultures in weeks 2–3.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what clinical clues point to schistosomiasis and leptospirosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Schistosomiasis: eosinophilia + travel to Africa/Middle East/SE Asia + water exposure; Katayama fever at 4–8 weeks post-exposure. Leptospirosis: distinctive features are conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without discharge) + jaundice + renal failure; associated with water sports/occupational exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the orienting framework for grouping antibiotic classes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Every class is grouped by where it acts; the mechanism and the side-effect/resistance logic follows from that.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotic classes act on cell wall synthesis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems (β-lactams); and glycopeptides (vancomycin — a non-β-lactam).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics inhibit protein synthesis at the 30S ribosome, and what mnemonic helps?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines — remember 'buy AT 30' (A = aminoglycosides, T = tetracyclines at 30S).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics inhibit protein synthesis at the 50S ribosome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Macrolides, lincosamides (clindamycin), chloramphenicol, and linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics act on DNA gyrase/topoisomerase, RNA polymerase, and nucleic acid/DNA damage?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: DNA gyrase/topoisomerase — fluoroquinolones. RNA polymerase — rifampicin. Nucleic acid/DNA damage — metronidazole, nitrofurantoin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics act on folate synthesis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole (sequential blockade), and sulfonamides.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics are bactericidal versus bacteriostatic, and when is bactericidal preferred?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cidal: β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole. Static: macrolides, tetracyclines, clindamycin, trimethoprim. Prefer bactericidal in serious infection / immunocompromise / endocarditis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How are Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria distinguished structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer lipid membrane. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan + outer lipid membrane.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of Gram-positive organisms by morphology.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cocci: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Enterococcus. Rods: Corynebacterium, Mycobacteria, Listeria, Bacillus, Nocardia. Anaerobes: Clostridium, Lactobacillus, Actinomyces, Propionibacterium.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of Gram-negative and atypical organisms.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Gram-negative: Neisseria (meningitidis, gonorrhoeae), H. influenzae, E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Moraxella catarrhalis. Atypicals (no cell wall): Legionella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Coxiella burnetii.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is MRSA, by what mechanism is it resistant, and what are the treatment options?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staph aureus resistant to beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a). Treatment: doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do penicillins (beta-lactams) work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit cell wall synthesis (block transpeptidation). Examples include amoxicillin. Side effects: allergy, drug-induced liver injury (also amoxicillin), hypernatraemia (piperacillin); amoxicillin + EBV = rash.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do glycopeptides (vancomycin) work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by a non-beta-lactam mechanism — binding D-Ala-D-Ala. Side effects: nephrotoxicity, red man syndrome (vancomycin — slow the infusion to prevent), and ototoxicity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do aminoglycosides work, and what are their key cautions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit protein synthesis (30S ribosome); e.g. gentamicin. Cautions: contraindicated in myasthenia gravis (blocks NMJ); dose by ideal body weight in obese patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do tetracyclines work, what are their key side effects, and what are they used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit protein synthesis (30S ribosome); e.g. doxycycline. Side effects: photosensitivity, teeth discolouration (avoid in children <8 and pregnancy). Used for atypicals, Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Lyme disease, brucellosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do macrolides work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit protein synthesis (50S ribosome — block translocation); e.g. clarithromycin, erythromycin. Side effects: QTc prolongation, P450 inhibitor (↑ statin levels → myopathy/rhabdomyolysis), cholestatic jaundice, tinnitus, GI upset. Do NOT use with statins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do lincosamides (clindamycin) work, what is their main risk, and what are they used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit protein synthesis (50S ribosome). Main risk: C. diff infection (highest risk). Used for anaerobic infections, dental abscesses, and bone/joint infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do fluoroquinolones work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II); oral, with excellent bioavailability; e.g. ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin. Side effects: C. diff risk, tendonitis/Achilles rupture, lowers seizure threshold, dizziness, photosensitivity, prolongs QTc. Avoid in epilepsy and pregnancy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do folate antagonists (trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole) work, and what are they used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit folate synthesis (sequential blockade). Nitrofurantoin is now first-line for uncomplicated lower UTI (NICE NG109); trimethoprim is a second choice only where local resistance is known to be low. Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole) = PCP treatment/prophylaxis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key side effects of trimethoprim and of sulfonamides?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist → teratogenic (1st trimester) + hyperkalaemia + raised creatinine. Sulfonamides → Stevens-Johnson, and haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does metronidazole work, what does it cover, and what is its classic side effect?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bactericidal vs anaerobes + protozoa (C. diff, Giardia, bacterial vaginosis, abscesses) — causes DNA damage. Classic side effect: disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; also peripheral neuropathy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is nitrofurantoin used, and what are its key cautions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Concentrated in urine → for uncomplicated UTI only. Avoid at term (neonatal haemolysis) and in significant renal impairment (needs renal function to concentrate in urine).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the penicillin allergy cross-reactivity, and what is the rule for true anaphylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: About 10% cross-reactivity with cephalosporins and about 1% with carbapenems. True anaphylaxis to penicillin → avoid ALL β-lactams; use a non-β-lactam.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: First-line antibiotic(s) for MRSA and for Pseudomonas.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: MRSA: vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid, doxycycline. Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, meropenem, gentamicin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: First-line antibiotic(s) for anaerobes, atypicals, ESBL, and C. diff.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anaerobes: metronidazole, co-amoxiclav, clindamycin. Atypicals (Legionella/Mycoplasma/Chlamydia): macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (no cell wall → β-lactams useless). ESBL: meropenem (carbapenem). C. diff: oral vancomycin / fidaxomicin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the atypicals reasoning step for antibiotic choice?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) have no cell wall, so cell-wall agents (β-lactams) don't work → reach for protein-synthesis (macrolides/tetracyclines) or DNA-targeting (quinolones) drugs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Resistance mechanism — altered target: what does it involve, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A mutation in the target site: RNA polymerase (rifampicin), DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin), 30S ribosome (streptomycin); and altered PBP in MRSA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Resistance mechanism — enzymatic inactivation: what does it involve, and how is it overcome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Beta-lactamase destroys the beta-lactam ring (penicillinase, ESBLs); aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes also occur. Overcome with combinations such as co-amoxiclav = amoxicillin + clavulanate (a beta-lactamase inhibitor).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Resistance mechanisms — efflux pumps and alternative target/reduced permeability: describe each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Efflux pumps: active transport pumps antibiotic out of the cell (affects tetracyclines, quinolones, beta-lactams, macrolides; common in Pseudomonas). Alternative target/reduced permeability: using an alternative metabolic pathway (vancomycin resistance: D-Ala-D-Lac), reduced outer membrane porins (Pseudomonas), and biofilm formation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: On what shared principle do all antifungals act, and why?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They all act on fungal cell wall/membrane synthesis, because fungi have ergosterol (not cholesterol).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Azoles: mechanism, key interaction issue, and drugs of choice for Candida and Aspergillus.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit ergosterol synthesis (lanosterol 14α-demethylase); they are P450 inhibitors → many drug interactions. Fluconazole for Candida; voriconazole for Aspergillus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin): mechanism, key toxicity, and role.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bind ergosterol → pore formation → membrane leak → cell death. Amphotericin B is highly nephrotoxic with electrolyte imbalances; reserve for life-threatening infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Echinocandins (micafungin, caspofungin): mechanism, use, and toxicity compared to amphotericin.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit beta-glucan synthesis → cell wall formation. Good for invasive Candida/Aspergillus; less toxic than amphotericin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what is the C. diff risk hierarchy, and the current first-line treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: C. diff risk hierarchy: clindamycin > cephalosporins > fluoroquinolones > broad-spectrum penicillins. First-line treatment is now oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin (NICE — fidaxomicin increasingly first-line); metronidazole is no longer first-line; oral, not IV — it must reach the bowel lumen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what monitoring and cautions apply to gentamicin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Peak and trough levels are needed; ototoxicity is irreversible — stop if hearing changes. Check levels after 3 doses (or daily in CKD). Do not use in myasthenia gravis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what is the fluconazole + warfarin interaction?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fluconazole causes CYP450 inhibition → ↑warfarin levels → bleeding risk. Always check P450 interactions with azoles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: how are ESBL-producing organisms and increasing CRE treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ESBL-producing organisms (Klebsiella, E. coli) are resistant to all penicillins and cephalosporins → treat with meropenem (carbapenem). For increasing CRE, use colistin as a last resort.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the cell membrane described as a selective barrier, and what does this control create?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It controls what enters and leaves the cell, and this control creates the ion gradients that underlie the resting membrane potential (the electrical charge across the membrane) essential for all excitable tissue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of the cell membrane's transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The membrane is selectively permeable, using different transport mechanisms for different substances; the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase sets up ion gradients that (with the membrane's K⁺ permeability) create the resting membrane potential — the foundation for nerve, muscle, and cardiac action potentials.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the basic structure of the cell membrane.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A phospholipid bilayer (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in) with embedded proteins (channels, transporters, receptors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the permeability principle of the lipid bilayer — what crosses freely and what is blocked?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The lipid bilayer lets small, lipid-soluble (non-polar) molecules cross freely (O₂, CO₂, steroids, lipid-soluble drugs), but blocks large or charged/polar molecules (ions, glucose) → these need transport proteins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the consequence of the membrane's selective permeability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It allows the cell to maintain a different internal environment from the outside, including the ion gradients that create the membrane potential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Simple diffusion: is it passive or active, which direction does it move, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Passive (no ATP); moves down the gradient; examples are O₂, CO₂, and lipid-soluble molecules crossing the bilayer directly.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Facilitated diffusion: is it passive or active, which direction, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Passive; moves down the gradient; examples are glucose (GLUT) and ions through channels — via a protein.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Osmosis: is it passive or active, which direction does water move, and via what?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Passive; water moves down its osmotic gradient; via aquaporins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Primary active transport: what energy source does it use, which direction, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active — uses ATP directly; moves against the gradient; examples are Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, Ca²⁺ ATPase, and the proton pump.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Secondary active transport: what energy source does it use, which direction, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active — uses an ion gradient rather than ATP directly; moves against the gradient; examples are glucose-Na⁺ cotransport (SGLT) and Na⁺/H⁺ exchange.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise the passive-vs-active transport distinction.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Passive = down the gradient, no energy (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis). Active = against the gradient, needs energy (directly as ATP, or borrowed from an ion gradient).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield mechanism of secondary active transport with an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It doesn't use ATP directly — it uses the energy stored in an ion gradient (usually the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) to move something else against its gradient, e.g. SGLT (glucose rides in on the Na⁺ gradient).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump per ATP, and what gradients does this maintain?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It pumps 3 Na⁺ OUT and 2 K⁺ IN per ATP (against their gradients), maintaining high Na⁺ outside and high K⁺ inside — the fundamental cellular ion gradients. It is found in every cell.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three main 'payoffs' of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1) It sets up the gradients for the resting membrane potential and all action potentials; 2) it powers secondary active transport (the Na⁺ gradient drives glucose/amino acid uptake); 3) it's electrogenic (3 out, 2 in → net loss of positive charge → contributes slightly to the negative resting potential).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase described as electrogenic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It pumps 3 positive ions out for every 2 in, causing a net loss of positive charge, which contributes slightly to the negative resting potential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the clinical link between digoxin and the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase in cardiac muscle → ↑intracellular Na⁺ → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange) → ↑contractility (positive inotrope).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: At rest, what is the inside of the cell relative to the outside, and what are the typical values?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The inside is negative relative to the outside — about −70 mV in neurons and about −90 mV in cardiac/skeletal muscle.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What three factors contribute to the resting membrane potential and how?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1) Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase — sets up the ion gradients (high K⁺ in, high Na⁺ out); 2) K⁺ leak channels — the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest, so K⁺ leaks out down its gradient, leaving the inside negative; 3) large intracellular anions — proteins/phosphates (negative, can't leave) add to the negativity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the resting potential set mainly by potassium?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest, the resting potential sits close to the K⁺ equilibrium potential (about −90 mV). K⁺ leaking out is what makes the inside negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an equilibrium potential, and what gives it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Each ion has an equilibrium potential — the voltage at which its electrical and chemical gradients balance. The Nernst equation gives it; the resting potential is a weighted average dominated by the most permeable ion (K⁺).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is the resting potential the starting point for an action potential?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A stimulus depolarises the membrane toward threshold → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → the action potential fires.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield electrolyte link: how does hyperkalaemia affect the resting membrane potential and excitability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hyperkalaemia (↑extracellular K⁺) → ↓the K⁺ gradient → depolarises the resting potential → initially more excitable, then (sustained) inactivates Na⁺ channels → inexcitable → cardiac arrest.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does hypokalaemia affect the membrane, and what is the risk?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hypokalaemia hyperpolarises the membrane → arrhythmia risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why are potassium disorders considered cardiac emergencies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because they directly alter the resting membrane potential of excitable tissue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do SGLT2 inhibitors and local anaesthetics act, in terms of membrane transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: SGLT2 inhibitors block Na⁺-glucose cotransport (secondary active transport) in the kidney. Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → no action potential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do oral rehydration therapy and diuretics relate to membrane transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Oral rehydration therapy: glucose-Na⁺ cotransport (SGLT) drives water absorption. Diuretics: act on tubular transporters (NKCC2, NCC, ENaC).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cerebral/cellular oedema relate to membrane transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It results from osmotic water movement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do cells communicate, and what is the basis of coordinated body function?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cells communicate via chemical signals (hormones, neurotransmitters, local mediators) that bind receptors and trigger a response — the basis of coordinated body function.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of cell signalling?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Signalling depends on where the receptor is, which is determined by whether the signal molecule is water-soluble (can't cross the membrane → surface receptors) or lipid-soluble (crosses the membrane → intracellular receptors). The receptor type then determines the speed and mechanism of the response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify the four types of chemical signalling by distance, with where the signal travels and an example of each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Endocrine — via the blood to distant targets (hormones: insulin, thyroid, cortisol). Paracrine — to nearby cells by local diffusion (local mediators: histamine, prostaglandins). Autocrine — back to the same cell (growth factors, some immune signals). Neuronal/synaptic — across a synapse (neurotransmitters).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What common principle unites endocrine and neuronal signalling, and how do they mainly differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The same principle (signal → receptor → response) operates whether the signal travels body-wide (endocrine) or just across a synapse (neuronal) — they differ mainly in distance and speed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Water-soluble signals: give examples, state whether they cross the membrane, and where their receptors are.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Examples: peptide hormones (insulin, ADH, most), catecholamines, neurotransmitters. They cannot cross the membrane (polar). Their receptors are at the cell surface (membrane receptors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Lipid-soluble signals: give examples, state whether they cross the membrane, and where their receptors are.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Examples: steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids), thyroid hormone, vitamin D. They can cross the membrane (lipophilic). Their receptors are intracellular (cytoplasm/nucleus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare the mechanism, speed, and duration of water-soluble versus lipid-soluble signals.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water-soluble: act via second messengers; fast (seconds–minutes); short duration. Lipid-soluble: directly alter gene transcription; slow (hours — needs new protein synthesis); long duration.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the whole cell-signalling framework in one linked sentence.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water-soluble → surface receptor → second messenger → fast, short; lipid-soluble → intracellular receptor → gene transcription → slow, long. This single divide explains why adrenaline acts in seconds but cortisol/thyroid hormone take hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the transport corollary for lipid-soluble hormones in the blood?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid) are carried bound to plasma proteins in the blood (they're not water-soluble), and only the free fraction is active (e.g. free T4).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must water-soluble signals use surface receptors and second messengers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water-soluble signals can't enter the cell, so they bind surface receptors that relay the signal inward via second messengers.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): what is their mechanism and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They activate a G-protein → second messengers (cAMP, IP₃/Ca²⁺). Examples: adrenergic, muscarinic, and many hormones — the biggest drug-target family.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Receptor tyrosine kinases: what is their mechanism and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The receptor has enzyme activity → a phosphorylation cascade. Examples: insulin, growth factors.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Ligand-gated ion channels: what is their mechanism and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The receptor is an ion channel → it opens on binding. Examples: nicotinic ACh (NMJ), GABA-A.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the major second messengers and their sources.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: cAMP (from GPCRs via adenylyl cyclase) — the classic; IP₃ + DAG → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ (another major pathway); Ca²⁺ itself (a key intracellular signal).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield amplification point of second-messenger signalling.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: One hormone molecule → activates many G-proteins → each makes many cAMP → each activates many enzymes → a cascade that massively amplifies a tiny signal (which is why hormones work at nanomolar concentrations).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do lipid-soluble signals act via the slow (intracellular) pathway?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lipid-soluble signals (steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D) cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors (cytoplasm/nucleus); the hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor → binds DNA → alters gene expression → new protein synthesis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the consequences of the intracellular gene-transcription pathway in terms of speed and duration?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is slow (hours–days — takes time to make new proteins) but produces lasting effects — which is why steroid effects (cortisol, aldosterone) build up over hours and persist.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the steroid pharmacology link arising from the intracellular pathway?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It explains why therapeutic steroids take time to work and why they have widespread effects (altering transcription across many tissues).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define an agonist and an antagonist in receptor pharmacology, with an example of each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Agonist — binds and activates the receptor (mimics the natural signal), e.g. salbutamol (β2 agonist). Antagonist — binds and blocks the receptor (no activation), e.g. β-blockers, antihistamines.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define a partial agonist and the competitive vs non-competitive distinction.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Partial agonist — activates, but sub-maximally, e.g. buprenorphine. Competitive vs non-competitive — reversible (surmountable) vs not — relevant to overdose/reversal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key receptor-pharmacology point about how most drugs work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most drugs work by mimicking (agonist) or blocking (antagonist) endogenous signalling → knowing the receptor and its second-messenger system predicts the effect.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does chronic overstimulation versus chronic blockade affect receptors, and what is a clinical consequence?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chronic overstimulation → downregulation/desensitisation; chronic blockade → upregulation — which is why abruptly stopping β-blockers causes rebound tachycardia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Cell signalling explanation: why are some hormones fast and others slow?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Peptide/catecholamine hormones use surface receptors → act in seconds; steroid/thyroid hormones use intracellular receptors → act over hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does insulin act at the receptor level, and what does it recruit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Insulin acts via a receptor tyrosine kinase → GLUT4, producing metabolic effects (cross-ref glucose homeostasis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cholera toxin cause disease at the signalling level?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It locks the G-protein 'on' → ↑↑cAMP → massive secretory diarrhoea (a signalling disease).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cell signalling relate to cancer?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many oncogenes are mutated signalling proteins (growth factor receptors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is body water distributed, and what drives water movement between compartments?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Body water is distributed between compartments (inside vs outside cells, and within the extracellular space); water moves between them by osmosis — driven by solute concentrations.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of body fluid compartments?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Total body water splits into intracellular and extracellular compartments, kept separate by cell membranes; water moves freely between them by osmosis (following solutes), while the solutes that can't cross determine where water goes. Sodium is the main extracellular solute (so it governs extracellular volume), and osmosis explains fluid shifts, oedema, and IV fluid behaviour.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is total body water as a fraction of body weight, and what is the '60-40-20 rule'?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Total body water is about 60% of body weight. The 60-40-20 rule: total body water ~60%, intracellular fluid (ICF) ~40%, extracellular fluid (ECF) ~20% of body weight.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What fraction of total body water is intracellular versus extracellular (the key split)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular. Of the ECF: three-quarters interstitial + one-quarter plasma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Break down the ECF: what percentage of body weight and fraction of ECF are interstitial fluid and plasma?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Interstitial (between cells) ~15% of body weight (~¾ of ECF); plasma (intravascular) ~5% of body weight (~¼ of ECF).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two barriers separating the fluid compartments, and what crosses each?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The cell membrane separates ICF from ECF (water crosses freely, solutes selectively). The capillary wall separates plasma from interstitium (water + small solutes cross, proteins mostly don't).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What determines where water goes between compartments?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water follows osmotically active solutes — but which compartment a solute is confined to determines where it pulls water.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which compartment is sodium confined to, what confines it there, and what does it govern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sodium is confined to the extracellular compartment (pumped out by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase) and governs ECF volume (it's the main extracellular osmole).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which compartments are potassium and plasma proteins (albumin) confined to, and what do they govern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Potassium is confined to the intracellular compartment and governs the ICF. Plasma proteins (albumin) are confined to plasma (can't cross the capillary) and govern plasma volume via oncotic pressure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield 'sodium = volume' point.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because sodium is the main extracellular solute, total body sodium determines ECF volume — so sodium = volume. Add sodium → hold water in the ECF → ↑volume; lose sodium → lose ECF volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the corollary distinguishing control of water balance from control of sodium?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water balance (osmolality) is controlled by ADH; sodium (volume) is controlled by aldosterone/RAAS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define osmosis in terms of solute and water concentration.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Osmosis is water moving across a semipermeable membrane from low solute (high water) → high solute (low water) concentration → water follows solute.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define osmolality and give its normal range.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Osmolality is the concentration of osmotically active particles (mainly Na⁺, glucose, urea in the ECF); normal is about 285–295 mOsm/kg.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is tonicity, and why is it the clinically useful concept?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tonicity is the effective osmolality — how a solution affects cell volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the effect on cells of an isotonic solution, and give an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: No net water movement (cells stay the same) — e.g. 0.9% saline.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the effect on cells of a hypotonic solution, and give an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water moves into cells → cells swell (can lyse) — e.g. giving too much free water.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the effect on cells of a hypertonic solution, and give an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water moves out of cells → cells shrink — e.g. hypernatraemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do changes in ECF osmolality shift water, and why is hyponatraemia dangerous?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Changes in ECF osmolality shift water in or out of cells. Hyponatraemia (low ECF osmolality) → water moves into cells → cellular swelling (dangerous in the brain → cerebral oedema); hypernatraemia → cells shrink.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an effective versus ineffective osmole, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Urea crosses membranes freely so it's an ineffective osmole (doesn't shift water); Na⁺ and glucose are effective osmoles (they do shift water) — which is why hyperglycaemia causes hyponatraemia by pulling water out of cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: IV fluids: where does 0.9% saline / Hartmann's distribute, and what is it used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 0.9% saline / Hartmann's (isotonic crystalloid) stays in the ECF (¼ intravascular, ¾ interstitial); used for volume resuscitation and replacement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: IV fluids: where does 5% dextrose distribute, and what is it used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The glucose is metabolised → leaves free water → distributes across all compartments (mostly into cells); used for free water replacement (rarely for resuscitation — little stays intravascular).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: IV fluids: where do colloids/albumin distribute, and what is their use?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They stay intravascular (large molecules); limited use for plasma volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the high-yield point comparing isotonic crystalloids and 5% dextrose for resuscitation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Isotonic crystalloids expand the ECF (good for resuscitation, though only ¼ stays intravascular); 5% dextrose gives free water (spreads everywhere, a poor volume expander — and giving too much → hyponatraemia/cellular swelling).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Fluid shifts: what happens in dehydration?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ECF volume loss → ↑osmolality (if water is lost) → water shifts out of cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Fluid shifts: what causes oedema (excess interstitial fluid)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Excess interstitial fluid from ↑hydrostatic pressure (heart failure), ↓oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia), ↑permeability (sepsis), or lymphatic block — a Starling-force imbalance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Fluid shifts: describe the water movement in hyponatraemia versus hypernatraemia.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hyponatraemia: ↓ECF osmolality → water into cells → cerebral oedema. Hypernatraemia: ↑ECF osmolality → water out of cells → cellular shrinkage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is third-spacing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fluid shifts into a non-functional compartment (e.g. bowel in obstruction, ascites).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must hyponatraemia be corrected slowly?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because ↓osmolality → cellular swelling → cerebral oedema, but correcting too fast risks osmotic demyelination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Clinically, how does hyperglycaemia cause hyponatraemia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Glucose (an effective osmole) pulls water out of cells → dilutional hyponatraemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define homeostasis.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes — the fundamental organising principle of all physiology.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of homeostasis, and what three components make up its control systems?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The body keeps regulated variables (temperature, pH, glucose, ions, blood pressure, osmolality) within narrow ranges using negative feedback control systems — a sensor, control centre, and effector. This framework makes every regulatory system an instance of the same logic, and disease is often a failure of homeostasis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which systems regulate temperature, blood glucose, and pH?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Temperature — hypothalamus (thermoregulation); blood glucose — insulin/glucagon (glucose homeostasis); pH — lungs + kidneys (acid-base).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which systems regulate ions, osmolality/water, blood pressure/volume, and O₂/CO₂?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺) — kidneys + hormones (electrolyte handling, calcium homeostasis); osmolality/water — ADH + thirst; blood pressure/volume — baroreceptors + RAAS; O₂/CO₂ — respiratory control.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a set point, and what corrects deviations from it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Each regulated variable has a set point (the target value) and a control system that corrects deviations — every regulatory system is one of these.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is negative feedback, and how does it act on the variable?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Negative feedback is where the response opposes the change, pulling the variable back toward the set point. Almost all homeostasis works this way.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the three components of a feedback loop and their roles, using temperature as the example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sensor (receptor) — detects the change (thermoreceptors); control centre — compares to the set point and coordinates the response (hypothalamus); effector — produces the corrective response (sweating/shivering, vasodilation/constriction).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the logic of a negative feedback loop step by step.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A deviation from the set point → detected → triggers a response that opposes/reverses the deviation → the variable returns toward normal → the response switches off. The response counteracts the stimulus (hence 'negative').

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give the high-yield universality point — how blood glucose and blood pressure illustrate the same negative-feedback structure.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The same structure runs every regulatory system: ↑blood glucose → (sensor: β-cells) → insulin → (effector: cells take up glucose) → glucose falls; ↑BP → (baroreceptors) → ↓sympathetic → ↓BP; ↑cortisol → suppresses CRH/ACTH — all the same negative-feedback logic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is positive feedback, and what is it used for (in contrast to negative feedback)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Positive feedback amplifies the change (the response reinforces the stimulus) → not for maintaining stability, but for driving a process rapidly to completion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the amplifying loop of the LH surge → ovulation as a positive-feedback example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Oestrogen peak → ↑LH → more oestrogen → ovulation (cross-ref menstrual cycle).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give the amplifying loops for blood clotting and labour/uterine contractions.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Blood clotting: activated factors activate more factors (the cascade). Labour/uterine contractions: contractions → ↑oxytocin → stronger contractions → delivery.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is the action potential upstroke an example of positive feedback?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Depolarisation → opens Na⁺ channels → more depolarisation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key distinction between negative and positive feedback, and which loops are the classic positive-feedback exceptions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Negative feedback = stability (the norm); positive feedback = amplification to an endpoint (the rare exceptions). The few positive-feedback loops — the LH surge, clotting, labour, and the AP upstroke — are worth knowing precisely because they're exceptions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is feedforward control, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Feedforward control is where the body anticipates a change before it happens (e.g. the cephalic phase of digestion — seeing food triggers acid/insulin release before eating; the anticipatory ↑heart rate before exercise) → it prepares in advance rather than just correcting after.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How can set points be reset, using fever as the example?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Set points can be reset: in fever, infection resets the hypothalamic temperature set point higher (via pyrogens) → the body actively defends the new higher temperature (which is why you shiver with a fever).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain 'disease as failure of homeostasis' with the examples of diabetes, hypertension, and heart failure.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many diseases are a breakdown of homeostatic control: diabetes = failure of glucose homeostasis; hypertension = dysregulated BP control; heart failure = maladaptive compensation (RAAS activation worsens congestion).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which homeostatic failures underlie acid-base disorders and fluid/electrolyte disorders?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acid-base disorders = failure of pH regulation; fluid/electrolyte disorders = failure of osmotic/volume/ion regulation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield maladaptive-compensation point using heart failure.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sometimes the homeostatic response itself becomes harmful — e.g. in heart failure, RAAS activation (a normal 'low perfusion' response) causes fluid retention that worsens the failure → a homeostatic loop turned pathological.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does drug logic relate to homeostasis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many drugs support or replace a failed homeostatic mechanism (e.g. insulin, antihypertensives).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is genetics, in terms of storage, expression, and inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetics is the molecular basis of inheritance — how information is stored (DNA), expressed (→ protein), and passed on — and how variations cause inherited disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of genetics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma); it's packaged into chromosomes and inherited in predictable patterns (dominant, recessive, X-linked); mutations disrupt this and cause disease. Recognising the inheritance pattern predicts recurrence risk and which relatives are affected.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the three steps of the central dogma (DNA to protein).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: DNA — the stored code (in the nucleus), organised into genes on chromosomes. Transcription — DNA → mRNA (in the nucleus). Translation — mRNA → protein (at the ribosome, using the genetic code — codons).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key concept linking genes, DNA sequence, and disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genes code for proteins; the sequence of DNA bases → the sequence of amino acids → the protein's structure/function → so a mutation in the DNA → an altered protein → disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How many chromosomes do humans have, and how are they arranged?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Humans have 46 (23 pairs) — 22 autosomal pairs + 1 sex pair (XX female, XY male); one of each pair comes from each parent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define gene and allele.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Gene — a segment of DNA coding for a protein. Allele — a version of a gene (one from each parent).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define genotype and phenotype.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genotype — the genetic makeup. Phenotype — the observable trait/expression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define homozygous and heterozygous.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Homozygous — two identical alleles. Heterozygous — two different alleles (a 'carrier' if recessive).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define dominant and recessive.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Dominant — expressed even with one copy. Recessive — expressed only with two copies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autosomal dominant inheritance: state the rule, examples, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rule: one copy → affected; 50% risk to offspring; affects every generation. Examples: Huntington's, familial hypercholesterolaemia, ADPKD, Marfan's, neurofibromatosis. Key features: vertical transmission; both sexes; often later-onset.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autosomal recessive inheritance: state the rule, examples, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rule: two copies needed; carriers unaffected; 25% risk if both parents are carriers. Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia, most metabolic disorders. Key features: can skip generations; consanguinity increases risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: X-linked recessive inheritance: state the rule, examples, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rule: on the X; males affected (only one X), females usually carriers. Examples: haemophilia A/B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency, red-green colour blindness. Key features: no male-to-male transmission; affects mostly males.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: X-linked dominant inheritance: state the rule and key feature.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rule: on the X, one copy is enough (rarer). Key feature: affected males → all daughters affected.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Mitochondrial inheritance: state the rule, an example, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rule: inherited only from the mother (mitochondria come from the egg). Example: mitochondrial myopathies. Key features: maternal inheritance, affects both sexes (all her children can be affected; affected fathers don't pass it on).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Pattern-recognition payoff: what are the hallmarks of autosomal dominant vs autosomal recessive inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Autosomal dominant: affects every generation (vertical), 50% risk — e.g. Huntington's. Autosomal recessive: skips generations, carriers common, 25% risk if both parents are carriers — e.g. CF, sickle cell.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Pattern-recognition payoff: what are the hallmarks of X-linked recessive and mitochondrial inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: X-linked recessive: mostly males affected, no male-to-male transmission, females carriers — e.g. haemophilia, DMD. Mitochondrial: only from the mother (all her children can be affected; affected fathers don't pass it on).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a point mutation, with a classic example?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A single-base change — e.g. sickle cell (a single base → a single amino acid change in β-globin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a frameshift mutation and its effect?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame → major disruption.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a trinucleotide repeat expansion, with examples and its characteristic feature?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Repeated sequences expand → Huntington's (CAG), fragile X, Friedreich's ataxia; the characteristic feature is anticipation (the disease worsens/appears earlier each generation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are chromosomal mutations, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Whole-chromosome abnormalities → Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner's (45,X), Klinefelter's (47,XXY).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield sickle cell point.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A single point mutation in β-globin → the disease — the classic example of how one base change → one amino acid change → an abnormal protein.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield concept of anticipation.
