conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: In trinucleotide repeat disorders (e.g. Huntington's), the repeat expands each generation → the disease appears earlier and more severe in successive generations.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define penetrance and expressivity.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Penetrance — the proportion with the genotype who show the phenotype (incomplete penetrance = not everyone with the gene is affected). Expressivity — how severely the phenotype shows (variable expressivity = different severity).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define codominance, with an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Codominance is where both alleles are expressed — e.g. ABO blood groups.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is polygenic/multifactorial inheritance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many genes + environment (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, most common diseases) — not simple Mendelian.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is pharmacogenomics, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetic variation in drug handling (e.g. fast/slow acetylators, CYP polymorphisms) — cross-ref drug biotransformation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does recognising the inheritance pattern help in genetic counselling?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The pattern predicts recurrence risk — recognising the inheritance pattern predicts which relatives are affected and the risk to offspring.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first division of immunity, and how do the two arms differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Innate (born with it, non-specific, immediate, no memory) vs adaptive (acquired, specific, slower first time but has memory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the decisive fork within the adaptive arm, and how does the whole topic hang together?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active vs passive — the whole topic hangs on a 2×2 (active/passive × natural/artificial).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the defining trade-off between active and passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active = slow onset but long-lasting (memory); passive = immediate but short-lived (no memory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the components of innate vs adaptive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Innate: granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages), NK cells, complement. Adaptive: T-cells, B-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do innate and adaptive immunity differ in response speed and recognition?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Innate: nonspecific, rapid; recognises PAMPs via TLRs. Adaptive: specific, slow first time and faster on re-exposure; uses T-cell + B-cell receptors.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which immune arm has memory, and what does this underpin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Adaptive immunity has memory (innate does not) — this is the basis of vaccination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism of active vs passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active: the host's own immune system is stimulated → makes its own antibodies + memory cells. Passive: pre-formed antibodies are given to the host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare active and passive immunity by onset, duration and memory.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active: slow onset (days-weeks), long-lasting (memory), memory = yes. Passive: immediate onset, short-lived (antibodies degrade, no memory), memory = no.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of active vs passive immunity.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active: infection, vaccination. Passive: placental IgG, breast-milk IgA, immunoglobulin injection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: In one line, when should passive immunity be used?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active is slow but durable; passive is instant but temporary — so use passive when you need protection NOW and there's no time to mount a response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the examples in the NATURAL row of the active/passive × natural/artificial 2×2?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Natural active: infection → immune response + memory. Natural passive: placental transfer (IgG) to fetus; breast milk (IgA) to neonate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the examples in the ARTIFICIAL row of the active/passive × natural/artificial 2×2?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Artificial active: vaccination. Artificial passive: immunoglobulin administration — anti-tetanus Ig, anti-rabies Ig, hepatitis B Ig, anti-D, antivenom, monoclonal antibodies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is active immunity generated, and what does it prime?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Generated by infection (natural) or vaccination (artificial); both prime B/T cells to produce antibodies + memory cells → a faster, stronger response on re-exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do live attenuated and killed/inactivated vaccines differ in the immunity they produce?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated: better cell-mediated immunity; produces IgA + IgG. Killed/inactivated: IgG only.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do live attenuated and killed/inactivated vaccines differ in dosing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated: often single dose, no adjuvant needed. Killed/inactivated: needs adjuvant + boosters.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key caveat for live attenuated vs killed/inactivated vaccines?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated: may cause mild disease; avoid in immunocompromised/pregnancy. Killed/inactivated: safe in immunocompromised.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of live attenuated vs killed/inactivated vaccines.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated: MMR, BCG, oral rotavirus, varicella. Killed/inactivated: hepatitis B, polio (IPV), pertussis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the principle of passive immunity, and what role does it serve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It gives instant protection when there's no time to wait for an active response — a bridge, not a long-term solution.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the forms of natural passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Placental IgG (the only Ig crossing the placenta → protects the neonate ~6 months) and breast-milk IgA (mucosal protection).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the clinical uses of artificial passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Post-exposure prophylaxis (tetanus Ig, rabies Ig, hepatitis B Ig, VZV Ig), anti-D (prevents rhesus sensitisation), antitoxins/antivenoms, and monoclonal antibodies (e.g. palivizumab for RSV).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the limitation of passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It wears off as antibodies degrade; no memory — so it doesn't protect against future exposures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgG?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most abundant; the only Ig that crosses the placenta; main secondary-response antibody; long-lived. Clinical relevance: natural passive immunity to the neonate; basis of therapeutic Ig; IgG = past infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgA?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Found in mucosal secretions, breast milk, gut/respiratory linings. Clinical relevance: mucosal defence; natural passive immunity via breast milk; IgA deficiency → GI/resp infections (Giardia, Cryptosporidium).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgM?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Largest (pentamer); first antibody in the primary response; can't cross the placenta. Clinical relevance: acute/recent infection marker (IgM = current infection).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgE?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Binds mast cells/basophils. Clinical relevance: type I hypersensitivity (allergy), anaphylaxis, parasites.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mostly on the naïve B-cell surface. Clinical relevance: B-cell activation; minor role.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What two anchors tie the immunoglobulin classes to the active/passive topic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IgG crosses the placenta + IgA in breast milk = the natural passive box; IgM-vs-IgG = recent-vs-past infection (ties to hepatitis serology + autoimmune liver notes).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does IgG deficiency predispose to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Encapsulated bacteria risk (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are interleukins, and which IL causes fever as an endogenous pyrogen?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Interleukins = cytokines (chemical messengers between immune cells). IL-1 is an endogenous pyrogen → fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the one thing to remember for IL-2 and IL-6?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IL-2: T-cell proliferation. IL-6: acute-phase response + fever (drives CRP).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the one thing to remember for IL-4 and IL-5?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IL-4: IgE class switch + B-cell proliferation (Th2/allergy). IL-5: IgA class switch + eosinophil growth (allergy, parasites).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the one thing to remember for IL-8 and IL-10?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IL-8: neutrophil chemotaxis. IL-10: inhibits the Th1/inflammatory response (anti-inflammatory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the grouping logic for the high-yield interleukins?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever (1, 6); recruit/activate a specific cell (2→T-cells, 5→eosinophils, 8→neutrophils); drive allergy (4, 5); switch off (10).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do Th1 and Th2 responses differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Th1 = cell-mediated (IL-12 → IFN-γ); Th2 = humoral (IL-4).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is antimicrobial stewardship (AMS)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The coordinated effort to promote and monitor the responsible use of antimicrobials to preserve their future effectiveness — a public-health and patient-safety strategy, not a clinical condition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the driving problem AMS addresses, and how significant is it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — a global threat (projected ~10 million deaths/year by 2050) driven substantially by inappropriate antibiotic use.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is 'the spine' of the AMS topic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Why AMR happens → the goals of stewardship → how it's done (Start Smart Then Focus) → resistance mechanisms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the goals of stewardship (promoting judicious antibiotic use)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Reduce inappropriate use, improve patient outcomes, increase guideline adherence, decrease resistance, and reduce healthcare costs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the conceptual heart of AMS — the balance it strikes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Safeguard the quality of care for the patient in front of you while protecting antibiotics for future patients — the individual-vs-population tension is the conceptual heart.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the drivers of antimicrobial resistance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Over-prescribing (including for viral infections), broad-spectrum use when narrow would do, inadequate dosing/duration and poor adherence, and agricultural antibiotic use / global spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the consequences of antimicrobial resistance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Untreatable infections, longer admissions, higher mortality; reliance on toxic/last-line agents; and C. difficile and MRSA emergence from broad-spectrum overuse.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the underlying principle linking antibiotic exposure to resistance, and the resulting goal?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Every antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure favouring resistant organisms — so the goal is 'the right drug, for the right bug, at the right dose, for the right duration'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'Start Smart, Then Focus' framework, and where is it from?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The two-phase model (UKHSA / NICE NG15) applied to every antibiotic prescription.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does Phase 1 — Start Smart (at initiation) involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Don't start without clinical evidence of infection (avoid treating contamination/colonisation/viral illness); take cultures before starting (especially blood cultures); follow local prescribing guidelines (reflecting local resistance patterns); document indication, drug, dose, route, and a review/stop date on the chart; consider severity, immunocompromise, resistance risk, and prior antibiotic exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does Phase 2 — Then Focus involve, and when is it done?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Review the diagnosis and continuing need at 48-72 hours, and document a clear plan — one of five outcomes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the five outcomes of the antibiotic review at 48-72 h?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Stop (no evidence of infection → cease); Switch (IV → oral when stable); Change (de-escalate to a narrower-spectrum agent, or broaden if needed, per culture results); Continue (document review date); OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the pivotal AMS action at the focus stage?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: De-escalation — empirical broad-spectrum → narrow targeted once sensitivities return.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'right' mnemonic for practical stewardship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Right drug, dose, route, duration, for the right diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What practical stewardship measures relate to route and duration of antibiotics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: IV-to-oral switch as soon as appropriate (reduces line infections, length of stay); shortest effective duration (the old 'always finish the course' dogma is dropped where evidence supports shorter courses).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What practical stewardship measures relate to spectrum and last-line agents?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Use the narrowest effective spectrum; reserve last-line agents (carbapenems, vancomycin) via restriction/approval.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What practical stewardship measures relate to cultures and biomarkers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cultures before antibiotics; use biomarkers (e.g. procalcitonin) to guide stopping where available.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who makes up an AMS team, and what organisational measures support stewardship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: AMS teams (microbiologist + antimicrobial pharmacist), local guidelines, audit/feedback, prescriber education, ward rounds.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What public/prescriber education measures support stewardship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics don't treat viral infections; delayed prescribing in primary care.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'altered target' mechanism of resistance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Altered target: RNA polymerase (rifampicin), DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin), 30S ribosome (streptomycin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'alternative target' mechanism of resistance, with its example?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Alternative target: altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'drug modification / breakdown' mechanism of resistance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Drug modification / breakdown: β-lactamases (penicillins), aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'efflux pumps' mechanism of resistance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Efflux pumps: tetracyclines, quinolones, β-lactams.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is MRSA the archetype of resistance, and how is it treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via an altered PBP → treated with doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, or linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO), and how should it be conceptualised?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Not a disease but a diagnostic problem: a prolonged fever that remains undiagnosed despite a proper initial workup. The topic is about a structured approach to a defined differential, not a single condition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is 'the spine' of the approach to PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Define it → place the patient in the right sub-type → work through the four cause-buckets → investigate in a staged, history-led way.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the decisive feature of PUO, and why does it narrow the causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The precise definition (Petersdorf & Beeson) — the '3 weeks + appropriate investigation' criterion separates true PUO from an ordinary acute fever and narrows the likely causes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the Petersdorf & Beeson criteria for PUO (temperature, duration, investigation)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Temperature: >38.3°C on several occasions. Duration: fever persisting ≥3 weeks. Investigation: no diagnosis despite appropriate workup — originally 1 week inpatient, now revised to 3 outpatient visits or 3 days of inpatient / intensive ambulatory investigation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does the '≥3 weeks + investigated' criterion matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: By definition these patients have already resisted classification on baseline investigation, so the differential is a specific (often smaller, often serious) set — most self-limiting viral fevers have resolved or declared themselves by 3 weeks.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Classic sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Patient: immunocompetent, no specific risk factors. Dominant causes: the full four-bucket differential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Healthcare-associated (nosocomial) sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Patient: inpatient, fever developing in hospital. Dominant causes: line/catheter sepsis, C. diff, drug fever, VTE/PE, sinusitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Immunocompromised / neutropenic sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Patient: chemotherapy, immunosuppression. Dominant causes: opportunistic infection (fungal — Candida/Aspergillus, bacterial) — investigate + treat urgently.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the HIV-associated sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Patient: known/suspected HIV. Dominant causes: opportunistic infections (TB, MAC, PCP, CMV), HIV itself, lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why establish the PUO sub-type first?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It reshapes the differential and the urgency — neutropenic PUO is an emergency; classic PUO is a methodical workup.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Infection bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A large group (especially in the developing world): TB (especially miliary/extrapulmonary — the classic PUO cause), occult abscess (subphrenic, pelvic, dental), infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, HIV, EBV/CMV, brucellosis, hidden empyema.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Malignancy bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lymphoma (the classic), leukaemia, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, atrial myxoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Non-infectious inflammatory bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Predominates in the developed world: adult-onset Still's disease, giant cell arteritis / PMR (especially elderly), SLE, vasculitides, IBD (can present as isolated PUO).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Miscellaneous bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Drug fever, VTE/PE, hyperthyroidism / subacute thyroiditis, factitious fever, familial Mediterranean fever, sarcoidosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the reality of PUO outcomes by geography and overall?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infection predominates in developing nations, non-infectious inflammatory disease in industrialised nations — and a large proportion (up to ~half in some series) remain undiagnosed despite full workup (many resolve spontaneously, a reassuring point).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic don't-miss trio in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: TB, lymphoma, and giant cell arteritis (GCA especially in the elderly — treatable, sight-threatening).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the highest-yield step in PUO assessment, and what should the history cover?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: History is the highest-yield step: fever pattern/duration; travel (malaria, typhoid, TB); animal/occupational exposure (brucellosis, Q fever); sexual history (HIV); drug history (drug fever); TB risk/contacts; weight loss / night sweats (B symptoms → lymphoma/TB); joint/skin/eye symptoms (connective tissue); family history (FMF); recent surgery/lines (nosocomial).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is repeated, thorough examination essential in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A meticulous, repeated examination is essential — new signs (a murmur, lymphadenopathy, a rash, temporal artery tenderness, splenomegaly) often emerge over time and provide the diagnostic lead.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Weight loss + night sweats (malignancy/TB), new murmur (endocarditis), localising signs, immunocompromise/neutropenia (urgent).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the first-line (baseline) investigations in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: FBC + film, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, blood cultures (×3 from 3 different sites, before antibiotics), urinalysis + culture, CXR, HIV test, autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA, RF), TFTs, LDH, blood film for malaria if travel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the second-line (directed) investigations in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, malignancy), echocardiography (endocarditis — TTE → TOE), viral serology (EBV, CMV, hepatitis), TB workup (sputum, IGRA, biopsy), tumour markers.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the third-line (specialist) investigations in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: PET-CT (increasingly useful for occult malignancy/inflammation/infection), biopsy (lymph node, bone marrow, temporal artery, liver), invasive imaging.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the governing principle of investigating PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Investigate logically and in a directed way — let history and examination steer the next test rather than ordering everything at once. Avoid empirical 'blind' antibiotics/steroids unless the patient is unstable, as they obscure the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the fundamental management principle of PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Treat the underlying cause once found — PUO itself isn't treated, the diagnosis is.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When should blind empirical treatment be avoided in PUO, and what are the exceptions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Avoid blind empirical treatment (antibiotics/steroids) in the stable patient — it masks the picture. Exceptions: neutropenic/immunocompromised (urgent empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics), strong suspicion of GCA (urgent steroids to prevent blindness), or clinical instability/sepsis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the appropriate approach in the stable, improving PUO patient who remains undiagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A significant proportion resolve spontaneously undiagnosed — careful follow-up rather than ever-more-invasive testing is appropriate in the stable, improving patient.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two linked jobs of travel medicine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The pre-travel consultation (risk assessment, vaccines, advice) and specifically malaria prophylaxis (the most examinable part).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the ABCD organising framework for malaria prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Awareness of risk; Bite prevention; Chemoprophylaxis; Diagnose promptly (treat any fever after travel as malaria until proven otherwise).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the single most important safety message in malaria prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: No prophylaxis is 100% effective — any fever during or after travel to an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and bite avoidance matters as much as the drugs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the risk assessment in a pre-travel consultation cover?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Destination, rural vs urban, duration, season, activities, accommodation; plus patient factors (age, pregnancy, immunosuppression, comorbidities, current meds).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What travel vaccines are considered in a pre-travel consultation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Routine boosters + destination-specific — hepatitis A, typhoid, yellow fever (certificate may be legally required for entry), rabies, Japanese encephalitis, cholera, meningococcal ACWY (e.g. Hajj).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What general advice is given in a pre-travel consultation, and what is the commonest cause of traveller death?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Food/water hygiene (travellers' diarrhoea), sun/heat, accident/road-traffic risk (the commonest cause of traveller death), STI/blood-borne risk, travel insurance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does bite avoidance (the 'B', which applies to all) involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: DEET repellent, covering skin at dawn/dusk, insecticide-treated bed nets, air conditioning.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What organism causes malaria, how is it transmitted, and which species is the deadly one?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Caused by Plasmodium (mosquito-borne, Anopheles); five species, but P. falciparum is the deadly one (cerebral malaria, the bulk of travel deaths).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which malaria species have a dormant liver stage, and why does this matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: P. vivax and P. ovale have a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites) → they can relapse months later even after correct prophylaxis (the key to understanding primaquine).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why are standard prophylactic drugs called 'suppressive', and what follows from this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Standard prophylactic drugs (chloroquine, mefloquine, doxycycline, atovaquone-proguanil) are 'suppressive' — they act on the blood stage, NOT on initial infection or liver hypnozoites. This is why they must be continued for 4 weeks after leaving (to cover parasites emerging from the liver), and why vivax/ovale can still relapse.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone): dosing, timing, side effects and notes.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Daily dosing; start 1-2 days before, 1 week after. Best tolerated overall; GI upset. Shortest post-travel course (acts on the liver stage too); expensive; good for short trips.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe doxycycline: dosing, timing, side effects and contraindications.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Daily dosing; start 1-2 days before, 4 weeks after. GI upset, pill oesophagitis, photosensitivity, Candida vaginitis. Cheapest; contraindicated in pregnancy + children <12; take with food, stay upright.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe mefloquine (Lariam): dosing, timing, side effects and contraindications.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Weekly dosing; start 2-3 weeks before, 4 weeks after. Neuropsychiatric side effects — vivid dreams, anxiety, depression, psychosis. Contraindicated in epilepsy, depression/psychiatric history; the weekly dose aids adherence; start early to detect side effects.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe chloroquine (± proguanil): dosing, timing, side effects and notes.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Weekly dosing; start 1 week before, 4 weeks after. GI upset, retinopathy (long-term). Only for chloroquine-sensitive areas (now limited).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the '4 weeks after' vs '1 week after' rule for malaria prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Only atovaquone-proguanil stops at 1 week (it hits the liver stage); the suppressive agents (doxycycline, mefloquine, chloroquine) need 4 weeks to cover emerging blood-stage parasites.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the selection logic for choosing a malaria chemoprophylaxis agent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline are first-choice for most (best tolerated); mefloquine's neuropsychiatric profile makes it the one to avoid in psychiatric/epilepsy history, but its weekly dose suits long trips. Choice also depends on the resistance pattern of the destination, cost, pregnancy, and tolerability.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria prophylaxis approached in pregnancy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Malaria is more severe in pregnancy; mefloquine can be used; chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate; doxycycline is contraindicated; atovaquone-proguanil generally avoided (verify against current UK guidance).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the role of primaquine in relapse prevention, and what must be checked first?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primaquine is the only drug acting on liver hypnozoites — used as presumptive anti-relapse therapy after significant exposure (P. vivax / ovale); must check G6PD first (primaquine → haemolysis in G6PD deficiency).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria prophylaxis managed in children, the immunocompromised, and long-term travellers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Individualised, specialist advice.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'D' (diagnose promptly) can't-miss rule for malaria?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area = malaria until excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria diagnosed, and what is needed to exclude it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Thick and thin blood films (thick = detect parasites, thin = speciate + quantify) — three negative films over 48 h to exclude; rapid antigen tests as an adjunct.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is falciparum malaria significant, and what is its public-health status?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Falciparum is a medical emergency → urgent treatment. Malaria is a notifiable disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is infective diarrhoea (gastroenteritis), and what is the examined skill?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: GI infection causing diarrhoea ± vomiting — mostly self-limiting and managed with rehydration. The skill examined is recognising the specific organisms by their clinical signatures and knowing the few that change management.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is Fork 1 (bloody vs non-bloody) in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inflammatory / invasive (bloody) vs secretory / watery (non-bloody).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is Fork 2 (antibiotics or not) — the highest-yield rule in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible — they increase HUS risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Campylobacter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: undercooked poultry, travellers' diarrhoea. Incubation 2-5 days. Bloody diarrhoea. Signature: severe abdo pain (mimics appendicitis); Guillain-Barré + reactive arthritis sequelae. It is the commonest bacterial cause.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of E. coli O157 (STEC)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: undercooked beef, unpasteurised milk. Incubation 1-8 days. Bloody diarrhoea. Signature: Shiga toxin → HUS; antibiotics increase HUS risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Salmonella?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: eggs, poultry, raw food. Incubation 12-48 h. ± bloody diarrhoea. Signature: can cause bacteraemia; reactive arthritis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Shigella?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: faecal-oral, contaminated water. Incubation 1-2 days. Bloody diarrhoea. Signature: also Shiga toxin → HUS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Staph aureus (toxin)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: reheated / handled food. Incubation 1-6 h (fast). Watery diarrhoea. Signature: rapid-onset vomiting (preformed enterotoxin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Bacillus cereus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: reheated rice. Incubation 1-5 h (emetic). Watery diarrhoea. Signature: the 'fried rice' vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of C. difficile?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: post-antibiotics. Incubation variable. ± bloody diarrhoea. Signature: pseudomembranous colitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Norovirus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: outbreaks (cruise ships, wards). Incubation 24-48 h. Watery + vomiting. Signature: highly contagious. It is the commonest viral cause.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Rotavirus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: children. Incubation 1-2 days. Watery diarrhoea. Signature: vaccine-preventable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Giardia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: travel, contaminated water. Incubation 1-3 weeks. Chronic, non-bloody, fatty diarrhoea. Signature: malabsorption / steatorrhoea → metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two timing extremes worth holding in infective diarrhoea, and what does bloody diarrhoea imply?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Very fast (1-6 h) = preformed toxin (Staph aureus, Bacillus cereus). Bloody = invasive (Campylobacter, E. coli O157, Salmonella, Shigella).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Campylobacter in detail — type, presentation and incubation.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A Gram-negative, curved/spiral rod; the commonest bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide; from undercooked poultry, untreated water, unpasteurised milk; common travellers' diarrhoea. Incubation 2-5 days; resolves in 3-6 days: abdo cramps (can mimic appendicitis), bloody diarrhoea, fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When are antibiotics used for Campylobacter, and what is first-line? What are its sequelae?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics only after isolating the organism if severe or high-risk (immunocompromised, HIV, heart failure): clarithromycin first-line (azithromycin / ciprofloxacin alternatives). Sequelae (high-yield): Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does E. coli O157:H7 (STEC) cause its key complication?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It produces Shiga toxin → abdominal cramps, bloody diarrhoea, vomiting. The toxin binds Gb3 receptors on (mainly renal) endothelium, causing endothelial injury and microthrombi that mechanically shear red cells — a MICROangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — producing haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI). Avoid antibiotics (they increase HUS risk).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is THE RULE for E. coli O157, and what is its source?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics increase the risk of HUS → avoid antibiotics if E. coli O157 is possible (the single most-tested fact in this topic). Source: undercooked beef, unpasteurised dairy, petting farms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the HUS triad, and how common is it in O157 infections?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: AKI + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia — commonest in children, ~6% of O157 infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Salmonella gastroenteritis — source, incubation, presentation and antibiotic approach.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: From eggs, poultry, raw foods; incubation 12-48 h; watery (± bloody) diarrhoea, cramps, fever, vomiting. Usually self-limiting; antibiotics only if severe/invasive or high-risk (risk of prolonging carriage); can cause bacteraemia and reactive arthritis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is Salmonella gastroenteritis distinct from typhoid / enteric fever?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Typhoid / enteric fever (Salmonella typhi) is a systemic illness — distinct from Salmonella gastroenteritis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What should the history cover in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Onset/duration, blood in stool, vomiting, food / travel / contact history, antibiotic use (C. diff), immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the main thing that matters on clinical assessment of infective diarrhoea, and what are its signs?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Assess dehydration — the priority assessment in the unwell patient: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine output, prolonged CRT.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bloody diarrhoea, high fever; signs of HUS (reduced urine / pallor / bruising); severe dehydration / shock, immunocompromise, recent hospital / antibiotics (C. diff).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Do most cases of infective diarrhoea need investigation, and when is stool MC&S indicated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most cases need no investigation — it is self-limiting and a clinical diagnosis. Stool MC&S (+ ova/cysts/parasites) if: bloody diarrhoea, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, recent travel, suspected outbreak, or symptoms >7 days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What targeted investigations are used in infective diarrhoea (Shiga-toxin, C. diff, bloods)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Stool Shiga-toxin / E. coli O157 testing if bloody (informs the no-antibiotics decision); C. diff toxin if recent antibiotics; bloods if unwell — FBC (HUS — anaemia + thrombocytopenia + film for schistocytes), U&E (AKI + dehydration), CRP, cultures if septic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mainstay of management for infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rehydration — oral rehydration solution first-line; IV fluids if severe dehydration / shock / vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the supportive management of infective diarrhoea, and which agents must be avoided?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antiemetics if needed. Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) in bloody / inflammatory diarrhoea — risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged toxin exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise the selective antibiotic approach in infective diarrhoea.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Not routine — most are self-limiting; antibiotics can prolong carriage or precipitate HUS. Avoid entirely if E. coli O157 possible (raises HUS). Consider for: severe campylobacter/shigella, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, specific organisms (giardia → metronidazole, C. diff → vancomycin/fidaxomicin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the public-health measures for infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most are notifiable. Infection control: isolate, hand hygiene — alcohol gel is ineffective against C. diff / norovirus, so use soap and water. Exclusion from work/school until 48 h symptom-free (especially food handlers).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications of infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HUS (E. coli O157, Shigella — the can't-miss; don't give antibiotics); Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis (post-campylobacter); dehydration / AKI / shock; bacteraemia (Salmonella); toxic megacolon; post-infectious IBS; C. diff colitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is meningococcal disease, and what organism causes it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Invasive infection with Neisseria meningitidis (a Gram-negative diplococcus) — a medical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What distinguishes meningococcal meningitis from meningococcal septicaemia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningococcal meningitis: N. meningitidis infects the meninges + CSF → the meningitic picture. Meningococcal septicaemia: the bacteria invade the bloodstream → non-blanching rash + shock — the more lethal form.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the single most important action for suspected meningococcal disease in the community?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Urgent IM/IV benzylpenicillin and immediate transfer — do not wait.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast meningococcal meningitis and septicaemia by site and dominant features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningitis: site is meninges + CSF; dominant features are headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, fever. Septicaemia: site is the bloodstream; dominant features are a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash and shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast the key danger of meningococcal meningitis vs septicaemia.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningitis: raised ICP, neuro damage. Septicaemia: septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What causes the non-blanching rash in meningococcal disease, and what is the key caveat about its absence?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is caused by the septicaemia. It can be absent in meningococcal disease — its absence never excludes the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the bacterial causes of meningitis by age group?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Neonates → Group B Strep, E. coli, Listeria. Children/adults → N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae. Elderly/immunocompromised/pregnant → add Listeria.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the viral causes of meningitis, and how do they compare in frequency and severity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Enteroviruses, HSV, VZV — viral is the commonest overall and usually milder.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which two organisms are the big bacterial causes of meningitis in the immunocompetent child/adult?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningococcus + pneumococcus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic triad of the meningitic picture, and how sensitive is it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status — present in only ~60%, so its absence doesn't exclude it. Other features: headache, photophobia, vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the meningism signs Kernig's and Brudzinski's?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Kernig's: pain on knee extension with the hip flexed. Brudzinski's: involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the features of the septicaemic picture?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (the glass/tumbler test — doesn't fade under pressure), cold peripheries, limb pain, and signs of shock (tachycardia, hypotension, prolonged CRT).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does meningococcal disease present atypically in babies / young children?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Non-specific: fever, lethargy, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, hypotonia, seizures — easily missed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags for raised ICP that contraindicate a lumbar puncture?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Reduced/fluctuating GCS, focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema, and bradycardia + hypertension.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What blood investigations are used in meningococcal disease, and which is the key confirmatory test?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cultures, meningococcal PCR (key confirmatory test — remains positive after antibiotics), FBC, U&E, CRP, glucose, clotting (DIC), lactate, ABG.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When should a lumbar puncture be done in suspected meningitis, and when is it contraindicated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: LP + CSF analysis ideally before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics in an acutely unwell patient. Contraindicated if raised ICP / shock / coagulopathy (do CT + treat first).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: On CSF analysis, how do bacterial and viral meningitis differ in appearance and cell type?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacterial: cloudy/turbid appearance with markedly raised neutrophils. Viral: clear appearance with raised lymphocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: On CSF analysis, how do bacterial and viral meningitis differ in protein and glucose?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacterial: high protein, low glucose (CSF:plasma <½). Viral: normal/mildly raised protein, normal glucose.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do bacterial and viral meningitis produce their characteristic CSF patterns, and what is the TB/fungal pattern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria release proteins and consume glucose (→ high protein, low glucose); the immune system sends neutrophils to bacteria and lymphocytes to viruses. TB/fungal meningitis: lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the community / pre-hospital management of suspected bacterial meningitis or meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Urgent IM/IV benzylpenicillin (or IM ceftriaxone) while awaiting transfer — but it must NOT delay transfer; in true penicillin allergy, prioritise transfer.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mainstay empirical hospital antibiotic for meningococcal disease, and when is amoxicillin added?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) — a third-generation cephalosporin — is the mainstay. Add amoxicillin if Listeria risk (neonates, >50, immunocompromised, pregnant).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When is vancomycin added to empirical hospital treatment for meningitis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: If recent travel / penicillin-resistant pneumococcus risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the role of dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis, and when is it given?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It reduces complications, particularly hearing loss in bacterial meningitis (especially pneumococcal) — given with / just before antibiotics.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does supportive management of meningococcal disease involve, and what is the antibiotic duration?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Treat septic shock (Sepsis Six, fluids, vasopressors), manage raised ICP, correct DIC. Duration: meningococcal meningitis → ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) for a short course (~5-7 days) for uncomplicated recovery.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What public-health step must not be forgotten in meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a notifiable disease → inform public health / UKHSA immediately.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who needs contact prophylaxis in meningococcal disease, and why?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Close contacts (household, kissing contacts, same-room exposure) need post-exposure prophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first-line agent for contact prophylaxis in meningococcal disease, and who coordinates it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ciprofloxacin (single dose — now first-line, suits all ages + pregnancy) or rifampicin. Notify UKHSA, who coordinate contact tracing + prophylaxis. Vaccinate contacts if a vaccine-preventable serogroup.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the acute complications of meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Septic shock + DIC; Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage → adrenal failure); raised ICP / cerebral oedema, seizures, death.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the chronic / sequelae of meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sensorineural hearing loss (commonest — hence dexamethasone); neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, focal neurology; limb / digit loss (purpura fulminans / ischaemia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is meningococcal disease prevented?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vaccination: Men B (infants), Men ACWY (teenagers/students), Hib/Men C. Plus chemoprophylaxis for close contacts.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis, and why is it a time-critical emergency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. It is not the infection itself but the body's damaging reaction to it — a time-critical emergency where every hour of delayed antibiotics increases mortality.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is 'the spine' of the sepsis approach?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recognise early → deliver the Sepsis Six within 1 hour → identify and control the source.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the sepsis severity ladder?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infection → sepsis (organ dysfunction) → septic shock (refractory hypotension + raised lactate).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is septic shock defined under Sepsis-3?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is bacteraemia, and how does it differ from sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria in the blood — distinct from sepsis, as it may be transient or harmless.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the status of SIRS in the Sepsis-3 era?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: SIRS — the older systemic-inflammatory-response criteria — has been superseded by Sepsis-3's organ-dysfunction focus, but still appears as a screening tool.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the early pathophysiology of sepsis from infection to cytokine storm.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infection → release of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) → massive innate immune activation → cytokine storm (the dysregulation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does sepsis produce a 'warm' distributive shock?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The cytokine storm causes widespread vasodilation + capillary leak (NO-mediated) → distributive ('warm') shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does sepsis progress to multi-organ dysfunction at the microvascular level?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Microvascular thrombosis + endothelial injury → tissue hypoperfusion → lactate rises (anaerobic metabolism) → multi-organ dysfunction. It can also cause DIC (consumption of clotting factors), AKI, ARDS and encephalopathy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who is vulnerable to sepsis (risk factors)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Extremes of age (very young, elderly); immunocompromise (chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, HIV, asplenia); indwelling devices (lines, catheters); recent surgery / instrumentation; pregnancy / peripartum; IVDU and chronic disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Is sepsis a clinical or test-based diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis — no single test rules it in or out.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the preferred in-hospital screening tool for sepsis, and why?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: NEWS2 — 2026 Surviving Sepsis recommends NEWS2/NEWS/MEWS/SIRS over qSOFA; it is a track-and-trigger tool and the most sensitive.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the qSOFA criteria, and what is its current role?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A quick bedside score (≥2 = high risk): GCS <15, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100. It is no longer recommended as a sole screening tool — less sensitive than EWS — but remains useful as a predictor of poor outcome.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the SIRS score assess?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Temp, HR, RR and WCC derangement (the older criteria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags that prompt urgent action in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Altered mentation; SBP ≤90 (or a drop >40 from baseline); RR ≥25; SpO2 needing O2; lactate >2; reduced urine output; mottled/ashen skin; non-blanching rash.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Sepsis Six, and in what timeframe must it be delivered?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A bundle delivered within 1 hour, remembered as 'take 3, give 3'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three 'GIVE' components of the Sepsis Six?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1. Oxygen — target 94-98% (88-92% if a COPD retainer). 2. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (empirical, per local guidelines). 3. IV fluids (balanced crystalloid bolus, e.g. 500 mL, reassess).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three 'TAKE' components of the Sepsis Six?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1. Blood cultures (before antibiotics). 2. Lactate (via VBG/ABG). 3. Urine output (catheterise + monitor, aim >0.5 mL/kg/h).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is antibiotic timing the single most important intervention, and how does this interact with blood cultures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, ideally within 1 hour, for septic shock or high-likelihood sepsis. Take blood cultures before antibiotics where possible — but do not delay antibiotics for them in shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How should fluids be used in sepsis resuscitation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Use dynamic measures to guide resuscitation; reassess after each bolus — avoid both under- and over-resuscitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is source control, and why are antibiotics alone sometimes insufficient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics alone are not enough if there is a focus of infection that needs physical removal or drainage. Source control is the definitive step — a collection of pus under pressure will not clear with antibiotics alone.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the source control for an abscess, and for an obstructed + infected kidney?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Abscess → drainage (radiological or surgical). Obstructed + infected kidney → nephrostomy / stent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the source control for ascending cholangitis, and for an infected line/device?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ascending cholangitis → ERCP biliary decompression. Infected line / device → remove it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the source control for necrotising fasciitis / perforation, and for an empyema?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Necrotising fasciitis / perforation → urgent surgical debridement / repair. Empyema → chest drain.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the overarching principle of source control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Find the source and control it — the same logic as the cholangitis and infected-stone notes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How should a patient be reassessed after the Sepsis Six?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Repeat lactate; if not improving → escalate to HDU/ICU.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is septic shock managed when hypotension is fluid-refractory?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fluid-refractory hypotension → vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) to maintain MAP ≥65.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When and how are antibiotics de-escalated in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: De-escalate antibiotics once cultures/sensitivities return (empirical → targeted).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is organ dysfunction treated in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Treat organ dysfunction: AKI (may need RRT), ARDS (ventilation), and DIC.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications of sepsis, including long-term?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Septic shock, multi-organ dysfunction (AKI, ARDS, hepatic, encephalopathy), DIC, death. Long-term: post-sepsis syndrome (physical / cognitive impairment).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the significance of a lactate >2 in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It marks tissue hypoperfusion — and is the threshold in the septic shock definition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A medical student is asked to explain why antibiotics can kill bacteria without harming human cells. Which underlying difference best accounts for this 'selective toxicity'?
options: Bacteria and human cells share identical ribosomes
Bacteria are prokaryotes with a peptidoglycan wall and 70S ribosomes, which human (eukaryotic, 80S) cells lack
Human cells have a chitin wall that antibiotics spare
Bacteria have a nucleus that antibiotics target
Antibiotics act only on viruses, not human cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Bacteria are prokaryotes with a peptidoglycan wall and 70S ribosomes, which human (eukaryotic, 80S) cells lack
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Selective toxicity exploits prokaryote-specific targets — the peptidoglycan wall and the 70S ribosome — that human eukaryotic cells do not possess.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 72-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter has no fever, no suprapubic pain and normal inflammatory markers, but a routine urine culture grows E. coli. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: He has a confirmed urinary tract infection and needs IV antibiotics
This most likely represents colonisation rather than infection, and antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of symptoms/host response
He has urosepsis and needs the Sepsis Six
The culture proves contamination and should be ignored entirely
He requires immediate catheter removal and blood cultures
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: This most likely represents colonisation rather than infection, and antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of symptoms/host response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A positive culture without symptoms or a host response usually reflects colonisation (asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with catheters); treatment risks harm and resistance without benefit.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with Gram-negative bacteraemia develops fever, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which bacterial component is chiefly responsible for this systemic picture?
options: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide) from the Gram-negative outer membrane
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide) from the Gram-negative outer membrane
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Endotoxin (LPS), released from the Gram-negative outer membrane, non-specifically triggers the inflammatory cascade causing fever, sepsis, DIC and shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement best distinguishes an exotoxin from an endotoxin?
options: Exotoxin is LPS released on lysis; endotoxin is a secreted protein
Exotoxin is a secreted protein that can be made into a toxoid vaccine; endotoxin is the LPS of the Gram-negative wall
Endotoxin can be converted to a toxoid, but exotoxin cannot
Exotoxins are found only in Gram-negative organisms
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Exotoxin is a secreted protein that can be made into a toxoid vaccine; endotoxin is the LPS of the Gram-negative wall
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Exotoxins are secreted proteins (often Gram-positive), specific and convertible to toxoids; endotoxin is the LPS of the Gram-negative outer membrane and drives non-specific sepsis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with an infected prosthetic hip joint has an organism that persists despite prolonged antibiotics, and cure ultimately requires removal of the prosthesis. Which virulence mechanism most likely explains this?
options: Biofilm formation on the prosthetic surface
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Biofilm formation on the prosthetic surface
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Biofilms on prostheses and catheters protect organisms from antibiotics and immunity, causing chronic, resistant infection that often needs device removal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set correctly matches all six microbial groups to their defining feature?
options: Bacteria = eukaryote; viruses = have a nucleus; prions = RNA-based
Bacteria = prokaryote; viruses = acellular (DNA or RNA); fungi = eukaryote with chitin wall; parasites = eukaryote (protozoa/helminths); prions = protein with no nucleic acid
All six are prokaryotes with peptidoglycan walls
Fungi = acellular; prions = eukaryotes; viruses = chitin wall
Parasites = prokaryotes; bacteria = acellular; prions = DNA virus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Bacteria = prokaryote; viruses = acellular (DNA or RNA); fungi = eukaryote with chitin wall; parasites = eukaryote (protozoa/helminths); prions = protein with no nucleic acid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The six-fold framework: bacteria (prokaryote), viruses (acellular, DNA or RNA), fungi (eukaryote, chitin), parasites (eukaryote — protozoa/helminths), prions (protein, no nucleic acid).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A capsule is described as a key virulence factor in Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. What is its principal role?
options: It resists phagocytosis by host immune cells
It enables attachment to host epithelium
It forms a biofilm on catheters
It is the target of all beta-lactam antibiotics
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It resists phagocytosis by host immune cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis, a major reason encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus and meningococcus are virulent (and why capsular vaccines are effective).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: According to the 'chain of infection', which intervention breaks the link of transmission for a droplet-spread respiratory pathogen?
options: Isolating the patient and using appropriate respiratory precautions
Giving the patient a proton pump inhibitor
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Isolating the patient and using appropriate respiratory precautions
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Infection control works by breaking a link in the chain; isolation and respiratory precautions interrupt droplet/airborne transmission, just as hand hygiene interrupts contact spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A researcher wants to prove that a newly discovered bacterium causes a specific disease. Which framework classically sets out the criteria for establishing microbial causation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Koch's postulates set the classic criteria for proving causation: found in all cases, isolated in pure culture, reproduces disease in a healthy host, and re-isolated from that host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a recognised limitation of Koch's postulates?
options: They apply perfectly to every known pathogen
They fail for organisms that cannot be cultured, asymptomatic carriers, and many viruses
They require an electron microscope to apply
They only apply to Gram-positive bacteria
They have been shown to be entirely incorrect
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They fail for organisms that cannot be cultured, asymptomatic carriers, and many viruses
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Koch's postulates do not hold for uncultureable organisms, asymptomatic carriers or viruses, though they remain the conceptual foundation of causation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A previously healthy commensal organism from a patient's own skin causes a bloodstream infection only after a central venous catheter is inserted and the patient becomes neutropenic. This organism is best described as which type of pathogen?
options: A strict commensal that never causes disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An opportunistic pathogen is a commensal or low-virulence organism that causes disease only when host defences are breached or suppressed (e.g. a line in situ plus neutropenia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A blood culture from a septic patient shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The laboratory reports the organism is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which is the most likely organism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive (Staph, not Strep) and coagulase-positive identify Staphylococcus aureus; coagulase-negative staphylococci are epidermidis/saprophyticus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: During the Gram stain, what is the role of the alcohol step, and why do Gram-negative bacteria end up pink?
options: It fixes the crystal violet permanently into all cells
It decolourises the thin-walled Gram-negatives (which then take the pink safranin counterstain), while the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positives retains the crystal violet
It stains the outer membrane purple
It is a mordant that binds iodine to the wall
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It decolourises the thin-walled Gram-negatives (which then take the pink safranin counterstain), while the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positives retains the crystal violet
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Alcohol decolourises Gram-negatives (thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane), so they take the pink safranin; Gram-positives retain the crystal violet–iodine complex and stay purple.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A young adult with an atypical pneumonia fails to improve on amoxicillin. Serology later confirms Mycoplasma pneumoniae. What best explains the treatment failure, and what is appropriate?
options: Amoxicillin was underdosed; increase the dose
Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so wall-targeting β-lactams are ineffective — use a macrolide (or tetracycline/quinolone)
The organism produces a capsule that blocks amoxicillin; add a steroid
Mycoplasma is acid-fast and needs anti-tuberculous therapy
It is a viral pneumonia needing no antibiotic
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so wall-targeting β-lactams are ineffective — use a macrolide (or tetracycline/quinolone)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mycoplasma has no peptidoglycan wall, so β-lactams (which target the wall) don't work; atypicals are treated with macrolides, tetracyclines or quinolones.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Sputum from a patient with chronic cough, weight loss and haemoptysis is stained with Ziehl-Neelsen and shows red (acid-fast) bacilli. Which organism does this indicate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, resulting from the waxy mycolic-acid wall, indicate mycobacteria such as M. tuberculosis, which do not stain reliably by Gram.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has a deep, foul-smelling intra-abdominal abscess. Which class of organism predominates in such collections, and which antibiotic classically targets it?
options: Obligate aerobes; treated with an aminoglycoside
Microaerophilic organisms; treated with a macrolide
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Anaerobes dominate in abscesses, deep/necrotic tissue and the gut; metronidazole is the classic anti-anaerobe.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 40-year-old is due a splenectomy after trauma. Against which category of organism is vaccination especially important, and why?
options: Anaerobes, because the spleen filters them
Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib), because the spleen is key to clearing capsulated organisms
Acid-fast bacilli, because asplenia reactivates TB
Spirochaetes, because they evade the spleen
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib), because the spleen is key to clearing capsulated organisms
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Asplenic/hyposplenic patients are at high risk from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib) and should be vaccinated, as the capsule resists phagocytosis and the spleen is central to their clearance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A lumbar puncture in a teenager with meningism shows Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF. Which organism is most likely?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Gram-negative diplococci point to Neisseria meningitidis; S. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive diplococcus, and Listeria and Haemophilus have different morphologies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A ward outbreak of Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea prompts an infection-control review. Why is alcohol hand gel inadequate, and what is required?
options: C. difficile is Gram-negative and resists all measures
C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing plus sporicidal cleaning (e.g. chlorine) is needed
Alcohol gel is adequate and no change is needed
The organism is airborne, so respirators are the priority
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing plus sporicidal cleaning (e.g. chlorine) is needed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Spore-forming organisms such as C. difficile resist alcohol; mechanical removal by soap-and-water handwashing and sporicidal (chlorine-based) cleaning are required.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A throat swab from a child with tonsillitis grows a beta-haemolytic, Lancefield Group A streptococcus. Which organism is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Beta-haemolytic (complete haemolysis) Lancefield Group A streptococcus is S. pyogenes; Group B is S. agalactiae, and pneumococcus is alpha-haemolytic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A urine culture on MacConkey agar grows pink (lactose-fermenting) Gram-negative rods that are oxidase-negative. Which organism is most consistent with this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Lactose-fermenting (pink on MacConkey), oxidase-negative Gram-negative rods fit E. coli; Pseudomonas is oxidase-positive and a non-fermenter, and Salmonella/Shigella are non-fermenters.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which single laboratory result most reliably separates staphylococci from streptococci?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Catalase separates the Gram-positive cocci: staphylococci are catalase-positive, streptococci and enterococci are catalase-negative. Coagulase then separates S. aureus from other staphylococci.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A norovirus outbreak spreads through a ward despite staff using alcohol hand gel. What best explains this, and what should be done?
options: Norovirus is enveloped and resistant to alcohol; use more gel
Norovirus is non-enveloped and resistant to alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine-based cleaning are required
Norovirus is bacterial and needs antibiotics
The gel was expired; no other change is needed
Norovirus is airborne, so FFP3 masks are the key measure
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Norovirus is non-enveloped and resistant to alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine-based cleaning are required
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus resist alcohol; soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine (hypochlorite) cleaning are needed to control spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A renal transplant patient on immunosuppression develops fever, cytopenias and deranged LFTs, and CMV is detected. What is the underlying reason CMV has caused disease now?
options: CMV was newly acquired from the graft only
