Herpesviruses (including CMV) establish lifelong latency and reactivate when immunity falls, as with transplant immunosuppression
CMV is a non-enveloped virus resistant to the immune system
CMV integrates into the host genome like a retrovirus
CMV only causes disease in the immunocompetent
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Herpesviruses (including CMV) establish lifelong latency and reactivate when immunity falls, as with transplant immunosuppression
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Herpesviruses persist latently and reactivate under immunosuppression; CMV disease is characteristic in transplant recipients and HIV.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient newly diagnosed with HIV is started on antiretroviral therapy. Which virus-specific enzyme, unique to retroviruses, is a principal drug target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to convert RNA to DNA that integrates into the host genome; reverse-transcriptase (with integrase and protease) inhibitors are core antiretroviral targets.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An older adult develops a painful vesicular rash in a single dermatome. Which process explains this presentation?
options: Primary varicella infection acquired that week
Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from the dorsal root ganglia (shingles)
Bacterial superinfection of the skin only
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from the dorsal root ganglia (shingles)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Shingles is reactivation of VZV latent in the dorsal root ganglia, producing a dermatomal vesicular rash, typically when immunity wanes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Two patients have hepatitis. One acquired it from contaminated shellfish with an acute self-limiting illness; the other acquired it via blood and has developed chronic infection with cirrhosis. Which viruses are most likely, respectively?
options: Hepatitis A (faecal-oral, acute) and hepatitis B or C (blood-borne, chronic)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Hepatitis A (faecal-oral, acute) and hepatitis B or C (blood-borne, chronic)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hepatitis A is faecal-oral and acute; hepatitis B and C are blood-borne and can become chronic with progression to cirrhosis/HCC. Vowels (A/E) faecal-oral/acute; consonants (B/C/D) blood-borne/chronic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is aciclovir relatively non-toxic to human cells while effectively treating herpes simplex?
options: It is toxic to all dividing cells equally
It is only activated by the viral thymidine kinase, concentrating the active drug in infected cells (selective toxicity)
It dissolves the viral lipid envelope directly
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It is only activated by the viral thymidine kinase, concentrating the active drug in infected cells (selective toxicity)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Aciclovir is phosphorylated to its active form chiefly by viral thymidine kinase, so it is activated selectively in herpesvirus-infected cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 3-year-old has a runny nose, mild fever and cough for two days and looks well. The parents request antibiotics. What is the best explanation for withholding them?
options: Antibiotics are too expensive for viral illness
The illness is almost certainly viral; viruses lack the bacterial targets antibiotics act on, so antibiotics are ineffective and supportive care is appropriate
Antibiotics would cure it faster but are being rationed
The child is too young for any antibiotic
Antibiotics only work on non-enveloped viruses
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The illness is almost certainly viral; viruses lack the bacterial targets antibiotics act on, so antibiotics are ineffective and supportive care is appropriate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Uncomplicated URTIs are viral; antibiotics don't work on viruses (no wall/ribosome/metabolism to target), so supportive care and safety-netting are appropriate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Persistent infection with which virus is the principal cause of cervical cancer?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Persistent high-risk HPV infection causes cervical (and anogenital/oropharyngeal) cancer; HPV vaccination targets this.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why must the influenza vaccine be reformulated each year?
options: The vaccine degrades in storage annually
Influenza is an RNA virus with a high mutation rate (antigenic drift/shift), so circulating strains change
Influenza is a DNA virus that is highly stable
People lose all immune memory within weeks
Antibiotics have made the old vaccine obsolete
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Influenza is an RNA virus with a high mutation rate (antigenic drift/shift), so circulating strains change
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Influenza's RNA genome mutates rapidly (drift/shift), changing surface antigens, so the vaccine is updated to match circulating strains.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which type of virus is most likely to survive on environmental surfaces and spread by the faecal-oral route?
options: Non-enveloped (naked) viruses such as norovirus and rotavirus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Non-enveloped (naked) viruses such as norovirus and rotavirus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Non-enveloped viruses have a tough protein capsid, survive on surfaces and in the GI tract, and typically spread faecal-orally; enveloped viruses are fragile.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Oseltamivir is used in influenza. Which step of the viral life cycle does it inhibit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, blocking release of new influenza virions from infected cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 120 has three weeks of a dry cough, worsening exertional breathlessness and hypoxia, with bilateral perihilar infiltrates on chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: PCP is an AIDS-defining pneumonia at CD4 <200, with a dry cough, exertional hypoxia and bilateral perihilar infiltrates; treatment is co-trimoxazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with advanced HIV (CD4 40) has headache, fever and neck stiffness. CSF microscopy with India ink shows yeasts with a clear capsular halo. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An encapsulated yeast on India ink in an HIV patient with low CD4 indicates cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus neoformans); CrAg and culture confirm it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A diabetic patient in ketoacidosis develops facial pain, a black necrotic eschar on the palate and rapid orbital involvement. Which infection must be recognised urgently?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis is an aggressive angioinvasive mould infection in diabetic ketoacidosis/immunocompromise, presenting with necrotic (black) tissue — a surgical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neutropenic patient after chemotherapy develops persistent fever and pulmonary nodules; serum galactomannan is positive. Which infection is most likely?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Invasive aspergillosis is characteristic in the neutropenic and is supported by a positive galactomannan antigen; it carries a high mortality.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Amphotericin B is effective but nephrotoxic. What is its mechanism of action?
options: It inhibits β-glucan synthesis in the cell wall
It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Amphotericin (a polyene) binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores; because human membranes use cholesterol it is comparatively selective, but nephrotoxicity is a key limitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do the azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole) exert their effect?
options: By binding preformed ergosterol to make pores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Azoles inhibit 14α-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis; their similarity to human enzymes underlies hepatotoxicity and drug interactions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with poorly controlled asthma has recurrent wheeze, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, a high total IgE, eosinophilia and positive Aspergillus-specific IgE, with central bronchiectasis. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus in asthma/CF, with high IgE, eosinophilia, fleeting infiltrates and central bronchiectasis — distinct from invasive disease or a fungus ball.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A dimorphic fungus is described as growing as a mould in the environment and as a yeast in the body. Which phrase captures this behaviour?
options: 'Yeast in the cold, mould in the heat'
'Mould in the cold, yeast in the heat'
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: 'Mould in the cold, yeast in the heat'
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) are moulds in the cold environment and yeasts at body temperature — 'mould in the cold, yeast in the heat'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An infant on a course of antibiotics develops white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that leave a raw surface when scraped. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Oral thrush is caused by Candida, an opportunist favoured by antibiotics, inhaled steroids, extremes of age and immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why are antifungal drugs generally more toxic to patients than most antibacterial antibiotics?
options: Fungi are prokaryotes with many unique targets
Fungi are eukaryotes that share much cell machinery with human cells, leaving few selective targets
Fungi have no cell membrane to target
Antifungals target the human 80S ribosome deliberately
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Fungi are eukaryotes that share much cell machinery with human cells, leaving few selective targets
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Because fungi are eukaryotes like human cells, there are fewer fungus-specific targets, so antifungals (e.g. amphotericin, azoles) tend to be more toxic with a narrower therapeutic window.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has thickened, discoloured toenails and scaling between the toes; skin scrapings with KOH show hyphae. What is the first-line treatment for this dermatophyte infection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dermatophyte (tinea) infections are treated with terbinafine (topical or oral) or azoles; terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase in ergosterol synthesis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 28-year-old returns from Nigeria with cyclical fevers, rigors, headache and mild jaundice; the spleen is palpable. What is the single most important initial investigation?
options: Thick and thin blood films (repeated up to three times)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Thick and thin blood films (repeated up to three times)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fever in a returning traveller is malaria until proven otherwise; thick and thin blood films (×3 before exclusion) are the key investigation, with thick films to detect and thin films to speciate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A traveller treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria is at risk of relapse weeks later. What is the reason, and what additional treatment addresses it?
options: Re-infection from the ward; repeat artemisinin
Dormant liver hypnozoites; add primaquine (after checking G6PD status)
Incomplete blood-stage cure only; extend artesunate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Dormant liver hypnozoites; add primaquine (after checking G6PD status)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: P. vivax and ovale form dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapse; primaquine eradicates them, given after checking G6PD status to avoid haemolysis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A backpacker returns with several weeks of bloating, foul-smelling, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea and weight loss. Stool studies suggest a protozoan. What is the most likely organism and treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giardia causes chronic, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea with malabsorption ('backpacker's'); treatment is metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient returning from the tropics has bloody diarrhoea and, weeks later, right-upper-quadrant pain with a solitary liver lesion containing 'anchovy sauce' material. Which organism is responsible?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica causes bloody dysentery and amoebic liver abscess ('anchovy sauce' pus); treatment is metronidazole plus a luminal agent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with advanced HIV has headache and focal neurology; MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which parasitic infection is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii) is a classic opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, causing ring-enhancing brain lesions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 6-year-old has intense perianal itching at night; a parent has seen tiny white worms. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Threadworm (Enterobius) causes nocturnal perianal itch in children, is confirmed with the sellotape test, and is treated with mebendazole (treat the household).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A traveller who swam in a freshwater lake in sub-Saharan Africa develops painless visible haematuria weeks later. Which infection is most likely, and what is the treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Freshwater exposure with later haematuria suggests Schistosoma haematobium (which also predisposes to bladder cancer); treatment is praziquantel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A returning traveller has a chronic illness and a markedly raised eosinophil count. Which category of organism should this particularly prompt you to consider?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Eosinophilia with a travel history points to tissue-invading helminths; protozoa more typically cause acute fever/diarrhoea without eosinophilia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient from a rural area has iron-deficiency anaemia and a history of walking barefoot on contaminated soil. Which helminth is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hookworm larvae penetrate the skin of bare feet and cause chronic intestinal blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anaemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has intense generalised itch, worse at night, with burrows visible in the finger webs and wrists; household members are also itchy. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Scabies causes intense nocturnal itch with burrows in the finger webs/wrists and affects close contacts; treatment is topical permethrin, treating the whole household.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Before starting high-dose corticosteroids in a patient who lived for years in the tropics, which parasite is important to exclude/treat because of the risk of overwhelming hyperinfection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Strongyloides persists by autoinfection and can cause life-threatening hyperinfection with immunosuppression (e.g. steroids); at-risk patients are screened and treated (ivermectin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 65-year-old develops a dementia that progresses over weeks with prominent myoclonic jerks. He is afebrile, inflammatory markers and routine CSF are normal, and MRI shows cortical ribboning. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, no inflammation (normal CSF/markers) and cortical ribboning on MRI is characteristic of sporadic CJD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why are prions extraordinarily resistant to standard sterilisation methods such as autoclaving and alcohol?
options: They contain no nucleic acid for these methods to damage, and the misfolded protein is highly stable
They are enveloped and reseal after damage
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They contain no nucleic acid for these methods to damage, and the misfolded protein is highly stable
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Sterilisation largely works by damaging nucleic acid; prions have none and are extremely stable, so they resist heat/autoclave/formalin/alcohol/radiation and need special decontamination or single-use instruments.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A man in his late 20s develops psychiatric and behavioural changes with painful sensory symptoms, followed by neurological decline over more than a year; MRI shows the pulvinar sign. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Variant CJD affects younger patients, presents with psychiatric/sensory features first, runs a longer course and shows the pulvinar sign on MRI; it is linked to BSE-contaminated beef.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is there typically no fever, normal inflammatory markers and normal routine CSF in prion disease?
options: Because the patient is always immunosuppressed
Because the prion is a misfolded 'self' protein and provokes no immune/inflammatory response
Because prions replicate too slowly to be detected
Because antibiotics have already been given
Because CSF is not affected by any brain disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because the prion is a misfolded 'self' protein and provokes no immune/inflammatory response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prions are misfolded host protein, seen by the body as 'self', so there is no immune response — hence no fever, normal inflammatory markers and normal routine CSF.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does a prion cause more prion protein to form?
options: By templating the conversion of normal PrP into the misfolded β-sheet form (conformational change)
By hijacking host ribosomes to translate viral RNA
By integrating into the host genome
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: By templating the conversion of normal PrP into the misfolded β-sheet form (conformational change)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prions propagate by conformational conversion — the misfolded PrP^Sc forces normal PrP^C to misfold — not by copying any genetic code.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which EEG finding is classically associated with sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease?
options: A completely normal EEG in all cases
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Periodic sharp-wave complexes are the classic EEG finding in sporadic CJD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with suspected CJD requires neurosurgery. What is the key infection-control principle regarding the instruments?
options: Prions resist standard sterilisation, so single-use instruments (or special decontamination) are used for CNS/eye/tonsil procedures
Alcohol wipes fully decontaminate the instruments
No precautions are needed as prions are non-infectious
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Prions resist standard sterilisation, so single-use instruments (or special decontamination) are used for CNS/eye/tonsil procedures
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Because prions resist standard sterilisation, high-risk (CNS/eye/tonsil) procedures use single-use instruments or special decontamination to prevent iatrogenic transmission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which CSF investigation has become a key test supporting the diagnosis of prion disease?
options: Oligoclonal bands as the definitive test
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Routine CSF is normal, but RT-QuIC (prion-seeding assay) and 14-3-3 protein support the diagnosis; RT-QuIC is increasingly the key test.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the commonest form of prion disease in humans?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Sporadic CJD accounts for roughly 85% of cases and arises from spontaneous misfolding, typically in older adults.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Kuru and iatrogenic CJD (from contaminated instruments, dura mater grafts or human growth hormone) are examples of which category of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Kuru (ritual cannibalism) and iatrogenic CJD are acquired/transmissible prion diseases; other categories are sporadic and inherited (PRNP mutations).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the unifying principle underlying the herpesvirus family?
options: They are all RNA viruses with no latency
Primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops
They only cause disease in the immunocompetent
They are cleared completely after primary infection
They are all treated with neuraminidase inhibitors
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The unifying herpesvirus principle is primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops, which is why they dominate in immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The '-ciclovir' antivirals (aciclovir, valaciclovir, ganciclovir) work by which mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The '-ciclovirs' inhibit viral DNA polymerase; resistance arises via mutation of viral thymidine kinase or DNA polymerase.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which herpesviruses form the neurotropic alpha group treated with aciclovir?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The alpha group of human herpesviruses — HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV — is neurotropic and treated with aciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient presents with fever, confusion, and seizures, and imaging suggests temporal lobe involvement. What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?
options: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe); urgent IV aciclovir
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe); urgent IV aciclovir
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1) affects the temporal lobe and is the can't-miss diagnosis requiring urgent IV aciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: When is a patient with chickenpox (primary VZV) most infectious?
options: Only once the rash has crusted
Only during the fever phase after the rash
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Primary VZV (chickenpox) presents with fever + a vesicular rash (lesions at different stages) and is most infectious 1–2 days before the rash appears.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has a painful vesicular rash confined to one dermatome that does not cross the midline. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Shingles (VZV reactivation) presents as a painful rash in a dermatomal distribution that doesn't cross the midline.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which complication of VZV involves the facial nerve, causing facial palsy plus ear vesicles?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a VZV complication affecting the facial nerve → facial palsy + ear vesicles. Ophthalmic zoster (V1) carries Hutchinson's sign and is sight-threatening.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: At what age is the shingles vaccine offered?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Since September 2023 the UK offers the shingles vaccine (Shingrix — recombinant, non-live, two doses) routinely at age 65 (with a catch-up 70 cohort during rollout, and from age 50 in immunocompromised patients). VZV is treated with aciclovir/valaciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A teenager with sore throat, fever, and lymphadenopathy is given amoxicillin and develops a florid maculopapular rash. What is the underlying diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giving amoxicillin/ampicillin to someone with EBV causes a florid maculopapular rash — a classic SBA clue for EBV infectious mononucleosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which investigation supports a diagnosis of EBV mononucleosis, and when does it become positive?
options: Monospot/heterophile antibody test, positive in the 2nd week
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Monospot/heterophile antibody test, positive in the 2nd week
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: EBV shows raised (atypical) lymphocytes and a positive Monospot/heterophile antibody test in the 2nd week.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient recovering from EBV mononucleosis asks about activity. What advice is given, and why?
options: Avoid contact sport ~4–6 weeks due to splenic rupture risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Avoid contact sport ~4–6 weeks due to splenic rupture risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: EBV mononucleosis is managed conservatively (resolves in 2–4 weeks), and contact sport should be avoided ~4–6 weeks because of the risk of splenic rupture.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which malignancy is associated with EBV?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: EBV is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has a mononucleosis-like illness but the Monospot test is negative. Which virus is most likely responsible?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CMV typically causes a mononucleosis-like illness but is Monospot-negative — the discriminator from EBV (which is Monospot-positive); CMV is dormant in monocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the most important manifestation of CMV in an HIV/AIDS patient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In the immunocompromised, CMV causes retinitis (HIV/AIDS), colitis, oesophagitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection. Which classic feature results from it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection and causes sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, and growth restriction.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the treatment for clinically significant CMV disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CMV is treated with ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with influenza is at risk and presents within 48 hours. What is the appropriate treatment and its mechanism?
options: Oral oseltamivir or inhaled zanamivir; neuraminidase inhibitors block sialic acid cleavage to prevent viral release
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Oral oseltamivir or inhaled zanamivir; neuraminidase inhibitors block sialic acid cleavage to prevent viral release
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: For at-risk influenza patients within 48h, oral oseltamivir or inhaled zanamivir (neuraminidase inhibitors) block sialic acid cleavage → prevent viral release; annual vaccination is used for prevention.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which organisms cause secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Influenza can be complicated by pneumonia — primary viral or secondary bacterial (Staph aureus, pneumococcus). Diagnosis is by viral nasal/throat swab PCR.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What virus causes COVID-19, and what is its incubation period?
options: A DNA herpesvirus; up to 21 days
SARS-CoV-2, a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; up to 14 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: SARS-CoV-2, a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; up to 14 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus, with an incubation up to 14 days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which presenting symptom and CXR finding are characteristic of COVID-19?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: COVID-19 presents with anosmia, cough, fever, myalgia, headache, and fatigue (respiratory failure if severe); the CXR shows bilateral lower-zone ground-glass infiltrates, and diagnosis is RT-PCR of an upper respiratory swab.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the management of hospitalised/severe COVID-19?
options: Dexamethasone + remdesivir (nucleotide analogue) + CPAP/respiratory support, escalating to ventilation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Dexamethasone + remdesivir (nucleotide analogue) + CPAP/respiratory support, escalating to ventilation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mild–moderate COVID-19 is supportive; hospitalised/severe disease is treated with dexamethasone + remdesivir (nucleotide analogue) + CPAP/respiratory support, escalating to ventilation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes EBV from CMV mononucleosis?
options: EBV is Monospot-negative; CMV is Monospot-positive
EBV is Monospot-positive; CMV is Monospot-negative
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: EBV is Monospot-positive; CMV is Monospot-negative
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Both cause mononucleosis, but EBV is Monospot-positive and CMV is Monospot-negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: At which age is the MMR vaccine first given in the UK childhood schedule?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MMR is first given at 12 months (12–13 months), along with Hib/MenC, pneumococcal booster, and MenB booster; the 2nd MMR dose is at 3–4 years.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are given at the 2-month visit in the UK schedule?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: At 2 months, the schedule gives the 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) + pneumococcal (PCV) + rotavirus (oral, live) + MenB.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The HPV vaccine is given at 12–13 years as a single dose. Which cancers and conditions does it protect against?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The HPV vaccine (given to girls + boys as a single dose since 2023) protects against HPV 16/18 (cervical/anal cancer) and 6/11 (genital warts).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are given at the 14-year visit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: At 14 years the schedule gives the 3-in-1 teenage booster (Td/IPV — tetanus, low-dose diphtheria, polio; NOT pertussis) plus MenACWY.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pregnant woman asks which vaccines she should receive. Which is recommended and at what timing?
options: Pertussis (Tdap) at 16–32 weeks (ideally 20 weeks) to protect the newborn
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pertussis (Tdap) at 16–32 weeks (ideally 20 weeks) to protect the newborn
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In pregnancy, only pertussis (Tdap) at 16–32 weeks (ideally 20 weeks — to protect the newborn from whooping cough), influenza (any trimester, inactivated), and COVID-19 booster (if eligible) are given; live vaccines are contraindicated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in pregnancy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy — MMR, varicella, and yellow fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: At what age is the shingles (VZV) vaccine given to adults, and how many doses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Since September 2023 the UK shingles vaccine is Shingrix (recombinant, non-live), given as TWO doses and offered routinely at age 65 (catch-up at 70 during rollout; from 50 if immunocompromised) — replacing the single-dose live Zostavax.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are recommended in a patient with asplenia/splenic dysfunction?
options: Pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In asplenia/splenic dysfunction, pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza are recommended.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines include MMR, VZV (shingles), rotavirus (oral), yellow fever, BCG, and nasal flu. IPV, DTaP, hepatitis B, and injectable influenza are killed/inactivated/subunit.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about live attenuated vaccines is correct?
options: They require multiple doses and a booster
A single dose is often sufficient, and they produce IgG + IgA antibodies with no adjuvant needed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A single dose is often sufficient, and they produce IgG + IgA antibodies with no adjuvant needed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines often need only a single dose (strong cell-mediated immunity), produce IgG + IgA, and need no adjuvant, but must not be given to immunocompromised or pregnant patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which feature distinguishes killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines from live vaccines?
options: They produce IgG + IgA and need no adjuvant
They produce IgG only (not IgA), need multiple doses + booster, and require an adjuvant
A single dose is always sufficient
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They produce IgG only (not IgA), need multiple doses + booster, and require an adjuvant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines produce IgG only (not IgA), need multiple doses + booster, require an adjuvant to boost immunogenicity, and are safe in pregnancy and immunocompromise.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do the diphtheria and tetanus vaccines generate immunity?
options: Toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Diphtheria + tetanus vaccines use toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant (inactivated toxin → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The meningococcus and Hib vaccines are conjugate vaccines. What does conjugation to a carrier protein achieve?
options: A T-independent response with no memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Meningococcus + Hib vaccines are capsular polysaccharide conjugated to a carrier protein, giving a T-cell-dependent response → memory.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does the hepatitis B vaccine generate immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant viral surface antigen (HBsAg).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is the MMR vaccine given at 12 months and not earlier?
options: Infants cannot mount any immune response before 12 months
Maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given earlier; it wanes by ~6 months
The vaccine is too toxic before 12 months
It requires an adjuvant only available later
It causes fever in younger infants
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given earlier; it wanes by ~6 months
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MMR is given from 12 months because maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given before this; maternal IgG wanes by ~6 months.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count <200 is being considered for vaccination. What is the rule regarding live vaccines?
options: Live vaccines are recommended to boost immunity
Live vaccines are an absolute contraindication due to risk of vaccine-strain disease
Live vaccines are safe if given with an adjuvant
Only inactivated vaccines cause vaccine-strain disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Live vaccines are an absolute contraindication due to risk of vaccine-strain disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live vaccines + immunocompromise is an absolute contraindication; in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <200, on biologics, post-stem cell transplant) live vaccines risk vaccine-strain disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why are unconjugated polysaccharide vaccines ineffective in children under 2 years?
options: They elicit a T-cell-dependent response with strong memory
They are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years
They require maternal IgG to work
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Conjugated polysaccharide vaccines (PCV, Hib, MenACWY) elicit a T-cell-dependent response → memory; unconjugated vaccines are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in children under 2.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is pertussis vaccination in pregnancy particularly important, and when is pertussis most dangerous?
options: It protects the mother only; pertussis is most dangerous in adults
Maternal antibodies are passively transferred to protect the newborn before their own vaccines; pertussis is most dangerous in infants under 3 months
It replaces the infant schedule entirely
It is a live vaccine that colonises the neonate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Maternal antibodies are passively transferred to protect the newborn before their own vaccines; pertussis is most dangerous in infants under 3 months
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Maternal pertussis vaccination at 16–32 weeks → antibodies passively transferred to the neonate → protects the newborn for the first few weeks before their own vaccines; this matters because pertussis is most dangerous in infants under 3 months.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about HPV epidemiology and vaccine coverage is correct?
options: HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers, and Gardasil 9 covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers, and Gardasil 9 covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers, HPV 6 + 11 cause 90% of genital warts, and Gardasil 9 (9-valent) now covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why was the whole-cell pertussis vaccine replaced by the acellular version?
options: The acellular version is live attenuated
The acellular version (5 purified protein components) replaced whole-cell due to side effects
The whole-cell version produced no immunity
The acellular version needs no doses
The whole-cell version was a toxoid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The acellular version (5 purified protein components) replaced whole-cell due to side effects
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The pertussis vaccine uses 5 purified protein components (acellular), which replaced the whole-cell vaccine due to side effects.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The rotavirus vaccine is given orally in the infant schedule. What type of vaccine is it, and why is it important?
options: Live attenuated, oral; rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea/hospitalisation in infants
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Live attenuated, oral; rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea/hospitalisation in infants
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The rotavirus vaccine is live attenuated and oral; rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea/hospitalisation in infants.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the central immunological problem in organ transplantation?
options: The donor immune system always attacks the recipient
The recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) and mounts a rejection response
The graft lacks any HLA molecules
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) and mounts a rejection response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The central problem is that the recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) → mounts a rejection response → graft damage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which HLA class is found on all nucleated cells and recognised by CD8+ T-cells?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MHC Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) is on all nucleated cells and recognised by CD8+ T-cells; MHC Class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) is on APCs/B-cells and recognised by CD4+ T-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the '6-antigen match', which HLA locus is the most significant to match?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The most important loci to match are HLA-A, -B, and -DR (the '6-antigen match'), and DR is the most significant.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: ABO incompatibility in transplantation leads to which type of rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: ABO incompatibility → hyperacute rejection, so ABO blood group must be compatible.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pre-transplant crossmatch tests recipient serum against donor lymphocytes. A positive crossmatch indicates what?
options: The transplant is safe to proceed
Pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies → risk of hyperacute rejection → contraindication
Chronic rejection is inevitable but treatable
The donor and recipient are ABO incompatible only
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies → risk of hyperacute rejection → contraindication
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The crossmatch detects pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies; a positive crossmatch means a risk of hyperacute rejection and is a contraindication.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In allorecognition, which pathway involves recipient T-cells recognising intact donor HLA on donor APCs, and what does it drive?
options: The direct pathway; acute rejection (early, vigorous)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The direct pathway; acute rejection (early, vigorous)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The direct pathway is where recipient T-cells recognise intact donor HLA on donor APCs → drives acute rejection (early, vigorous). The indirect pathway (recipient APCs process donor HLA) drives chronic rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A transplanted kidney becomes mottled and thrombosed within hours of reperfusion. Which rejection type is this, and what is the mechanism?
options: Hyperacute; pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Hyperacute; pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hyperacute rejection occurs in minutes–hours from pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis (Type II); it is irreversible, so the graft is removed, and it is prevented by crossmatch.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops rejection 3 months post-transplant that is T-cell-mediated with HLA mismatch. What is the type, hypersensitivity class, and typical outcome?
options: Acute; Type IV; often reversible with increased immunosuppression
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Acute; Type IV; often reversible with increased immunosuppression
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acute rejection occurs days–6 months, is T-cell-mediated (cellular) ± antibody with HLA mismatch, is Type IV, and is often reversible with increased immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Chronic rejection is characterised by which mechanism and outcome?
options: Antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy); largely irreversible → graft failure
Donor cells attacking the host; treatable
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy); largely irreversible → graft failure
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chronic rejection occurs over months–years, is antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy), is mixed hypersensitivity, and is largely irreversible → graft failure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which memory hook correctly links a rejection type to its mechanism?
options: Hyperacute = preformed antibodies (Type II, prevented by crossmatch)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Hyperacute = preformed antibodies (Type II, prevented by crossmatch)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The memory hook: hyperacute = preformed antibodies (Type II, prevented by crossmatch); acute = T-cells/HLA mismatch (Type IV, treatable); chronic = fibrosis (untreatable).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), what happens, and in which transplant setting?
options: The host rejects the graft; solid-organ transplant
The donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues; bone marrow/stem cell transplant
Pre-formed antibodies destroy the graft; kidney transplant
The graft becomes fibrotic; heart transplant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues; bone marrow/stem cell transplant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: GVHD is the opposite of rejection: in bone marrow/stem cell transplants, the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues (graft attacks host).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the classic triad of organs targeted in GVHD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The classic GVHD triad targets skin (rash), gut (diarrhoea), and liver (deranged LFTs/jaundice).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is GVHD prevented?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: GVHD is prevented by HLA matching + T-cell depletion; it is classified as acute (<100 days) vs chronic and managed with immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the general immunosuppression strategy after transplantation?
options: Induction (intense, peri-transplant) then maintenance (lifelong, lower-dose), usually triple therapy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Induction (intense, peri-transplant) then maintenance (lifelong, lower-dose), usually triple therapy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The strategy is induction (intense, peri-transplant) then maintenance (lifelong, lower-dose), usually as triple therapy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Tacrolimus and ciclosporin form the immunosuppression backbone. What is their mechanism and a key caution?
options: Block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation; nephrotoxic with a narrow therapeutic index requiring TDM
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation; nephrotoxic with a narrow therapeutic index requiring TDM
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, ciclosporin) block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation (the backbone); they are nephrotoxic with a narrow therapeutic index and need TDM.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Mycophenolate and azathioprine act by which mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antiproliferatives (mycophenolate, azathioprine) inhibit purine synthesis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Basiliximab (anti-IL-2R) and ATG are used for induction. What do they do?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Biologics used for induction — basiliximab (anti-IL-2R) and ATG — deplete/block T-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the standard maintenance immunosuppression regimen?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Standard maintenance is tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the first-line treatment for an episode of acute rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acute rejection is treated with high-dose steroids first-line ± antibody therapy; acute rejection is often reversible with increased immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A transplant patient on long-term immunosuppression is at risk of opportunistic infection. Which prophylaxis is given for PCP?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Immunosuppressed transplant patients have iatrogenic T-cell deficiency and are at risk of opportunistic infections (CMV, PCP, fungal, BK virus, TB/hepatitis reactivation); co-trimoxazole is used as PCP prophylaxis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which malignancy is EBV-driven and increased in transplant patients on immunosuppression?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Immunosuppression increases malignancy risk, including skin cancers (esp. SCC) and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD — EBV-driven).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which drug-specific complication is correctly matched?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, new-onset diabetes, hypertension, and tremor are associated with tacrolimus; gum hypertrophy/hirsutism is associated with ciclosporin, and marrow suppression with azathioprine.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Before starting azathioprine in a transplant patient, which test should be checked, and why?
options: TPMT, because of marrow suppression risk
ABO type, to prevent hyperacute rejection
HLA typing, to match the donor
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: TPMT, because of marrow suppression risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Azathioprine can cause marrow suppression, so TPMT is checked before starting it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Acute inflammation is best described as consisting of which two responses?
options: A humoral response and a cell-mediated response
A vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils)
A fibrotic response and a granulomatous response
An innate response and an adaptive response only
A systemic response and a wound-healing response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acute inflammation has a vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils to the site), driven by chemical mediators, producing the cardinal signs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which cardinal sign of inflammation is caused by increased vascular permeability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Swelling (tumor) is caused by increased vascular permeability → fluid leaks into tissue (exudate). Redness and heat are from increased blood flow, and pain is from mediators.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mediators sensitise nerves to produce the pain (dolor) of inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Pain (dolor) results from mediators — bradykinin and prostaglandins — sensitising nerves.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Vasodilation in the vascular response is mediated by which of the following?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Vasodilation → ↑blood flow to the area → redness + heat, mediated by histamine, prostaglandins, and NO.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What distinguishes an inflammatory exudate from a simple transudate?
options: The exudate is protein-rich, carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen
The transudate forms fibrin to wall off the area
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The exudate is protein-rich, carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Inflammatory exudate is protein-rich, carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen (which forms fibrin to wall off the area) — this distinguishes it from a simple transudate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the correct order of the cellular response (neutrophil recruitment)?
options: Margination → rolling + adhesion → diapedesis → chemotaxis → phagocytosis
Margination → diapedesis → rolling + adhesion → phagocytosis → chemotaxis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Margination → rolling + adhesion → diapedesis → chemotaxis → phagocytosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The sequence is margination → rolling + adhesion (selectins → integrins) → diapedesis/transmigration → chemotaxis (following gradients — chemokines, C5a) → phagocytosis (aided by opsonisation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: During rolling and adhesion, neutrophils bind the endothelium via which molecules?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In rolling + adhesion, neutrophils bind the endothelium via selectins → integrins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why does the FBC classically show neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection?
options: Macrophages arrive first in acute inflammation
Neutrophils arrive first in acute inflammation, with macrophages later
Neutrophils only appear in chronic inflammation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Neutrophils arrive first in acute inflammation, with macrophages later
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Neutrophils arrive first (acute inflammation), then macrophages later (clean-up + chronic) — which is why the FBC shows neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is opsonisation, and why does it matter?
options: Coating the pathogen with antibody/complement to make phagocytosis far more efficient
Neutrophils squeezing through the vessel wall
Slowed blood flow letting leucocytes marginate
Endothelial cells contracting to form gaps
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Coating the pathogen with antibody/complement to make phagocytosis far more efficient
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Opsonisation is coating the pathogen with antibody/complement, which makes phagocytosis far more efficient ('opsonins' = 'to prepare for eating').

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mediator is released by mast cells and blocked by antihistamines?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Histamine is released by mast cells and causes early vasodilation + ↑permeability; antihistamines block it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: NSAIDs exert their anti-inflammatory effect by inhibiting the production of which mediator, via which enzyme?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid via COX and cause vasodilation, pain, and fever; NSAIDs block COX → ↓prostaglandins → anti-inflammatory + analgesic + antipyretic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Leukotrienes are derived from arachidonic acid via which enzyme, and what is a key action?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Leukotrienes are made from arachidonic acid via lipoxygenase and cause bronchoconstriction and ↑permeability; leukotriene antagonists are used in asthma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mediators are produced by macrophages and act as biologic drug targets in the systemic response?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) are produced by macrophages and drive the systemic response (fever, acute-phase proteins); TNF/IL-6 are biologic drug targets.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do steroids act as the most powerful anti-inflammatories?
options: By broadly suppressing inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: By broadly suppressing inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Steroids broadly suppress inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway) — making them the most powerful anti-inflammatories.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Biologics such as anti-TNF and anti-IL-6 agents are used in which conditions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) block specific cytokines and are used in rheumatoid arthritis and IBD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does fever arise in the systemic inflammatory response?
options: Cytokines act on the hypothalamus to raise the temperature set point
The liver raises body temperature via CRP
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Cytokines act on the hypothalamus to raise the temperature set point
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fever occurs when cytokines act on the hypothalamus → ↑temperature set point.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which acute-phase protein is the clinical inflammatory marker, and what drives its production?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The liver produces CRP, fibrinogen, and ferritin (IL-6-driven); CRP is the clinical inflammatory marker.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do CRP and ESR compare as inflammatory markers?
options: CRP is slower and fibrinogen-related; ESR rises fast and is IL-6-driven
CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven); ESR is slower and fibrinogen-related
Both rise at exactly the same rate
CRP measures red cells; ESR measures protein
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven); ESR is slower and fibrinogen-related
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven) and ESR is slower (fibrinogen-related); both are clinical markers used to detect and monitor inflammatory/infective disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An overwhelming, dysregulated systemic inflammatory response to infection leading to organ dysfunction is described as:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The extreme of the systemic response is an overwhelming systemic inflammatory response → SIRS → sepsis (a dysregulated response to infection → organ dysfunction).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A localised collection of pus composed of dead neutrophils and debris is which outcome of acute inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An abscess is a localised collection of pus (dead neutrophils + debris) — one of the outcomes of acute inflammation, alongside resolution, chronic inflammation, and fibrosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which cells predominantly drive chronic inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chronic inflammation is macrophage + lymphocyte-driven (not neutrophils), with simultaneous tissue destruction + repair (fibrosis). The acute-vs-chronic cell distinction is: acute = neutrophils; chronic = macrophages + lymphocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Granuloma formation (organised macrophages) is characteristically seen in which conditions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chronic inflammation often involves granuloma formation (organised macrophages) — seen in TB, sarcoid, and Crohn's; chronic inflammation also underlies rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, and atherosclerosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What are the three phases of wound healing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Wound healing proceeds through inflammation → proliferation → remodelling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: By definition, when is an infection classified as healthcare-associated (an HCAI)?
options: When it is present on admission
When it is acquired ≥48h after admission and was not incubating on arrival
When it occurs within 24h of discharge
When it is caused by a resistant organism
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: When it is acquired ≥48h after admission and was not incubating on arrival
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HCAIs (healthcare-associated/nosocomial infections) are acquired ≥48h after admission and not incubating on arrival.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: According to the organising principle, what is the single most effective infection-control intervention?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Every infection follows the chain of infection, and breaking any single link prevents transmission; the single most effective intervention is hand hygiene.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the chain of infection, which measure breaks the 'mode of transmission' link?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The mode of transmission (contact/droplet/airborne/vehicle) is broken by hand hygiene, PPE, and isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Breaking which link of the chain of infection involves vaccination, treating comorbidity, and nutrition?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The susceptible host (the patient at risk) link is addressed by vaccination, treating comorbidity, and nutrition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Measles, TB, and varicella spread by which transmission route?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Airborne transmission involves small particles that stay suspended — TB, measles, and varicella.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: MRSA and C. difficile are chiefly spread by which route?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Contact transmission (direct/indirect) includes MRSA and C. diff.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A nurse is about to perform a clean/aseptic procedure. Which of the WHO '5 Moments for Hand Hygiene' does this represent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The WHO 5 Moments are: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has C. difficile infection. Which hand-hygiene method must be used, and why?
options: Alcohol gel, because it is faster
Soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill spores
Alcohol gel followed by gloves only
No hand hygiene is needed with gloves
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill spores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The classic exam point: alcohol gel is used for most situations, but soap and water (not alcohol gel) is needed for spore-forming organisms — C. difficile and norovirus — because alcohol doesn't kill spores.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with pulmonary TB requires isolation. Which precaution and room are needed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Airborne precautions (for TB, measles, varicella) require an N95/FFP3 respirator and a negative-pressure room; TB in fact needs airborne + contact + standard precautions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with influenza is admitted. Which transmission-based precautions apply?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Droplet precautions (for influenza, COVID-19, pertussis, meningococcus) require a surgical mask and single room.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which combination of precautions is required for a patient with C. difficile?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. diff needs contact + standard precautions; TB needs airborne + contact + standard.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which HCAI is antibiotic-associated and spore-forming, and how is it prevented?
options: C. difficile; stewardship, isolation, soap & water, oral vancomycin to treat
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: C. difficile; stewardship, isolation, soap & water, oral vancomycin to treat
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. difficile is antibiotic-associated (clindamycin/cephalosporins/fluoroquinolones) and spore-forming; prevention is stewardship, isolation, soap & water, with oral vancomycin to treat.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is MRSA prevented as an HCAI?
options: Contact precautions, screening + decolonisation (chlorhexidine wash, nasal mupirocin)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Contact precautions, screening + decolonisation (chlorhexidine wash, nasal mupirocin)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA (colonisation → infection; lines/wounds) is prevented with contact precautions and screening + decolonisation using chlorhexidine wash and nasal mupirocin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the key prevention strategy for catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)?
options: Prophylactic antibiotics for all catheterised patients
Avoid/remove catheters early and use aseptic insertion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Avoid/remove catheters early and use aseptic insertion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CAUTI (associated with urinary catheters) is prevented by avoiding/removing catheters early and using aseptic insertion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which measures are key to preventing central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)?
options: Insertion care bundles, aseptic technique, and early removal
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Insertion care bundles, aseptic technique, and early removal
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CLABSI (associated with central venous catheters) is prevented with insertion care bundles, aseptic technique, and early removal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set of measures reduces surgical site infection (SSI)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: SSI (associated with surgery) is reduced by prophylactic antibiotics, skin prep, and normothermia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Norovirus causes ward and cruise-ship outbreaks. Which prevention measures are appropriate?
options: Soap & water, ward closure, and isolation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Soap & water, ward closure, and isolation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Norovirus (faecal-oral, outbreaks on wards/cruises) is managed with soap & water, ward closure, and isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: MRSA is resistant to β-lactams by which mechanism, and how are patients screened on admission?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA is Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams via altered PBP2a; patients are screened on admission with a nasal/groin swab, then decolonised (mupirocin + chlorhexidine).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What are the '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics for C. difficile?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics for C. difficile are clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, and ciprofloxacin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the current first-line management of C. difficile infection?
options: Isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin, and stop the offending antibiotic (metronidazole no longer first-line)
Alcohol gel and continue the antibiotic
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin, and stop the offending antibiotic (metronidazole no longer first-line)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. diff management is isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin (metronidazole is no longer first-line), plus stopping the offending antibiotic. Antibiotic use → loss of gut flora → toxin-producing C. diff overgrowth → pseudomembranous colitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is antimicrobial stewardship considered a core part of infection control?
options: It replaces the need for hand hygiene
It prevents C. diff and resistance
It eliminates the need for isolation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It prevents C. diff and resistance
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antimicrobial stewardship is core infection control because it prevents C. diff and resistance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which sequence correctly describes outbreak management at the organisational level?
options: Identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, and involve the IPC team
Vaccinate staff, then close the hospital
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, and involve the IPC team
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Outbreak management involves identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, and involve the IPC (infection prevention and control) team.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is part of the standard precautions applied to every patient, always?
options: Sharps safety with no re-sheathing and use of sharps bins
Nasal mupirocin decolonisation for all patients
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Sharps safety with no re-sheathing and use of sharps bins
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Standard precautions (applied to every patient always) include hand hygiene, PPE, sharps safety (no re-sheathing; sharps bins), respiratory hygiene, safe waste/linen disposal, cleaning + decontamination, and aseptic technique.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the single organising principle when approaching immunodeficiency?
options: The severity of infection predicts the organism
The deficient component predicts the infection pattern — work out which arm has failed and you predict the bug
Age of onset determines the causative organism regardless of the arm
Only primary immunodeficiencies follow predictable patterns
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The deficient component predicts the infection pattern — work out which arm has failed and you predict the bug
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The single organising principle is that the deficient component predicts the infection pattern — work out which arm has failed, and you predict the bug.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is the correct top-level fork of immunodeficiency, and which is commoner?
options: Primary (genetic/intrinsic) vs secondary (acquired); secondary far commoner
Primary vs secondary; primary far commoner
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Primary (genetic/intrinsic) vs secondary (acquired); secondary far commoner
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The top-level fork is primary (genetic/intrinsic) vs secondary (acquired), and secondary is far commoner.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) and recurrent sinopulmonary infections after 6 months of age. Which arm is deficient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Humoral (B-cell/antibody) deficiency causes infections with encapsulated bacteria ('SHiN'), with the clue of recurrent sinopulmonary infections after 6 months of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A child presents with recurrent abscesses and osteomyelitis from Staph aureus and Aspergillus. Which immune arm is most likely deficient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Phagocyte deficiency causes infections with catalase-positive bacteria (Staph aureus) and fungi (Aspergillus), with the clue of abscesses and osteomyelitis in childhood.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has recurrent meningococcal disease. Which immune arm should be tested?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Complement deficiency (terminal C5–9/MAC) causes recurrent Neisseria, since the membrane attack complex is the only thing that kills Neisseria; the clue is recurrent meningococcaemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the single most common cause of secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Malnutrition is the most common cause of secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency worldwide; HIV is the most common infectious cause. Other causes include drugs, malignancy, protein loss (nephrotic syndrome), asplenia, diabetes and extremes of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Using the MHC 'Rule of 8', which cells recognise MHC class II, and what is the relationship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Rule of 8: Class II (HLA-DQ/DR/DP, on APCs + B-cells) is recognised by CD4 (CD4 × MHC II = 8); Class I is recognised by CD8 (CD8 × MHC I = 8).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which complement components function as anaphylatoxins causing mast cell degranulation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C3/4/5a are anaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation); C3b is opsonisation, C5a is neutrophil chemotaxis, and C5–9 is the membrane attack complex (kills Neisseria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A boy develops recurrent URTIs/LRTIs with encapsulated organisms starting after 6 months of age. Investigations show absent B-cells and absent antibodies. What is the diagnosis and its genetic defect?
options: Selective IgA deficiency; IgA gene deletion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: X-Linked Agammaglobulinaemia (XLA/Bruton's) is a BTK mutation → absent B-cells + absent antibodies; it presents after 6 months as maternal IgG wanes, with recurrent URTI/LRTI from encapsulated organisms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does CVID differ from XLA, and what are its associated risks?
options: It has absent antibodies and presents in infancy
It is less severe (low rather than absent antibodies), affects adults, and increases the risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma
It only affects IgA and is usually asymptomatic
It causes hypocalcaemia and cardiac defects
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It is less severe (low rather than absent antibodies), affects adults, and increases the risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CVID is like XLA but less severe (low rather than absent antibodies), affects adults, and carries an increased risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the most common primary immunodeficiency, and what transfusion precaution does it require?
options: Selective IgA deficiency; risk of anaphylaxis to blood products, so give washed/IgA-deficient products
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Selective IgA deficiency; risk of anaphylaxis to blood products, so give washed/IgA-deficient products
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency; it carries a risk of anaphylaxis to blood products, so washed/IgA-deficient products should be given if transfusing.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neonate presents with tetany/hypocalcaemia at birth and a conotruncal cardiac defect. Which syndrome should you think of, and what is its mechanism?
options: SCID; failure of B and T cells
DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion); loss of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal arch → thymic aplasia + hypoparathyroidism
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion); loss of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal arch → thymic aplasia + hypoparathyroidism
