options: From high solute (low water) to low solute (high water)
From low solute (high water) to high solute (low water)
Always into the cell regardless of solute
Always out of the cell regardless of solute
It does not move without active transport
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: From low solute (high water) to high solute (low water)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Osmosis is water moving from low solute (high water) to high solute (low water) concentration — water follows solute.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the normal plasma osmolality, and what particles mainly contribute to it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Osmolality is the concentration of osmotically active particles (mainly Na⁺, glucose, urea in the ECF); normal is about 285–295 mOsm/kg.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is tonicity best defined?
options: The total number of particles in a solution
The effective osmolality — how a solution affects cell volume
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The effective osmolality — how a solution affects cell volume
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Tonicity is the effective osmolality — how a solution affects cell volume — and is the clinically useful concept.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A hypotonic solution is administered. What happens to the cells?
options: No net water movement; cells stay the same
Water moves out of cells; cells shrink
Water moves into cells; cells swell and may lyse
Sodium moves into cells; cells depolarise
Cells become dehydrated but do not change size
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Water moves into cells; cells swell and may lyse
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: With a hypotonic solution, water moves into cells → cells swell (can lyse) — e.g. giving too much free water.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which solution causes no net water movement, leaving cell volume unchanged?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An isotonic solution such as 0.9% saline causes no net water movement, so cells stay the same.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is urea described as an ineffective osmole whereas glucose is an effective one?
options: Urea is larger than glucose, so it can't move water
Urea crosses membranes freely so it doesn't shift water, whereas glucose does shift water
Urea is confined to cells and glucose to plasma
Glucose crosses membranes freely and urea does not
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Urea crosses membranes freely so it doesn't shift water, whereas glucose does shift water
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Urea crosses membranes freely so it's an ineffective osmole (doesn't shift water); Na⁺ and glucose are effective osmoles that do shift water — which is why hyperglycaemia causes hyponatraemia by pulling water out of cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops acute hyponatraemia. What is the dangerous consequence and its mechanism?
options: Cells shrink due to raised ECF osmolality
Water moves into cells due to low ECF osmolality → cerebral oedema
Water leaves cells → dehydration of neurons
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Water moves into cells due to low ECF osmolality → cerebral oedema
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hyponatraemia (low ECF osmolality) causes water to move into cells → cellular swelling, which is dangerous in the brain (cerebral oedema); hypernatraemia causes cells to shrink.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A litre of 0.9% saline (isotonic crystalloid) is given for resuscitation. Where does it distribute?
options: Across all compartments, mostly into cells
It stays in the ECF (¼ intravascular, ¾ interstitial)
It is confined to the interstitium only
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It stays in the ECF (¼ intravascular, ¾ interstitial)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: 0.9% saline / Hartmann's (isotonic crystalloid) stays in the ECF — about ¼ intravascular and ¾ interstitial — and is used for volume resuscitation and replacement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is 5% dextrose a poor choice for volume resuscitation?
options: It stays entirely intravascular and overloads the circulation
The glucose is metabolised, leaving free water that distributes across all compartments (mostly into cells), so little stays intravascular
It is hypertonic and shrinks cells
It cannot cross the capillary wall
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The glucose is metabolised, leaving free water that distributes across all compartments (mostly into cells), so little stays intravascular
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In 5% dextrose the glucose is metabolised → free water → distributes across all compartments (mostly into cells); it is a poor volume expander and giving too much causes hyponatraemia/cellular swelling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which IV fluid characteristically stays intravascular because it contains large molecules?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Colloids/albumin stay intravascular because they are large molecules, and have limited use for plasma volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with heart failure develops peripheral oedema. Which mechanism of excess interstitial fluid does this represent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Oedema is excess interstitial fluid from ↑hydrostatic pressure (heart failure), ↓oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia), ↑permeability (sepsis), or lymphatic block — a Starling-force imbalance. Heart failure raises hydrostatic pressure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Fluid shifting into a non-functional compartment, such as bowel in obstruction or ascites, is termed:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Third-spacing is fluid shifting into a non-functional compartment (e.g. bowel in obstruction, ascites).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: When correcting hyponatraemia, why must it be done slowly?
options: Because rapid correction causes cerebral oedema
Because correcting too fast risks osmotic demyelination
Because sodium cannot be given intravenously
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because correcting too fast risks osmotic demyelination
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hyponatraemia lowers osmolality → cellular swelling → cerebral oedema, but it must be corrected slowly because correcting too fast risks osmotic demyelination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with marked hyperglycaemia is found to have a low measured sodium. What is the mechanism?
options: Glucose is an ineffective osmole and has no effect on sodium
Glucose, an effective osmole, pulls water out of cells → dilutional hyponatraemia
Hyperglycaemia raises ECF osmolality and shrinks the sodium pool
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Glucose, an effective osmole, pulls water out of cells → dilutional hyponatraemia
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Glucose is an effective osmole that pulls water out of cells → dilutional hyponatraemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following best defines homeostasis?
options: The amplification of a change to drive a process to completion
The maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes
The permanent resetting of the body's set points
The anticipation of a change before it occurs
The breakdown of regulatory control in disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes — the fundamental organising principle of all physiology.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: According to the organising principle, which three components make up a negative feedback control system?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The body uses negative feedback control systems made of a sensor, a control centre, and an effector to keep regulated variables within narrow ranges.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which system is responsible for regulating osmolality/water in the body?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Osmolality/water is regulated by ADH + thirst. Blood pressure/volume is regulated by baroreceptors + RAAS, pH by lungs + kidneys, glucose by insulin/glucagon, and O₂/CO₂ by respiratory control.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Blood pressure and volume are regulated by which of the following?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Blood pressure/volume is regulated by baroreceptors + RAAS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is meant by a 'set point' in homeostasis?
options: The maximum tolerable value before cell death
The target value that the control system corrects deviations toward
The point at which positive feedback begins
The threshold for an action potential
The concentration at which a hormone is inactive
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The target value that the control system corrects deviations toward
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Each regulated variable has a set point (the target value) and a control system that corrects deviations.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement correctly describes negative feedback?
options: The response reinforces the change, amplifying it
The response opposes the change, pulling the variable back toward the set point
The response anticipates the change before it happens
The response permanently raises the set point
The response has no effect on the stimulus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The response opposes the change, pulling the variable back toward the set point
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In negative feedback the response opposes the change, pulling the variable back toward the set point; almost all homeostasis works this way.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In thermoregulation, which structure acts as the control centre of the feedback loop?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The control centre compares to the set point and coordinates the response — in temperature regulation this is the hypothalamus. Thermoreceptors are the sensor, and sweating/shivering and vasodilation/constriction are the effector responses.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A rise in blood glucose is sensed by β-cells, which release insulin, causing cells to take up glucose so that glucose falls. This illustrates:
options: Negative feedback returning the variable toward its set point
A reset of the glucose set point
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Negative feedback returning the variable toward its set point
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: This is the same negative-feedback logic seen everywhere: ↑blood glucose → sensor (β-cells) → insulin → effector (cells take up glucose) → glucose falls.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does positive feedback differ from negative feedback in its purpose?
options: It maintains stability around a set point
It amplifies the change to drive a process rapidly to completion
It anticipates changes before they occur
It switches the response off once the deviation is detected
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It amplifies the change to drive a process rapidly to completion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies the change (the response reinforces the stimulus) — not for maintaining stability, but for driving a process rapidly to completion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a classic example of a positive-feedback loop?
options: Baroreceptors reducing sympathetic tone when BP rises
ADH conserving water when osmolality rises
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The LH surge → ovulation is a positive-feedback loop: oestrogen peak → ↑LH → more oestrogen → ovulation. The other options are negative-feedback systems.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: During labour, uterine contractions drive increasing oxytocin release, producing stronger contractions until delivery. This is an example of:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Labour is a positive-feedback loop: contractions → ↑oxytocin → stronger contractions → delivery.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The action potential upstroke — depolarisation opening Na⁺ channels causing more depolarisation — is an example of which control mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The AP upstroke is a positive-feedback loop: depolarisation → opens Na⁺ channels → more depolarisation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Seeing food triggers acid and insulin release before eating (the cephalic phase of digestion). Which type of control does this represent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Feedforward control is where the body anticipates a change before it happens (e.g. the cephalic phase of digestion, the anticipatory rise in heart rate before exercise), preparing in advance rather than just correcting after.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why does a patient shiver during a fever despite already being hot?
options: Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic temperature set point higher, so the body defends the new higher temperature
Positive feedback is amplifying the temperature indefinitely
The effector response is inappropriate and random
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic temperature set point higher, so the body defends the new higher temperature
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In fever, infection resets the hypothalamic temperature set point higher (via pyrogens), so the body actively defends the new higher temperature — which is why you shiver.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Under the concept 'disease as failure of homeostasis', which homeostatic failure corresponds to diabetes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Diabetes represents a failure of glucose homeostasis. Hypertension is dysregulated BP control, acid-base disorders are failure of pH regulation, and fluid/electrolyte disorders are failure of osmotic/volume/ion regulation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In heart failure, RAAS activation (a normal response to low perfusion) causes fluid retention that worsens the failure. This is best described as:
options: Maladaptive compensation — a homeostatic loop turned pathological
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Maladaptive compensation — a homeostatic loop turned pathological
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: This is the maladaptive-compensation point: sometimes the homeostatic response itself becomes harmful — in heart failure, RAAS activation causes fluid retention that worsens the failure, a homeostatic loop turned pathological.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which homeostatic failure underlies acid-base disorders?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acid-base disorders represent a failure of pH regulation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does drug logic relate to homeostasis, according to the note?
options: Many drugs support or replace a failed homeostatic mechanism, e.g. insulin, antihypertensives
Drugs reset every set point permanently
Drugs act only through feedforward control
Drugs have no relationship to homeostatic mechanisms
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Many drugs support or replace a failed homeostatic mechanism, e.g. insulin, antihypertensives
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Many drugs support or replace a failed homeostatic mechanism — for example, insulin and antihypertensives.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following correctly matches a regulated variable with its controlling system?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺) are regulated by kidneys + hormones (electrolyte handling, calcium homeostasis). pH is controlled by lungs + kidneys, temperature by the hypothalamus, O₂/CO₂ by respiratory control, and glucose by insulin/glucagon.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the negative-feedback logic, what happens once the variable returns toward normal?
options: The set point is reset higher
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In negative feedback, a deviation is detected → a response opposes/reverses it → the variable returns toward normal → the response switches off. The response counteracts the stimulus, hence 'negative'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Blood clotting, in which activated factors activate more factors in a cascade, is an example of which control mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Blood clotting is a positive-feedback example: activated factors activate more factors (the cascade).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The central dogma describes the flow of genetic information. Which sequence is correct?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma): DNA is transcribed to mRNA in the nucleus, and mRNA is translated to protein at the ribosome using codons.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: During which step of the central dogma is mRNA converted into protein, and where does it occur?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Translation is mRNA → protein at the ribosome, using the genetic code (codons). Transcription (DNA → mRNA) occurs in the nucleus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How many chromosomes do humans have, and how are they arranged?
options: 44 autosomes only, with no sex chromosomes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs): 22 autosomal pairs + 1 sex pair (XX female, XY male), with one of each pair from each parent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A person is heterozygous for a recessive condition. Which term best describes them?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Heterozygous means two different alleles — a 'carrier' if the condition is recessive, since a recessive trait is expressed only with two copies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A condition affects every generation, is transmitted vertically, affects both sexes, and carries a 50% risk to offspring. Which inheritance pattern is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Autosomal dominant: one copy → affected; 50% risk to offspring; affects every generation (vertical transmission); both sexes; often later-onset — e.g. Huntington's, ADPKD, Marfan's.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, and thalassaemia are classic examples of which inheritance pattern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia and most metabolic disorders are autosomal recessive: two copies needed, carriers unaffected, 25% risk if both parents are carriers; can skip generations, with consanguinity increasing risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Two unaffected parents who are both carriers of an autosomal recessive condition have a child. What is the risk that the child is affected?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In autosomal recessive inheritance, two copies are needed and carriers are unaffected; the risk is 25% if both parents are carriers.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which feature is characteristic of X-linked recessive inheritance?
options: Females are usually affected and males are carriers
No male-to-male transmission; affects mostly males, with females usually carriers
Inherited only from the mother's mitochondria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: No male-to-male transmission; affects mostly males, with females usually carriers
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: X-linked recessive: the gene is on the X, so males are affected (only one X) and females are usually carriers; there is no male-to-male transmission and it affects mostly males — e.g. haemophilia A/B, DMD, G6PD deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A boy has haemophilia. His unaffected mother carries the gene. This pattern of mostly-affected males with no father-to-son transmission indicates which mode of inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive: males affected (only one X), females usually carriers, and no male-to-male transmission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A condition is passed only from an affected mother to all of her children, and affected fathers never pass it on. Which inheritance pattern is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mitochondrial inheritance is only from the mother (mitochondria come from the egg); it affects both sexes, all her children can be affected, and affected fathers don't pass it on — e.g. mitochondrial myopathies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In X-linked dominant inheritance, what is the key feature regarding an affected male's children?
options: None of his children are affected
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: X-linked dominant: one copy on the X is enough, and an affected male's daughters are all affected.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Sickle cell disease results from a single base change producing a single amino acid change in β-globin. What type of mutation is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A point mutation is a single-base change — sickle cell is the classic example (a single base → a single amino acid change in β-globin → an abnormal protein).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An insertion or deletion of bases that shifts the reading frame and causes major disruption is called a:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A frameshift mutation is an insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame, causing major disruption.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Huntington's disease appears earlier and more severely in successive generations. What is this phenomenon called, and what causes it?
options: Penetrance — not everyone with the gene is affected
Anticipation — the trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expands each generation
Expressivity — variable severity from the same genotype
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Anticipation — the trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expands each generation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In trinucleotide repeat disorders such as Huntington's (CAG), the repeat expands each generation → the disease appears earlier and more severe in successive generations — this is anticipation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner's (45,X), and Klinefelter's (47,XXY) are examples of which type of mutation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner's (45,X), and Klinefelter's (47,XXY) are chromosomal mutations — whole-chromosome abnormalities.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Not everyone who carries a particular disease gene actually shows the trait. This concept is called:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Penetrance is the proportion with the genotype who show the phenotype; incomplete penetrance means not everyone with the gene is affected. (Expressivity refers to how severely the phenotype shows.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The ABO blood group system, in which both alleles are expressed, is an example of:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Codominance is where both alleles are expressed — e.g. ABO blood groups.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Diabetes and hypertension, which arise from many genes plus environment rather than a single gene, are best described as:
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Polygenic/multifactorial inheritance involves many genes plus environment (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, most common diseases) and is not simple Mendelian.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Genetic variation in drug handling, such as fast/slow acetylators and CYP polymorphisms, falls under which concept?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Pharmacogenomics is genetic variation in drug handling — e.g. fast/slow acetylators, CYP polymorphisms (cross-ref drug biotransformation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mutation type is specifically associated with the phenomenon of anticipation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Trinucleotide repeat expansions (e.g. Huntington's CAG, fragile X, Friedreich's ataxia) show anticipation — the disease worsens and appears earlier each generation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does recognising a condition's inheritance pattern help in genetic counselling?
options: It identifies the causative point mutation
It predicts recurrence risk and which relatives are affected
It confirms the diagnosis without testing
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It predicts recurrence risk and which relatives are affected
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Recognising the inheritance pattern predicts recurrence risk and which relatives are affected — the basis of genetic counselling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about autosomal recessive inheritance is correct?
options: It can skip generations, and consanguinity increases the risk
It is inherited only from the mother
One copy is sufficient to be affected
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It can skip generations, and consanguinity increases the risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Autosomal recessive inheritance can skip generations (carriers are unaffected) and consanguinity increases risk; two copies are needed to be affected.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do innate and adaptive immunity fundamentally differ?
options: Innate is specific with memory; adaptive is non-specific without memory
Innate is non-specific, immediate and has no memory; adaptive is specific, slower first time and has memory
Innate is acquired; adaptive is inborn
Adaptive is immediate; innate is slow
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Innate is non-specific, immediate and has no memory; adaptive is specific, slower first time and has memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Innate immunity is inborn, non-specific, immediate and has no memory, whereas adaptive immunity is acquired, specific, slower on first exposure and has memory (the basis of vaccination).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the defining trade-off between active and passive immunity?
options: Active = immediate but short-lived; passive = slow but long-lasting
Active = slow onset but long-lasting (memory); passive = immediate but short-lived (no memory)
Active has no memory; passive has memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Active = slow onset but long-lasting (memory); passive = immediate but short-lived (no memory)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The defining trade-off is that active immunity is slow in onset but long-lasting (memory), whereas passive immunity is immediate but short-lived (no memory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which immune arm has memory, and what does this underpin?
options: Adaptive immunity; the basis of vaccination
Innate immunity; the basis of vaccination
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Adaptive immunity; the basis of vaccination
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Adaptive immunity has memory (innate does not), which is the basis of vaccination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient is given pre-formed antibodies after a high-risk exposure. Which type of immunity is this, and what is its onset and durability?
options: Passive immunity; immediate onset, short-lived with no memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Passive immunity; immediate onset, short-lived with no memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giving pre-formed antibodies is passive immunity, which is immediate but short-lived (antibodies degrade) with no memory.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: When is passive immunity the appropriate choice?
options: When long-term durable protection is the priority
When you need protection NOW and there's no time to mount an active response
When the patient needs immune memory
When vaccination is contraindicated by cost only
When the patient has no risk of exposure
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: When you need protection NOW and there's no time to mount an active response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Active is slow but durable; passive is instant but temporary, so passive is used when protection is needed NOW and there's no time to mount an active response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the natural/artificial × active/passive 2×2, which is an example of NATURAL PASSIVE immunity?
options: Placental transfer of IgG to the fetus and breast-milk IgA to the neonate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Placental transfer of IgG to the fetus and breast-milk IgA to the neonate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Natural passive immunity is placental transfer of IgG to the fetus and breast-milk IgA to the neonate; vaccination is artificial active, and immunoglobulin/antivenom is artificial passive.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is an example of ARTIFICIAL ACTIVE immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Artificial active immunity is vaccination; artificial passive immunity is immunoglobulin administration (anti-tetanus, anti-rabies, hepatitis B Ig, anti-D, antivenom, monoclonal antibodies).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does a live attenuated vaccine differ from a killed/inactivated vaccine in the immunity it produces?
options: Live produces IgG only; killed produces IgA + IgG
Live gives better cell-mediated immunity and produces IgA + IgG; killed produces IgG only
Live produces no antibodies; killed produces all classes
Killed gives better cell-mediated immunity than live
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Live gives better cell-mediated immunity and produces IgA + IgG; killed produces IgG only
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines give better cell-mediated immunity and produce IgA + IgG, whereas killed/inactivated vaccines produce IgG only.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pregnant woman is due a vaccine. Which vaccine type should be avoided, and why?
options: Live attenuated, because it may cause mild disease and should be avoided in immunocompromise/pregnancy
Both types are contraindicated in pregnancy
Killed/inactivated, because it gives IgG only
Neither — all vaccines are safe in pregnancy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Live attenuated, because it may cause mild disease and should be avoided in immunocompromise/pregnancy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines may cause mild disease and should be avoided in immunocompromised patients and pregnancy; killed/inactivated vaccines are safe in immunocompromise.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines include MMR, BCG, oral rotavirus and varicella; hepatitis B, polio (IPV) and pertussis are killed/inactivated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about killed/inactivated vaccines is correct?
options: They are often single dose with no adjuvant
They need an adjuvant + boosters and are safe in the immunocompromised
They produce IgA + IgG and better cell-mediated immunity
They are contraindicated in the immunocompromised
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They need an adjuvant + boosters and are safe in the immunocompromised
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Killed/inactivated vaccines need an adjuvant plus boosters, produce IgG only, and are safe in the immunocompromised.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the principle and the key limitation of passive immunity?
options: It gives durable protection with memory; limitation is slow onset
It gives instant protection as a bridge; limitation is that it wears off as antibodies degrade with no memory, so it doesn't protect against future exposures
It generates memory cells; limitation is cost
It is only natural; limitation is that it cannot be given artificially
It is permanent; limitation is mild disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It gives instant protection as a bridge; limitation is that it wears off as antibodies degrade with no memory, so it doesn't protect against future exposures
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Passive immunity gives instant protection as a bridge (not a long-term solution); its limitation is that it wears off as antibodies degrade, with no memory, so it doesn't protect against future exposures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which immunoglobulin is the only one that crosses the placenta, and what is its clinical relevance?
options: IgG; provides natural passive immunity to the neonate and indicates past infection
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: IgG; provides natural passive immunity to the neonate and indicates past infection
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin and the only one that crosses the placenta, providing natural passive immunity to the neonate; it is the main secondary-response antibody and indicates past infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with recurrent GI and respiratory infections, including Giardia, is found to be deficient in which immunoglobulin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IgA provides mucosal defence and natural passive immunity via breast milk; IgA deficiency leads to GI/respiratory infections such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Serology shows a raised IgM against a pathogen. What does this indicate, and how does it contrast with IgG?
options: Chronic infection only; IgG = mucosal defence
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IgM is the largest (pentamer), the first antibody in the primary response and can't cross the placenta; it marks acute/recent (current) infection, whereas IgG indicates past infection — the IgM-vs-IgG recent-vs-past distinction.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which immunoglobulin binds mast cells/basophils and mediates type I hypersensitivity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IgE binds mast cells/basophils and mediates type I hypersensitivity (allergy), anaphylaxis and parasite responses.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: IgG deficiency predisposes particularly to infection with which group of organisms?
options: Encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IgG deficiency predisposes to encapsulated bacteria such as H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which interleukin acts as an endogenous pyrogen causing fever?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IL-1 is an endogenous pyrogen that causes fever; IL-6 also drives fever and the acute-phase response (CRP).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which interleukin drives the acute-phase response and CRP?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IL-6 drives the acute-phase response and fever, including CRP; IL-2 causes T-cell proliferation and IL-8 mediates neutrophil chemotaxis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which interleukin is responsible for neutrophil chemotaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IL-8 mediates neutrophil chemotaxis; the grouping logic is fever (1, 6), recruit/activate a specific cell (2→T-cells, 5→eosinophils, 8→neutrophils), drive allergy (4, 5) and switch off (10).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which interleukin is anti-inflammatory, inhibiting the Th1/inflammatory response?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IL-10 inhibits the Th1/inflammatory response and is anti-inflammatory — the 'switch off' interleukin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do Th1 and Th2 responses differ?
options: Th1 drives allergy; Th2 drives fever
Th1 = IgE class switch; Th2 = neutrophil chemotaxis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Th1 responses are cell-mediated (IL-12 → IFN-γ), whereas Th2 responses are humoral (IL-4).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What does antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) describe?
options: A clinical condition caused by antibiotic overuse
The coordinated effort to promote and monitor the responsible use of antimicrobials to preserve their future effectiveness
The treatment of resistant infections with last-line agents
A laboratory technique for detecting resistance
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The coordinated effort to promote and monitor the responsible use of antimicrobials to preserve their future effectiveness
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: AMS is the coordinated effort to promote and monitor the responsible use of antimicrobials to preserve their future effectiveness — a public-health and patient-safety strategy, not a clinical condition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the driving problem that AMS addresses, and its projected scale?
options: Drug fever — projected to double by 2050
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — a global threat projected to cause ~10 million deaths/year by 2050, driven substantially by inappropriate antibiotic use
Hospital-acquired pneumonia — projected to halve by 2050
Vaccine hesitancy — projected to plateau by 2050
Antibiotic allergy — projected to rise by 2050
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — a global threat projected to cause ~10 million deaths/year by 2050, driven substantially by inappropriate antibiotic use
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The driving problem is antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a global threat projected to cause ~10 million deaths/year by 2050, driven substantially by inappropriate antibiotic use.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is described as the conceptual heart of AMS?
options: Always using the broadest-spectrum agent available
The individual-vs-population tension — safeguarding care for the patient in front of you while protecting antibiotics for future patients
Minimising healthcare costs above all else
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The individual-vs-population tension — safeguarding care for the patient in front of you while protecting antibiotics for future patients
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The conceptual heart of AMS is the individual-vs-population tension: safeguarding the quality of care for the patient in front of you while protecting antibiotics for future patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a recognised driver of antimicrobial resistance?
options: Broad-spectrum use when a narrow agent would do
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Broad-spectrum use when a narrow agent would do
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Drivers of resistance include over-prescribing (including for viral infections), broad-spectrum use when narrow would do, inadequate dosing/duration with poor adherence, and agricultural use / global spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which two organisms are specifically noted to emerge from broad-spectrum antibiotic overuse?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Among the consequences of resistance, C. difficile and MRSA emergence from broad-spectrum overuse is specifically highlighted, alongside untreatable infections, longer admissions, higher mortality and reliance on toxic/last-line agents.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What underlying principle links every antibiotic exposure to resistance, and what goal follows?
options: Antibiotics are always harmless; the goal is to use as many as possible
Every antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure favouring resistant organisms — so the goal is 'the right drug, for the right bug, at the right dose, for the right duration'
Resistance only develops with IV antibiotics; the goal is oral therapy only
Resistance is purely genetic and unrelated to use; the goal is genetic testing
Only broad-spectrum agents cause resistance; the goal is to use them last
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Every antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure favouring resistant organisms — so the goal is 'the right drug, for the right bug, at the right dose, for the right duration'
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Every antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure favouring resistant organisms, so the goal is 'the right drug, for the right bug, at the right dose, for the right duration'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which framework is the UK two-phase model (UKHSA / NICE NG15) applied to every antibiotic prescription?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Start Smart, Then Focus is the two-phase model (UKHSA / NICE NG15) applied to every antibiotic prescription.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Under 'Start Smart' at initiation, which action is recommended?
options: Start antibiotics for any colonisation or contamination
Take cultures before starting, follow local guidelines, and document indication, drug, dose, route and a review/stop date
Avoid documenting the indication to save time
Use the broadest-spectrum agent by default
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Take cultures before starting, follow local guidelines, and document indication, drug, dose, route and a review/stop date
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Start Smart means not starting without clinical evidence of infection, taking cultures before starting, following local prescribing guidelines, documenting indication/drug/dose/route and a review/stop date, and considering severity, immunocompromise, resistance risk and prior exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: At what point is the 'Then Focus' antibiotic review carried out?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The 'Then Focus' review of diagnosis and continuing need is carried out at 48-72 hours, documenting a clear plan as one of five outcomes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is one of the five outcomes of the 48-72 h antibiotic review?
options: Double the dose regardless of cultures
Add a second broad-spectrum agent in all cases
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The five outcomes are Stop, Switch (IV → oral when stable), Change (de-escalate or broaden per cultures), Continue (document review date) and OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient on empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics has culture sensitivities return. What is the pivotal AMS action?
options: De-escalate from empirical broad-spectrum to narrow targeted therapy
Stop all antibiotics regardless of the result
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: De-escalate from empirical broad-spectrum to narrow targeted therapy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: De-escalation — empirical broad-spectrum to narrow targeted once sensitivities return — is the pivotal AMS action.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What does the 'right' mnemonic for practical stewardship stand for?
options: Right ward, right nurse, right time, right chart
Right drug, dose, route, duration, for the right diagnosis
Right culture, right biomarker, right lab, right report
Right patient, right bed, right consultant, right team
Right vaccine, right schedule, right dose, right age
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Right drug, dose, route, duration, for the right diagnosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The 'right' mnemonic is right drug, dose, route, duration, for the right diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What does the note say about antibiotic course duration in modern stewardship?
options: Always finish the full prescribed course in every case
Use the shortest effective duration — the old 'always finish the course' dogma is dropped where evidence supports shorter courses
Always extend courses to prevent resistance
Courses should never be shorter than 14 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Use the shortest effective duration — the old 'always finish the course' dogma is dropped where evidence supports shorter courses
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Practical stewardship favours the shortest effective duration; the old 'always finish the course' dogma is dropped where evidence supports shorter courses.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How are last-line agents such as carbapenems and vancomycin managed under stewardship?
options: Reserved via restriction/approval, using the narrowest effective spectrum
Given empirically to every febrile patient
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Reserved via restriction/approval, using the narrowest effective spectrum
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Stewardship uses the narrowest effective spectrum and reserves last-line agents (carbapenems, vancomycin) via restriction/approval.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which biomarker is given as an example to help guide stopping antibiotics where available?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cultures are taken before antibiotics, and biomarkers such as procalcitonin are used to guide stopping where available.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Who typically makes up an AMS team?
options: A microbiologist and an antimicrobial pharmacist
A GP and a health visitor
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A microbiologist and an antimicrobial pharmacist
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: AMS teams comprise a microbiologist and an antimicrobial pharmacist, supported by local guidelines, audit/feedback, prescriber education and ward rounds.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient resistant to rifampicin has resistance through an altered RNA polymerase. Which mechanism of resistance is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Altered target resistance includes RNA polymerase (rifampicin), DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin) and the 30S ribosome (streptomycin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: β-lactamases (against penicillins) and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes are examples of which resistance mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Drug modification / breakdown resistance includes β-lactamases (penicillins) and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: MRSA is the archetype of resistance. By what mechanism is it resistant to β-lactams?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA is resistant to β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via an altered penicillin-binding protein — an alternative-target mechanism.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set of agents is listed for treating MRSA?
options: Doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, or linezolid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, or linezolid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA, resistant to β-lactams via altered PBP, is treated with doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin or linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) best conceptualised?
options: A specific infectious disease with a defined organism
Not a disease but a diagnostic problem — a prolonged fever undiagnosed despite a proper initial workup, requiring a structured approach to a defined differential
Any fever lasting more than 48 hours
A fever that always has a malignant cause
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Not a disease but a diagnostic problem — a prolonged fever undiagnosed despite a proper initial workup, requiring a structured approach to a defined differential
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: PUO is not a disease but a diagnostic problem: a prolonged fever that remains undiagnosed despite a proper initial workup, approached through a structured framework rather than as a single condition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set correctly states the Petersdorf & Beeson criteria for PUO?
options: Temperature >37.5°C, fever ≥1 week, no workup required
Temperature >38.3°C on several occasions, fever persisting ≥3 weeks, no diagnosis despite appropriate workup (now 3 outpatient visits or 3 days inpatient / intensive ambulatory investigation)
Temperature >39°C once, fever ≥6 weeks, diagnosis confirmed on imaging
Any fever with a raised CRP for 2 weeks
Temperature >38.3°C, fever ≥3 days, single outpatient visit
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Temperature >38.3°C on several occasions, fever persisting ≥3 weeks, no diagnosis despite appropriate workup (now 3 outpatient visits or 3 days inpatient / intensive ambulatory investigation)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Petersdorf & Beeson: temperature >38.3°C on several occasions, fever persisting ≥3 weeks, and no diagnosis despite appropriate workup — originally 1 week inpatient, now revised to 3 outpatient visits or 3 days of inpatient / intensive ambulatory investigation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why does the '≥3 weeks + investigated' criterion matter for the differential?
options: It widens the differential to include all viral causes

By definition these patients have already resisted classification on baseline investigation, so the differential is a specific, often smaller, often serious set — most self-limiting viral fevers have resolved by 3 weeks
It means the fever is always factitious
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: By definition these patients have already resisted classification on baseline investigation, so the differential is a specific, often smaller, often serious set — most self-limiting viral fevers have resolved by 3 weeks
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The criterion matters because such patients have already resisted classification on baseline investigation, so the differential is a specific (often smaller, often serious) set; most self-limiting viral fevers resolve or declare themselves by 3 weeks.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An inpatient develops a new fever several days into a hospital admission with a central line. Which PUO sub-type is this, and what causes should be considered?
options: Classic PUO; the full four-bucket differential
Healthcare-associated (nosocomial) PUO; line/catheter sepsis, C. diff, drug fever, VTE/PE, sinusitis
HIV-associated PUO; TB, MAC, PCP, CMV
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Healthcare-associated (nosocomial) PUO; line/catheter sepsis, C. diff, drug fever, VTE/PE, sinusitis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fever developing in an inpatient is healthcare-associated (nosocomial) PUO, where dominant causes are line/catheter sepsis, C. diff, drug fever, VTE/PE and sinusitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neutropenic patient on chemotherapy develops a persistent fever. Why is establishing this sub-type so important?
options: It makes no difference to management
Neutropenic PUO is an emergency (opportunistic infection — investigate and treat urgently), whereas classic PUO is a methodical workup
It means the cause is always malignancy
It allows blind steroids to be started immediately
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Neutropenic PUO is an emergency (opportunistic infection — investigate and treat urgently), whereas classic PUO is a methodical workup
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Establishing the sub-type reshapes the urgency: the immunocompromised/neutropenic sub-type is an emergency with opportunistic infection (fungal — Candida/Aspergillus, bacterial) needing urgent investigation and treatment, unlike the methodical classic workup.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the HIV-associated sub-type of PUO, which causes dominate?
options: Opportunistic infections (TB, MAC, PCP, CMV), HIV itself, and lymphoma
Atrial myxoma and renal cell carcinoma
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Opportunistic infections (TB, MAC, PCP, CMV), HIV itself, and lymphoma
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HIV-associated PUO is dominated by opportunistic infections (TB, MAC, PCP, CMV), HIV itself, and lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Within the infection bucket of PUO causes, which is described as the classic PUO cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Within the infection bucket, TB — especially miliary/extrapulmonary — is the classic PUO cause; the bucket also includes occult abscess, infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, HIV, EBV/CMV, brucellosis and hidden empyema.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which malignancy is described as 'the classic' cause within the malignancy bucket of PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Lymphoma is 'the classic' malignancy cause of PUO; the bucket also includes leukaemia, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and atrial myxoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which condition belongs to the non-infectious inflammatory bucket of PUO and is especially important in the elderly?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giant cell arteritis / PMR is in the non-infectious inflammatory bucket and is especially important in the elderly; the bucket also includes adult-onset Still's disease, SLE, vasculitides and IBD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does the predominant cause of PUO differ by geography, and what is the overall outcome?
options: Inflammatory disease predominates everywhere; all cases are diagnosed
Infection predominates in developing nations and non-infectious inflammatory disease in industrialised nations; a large proportion (up to ~half) remain undiagnosed despite full workup
Malignancy predominates worldwide; none resolve spontaneously
Infection predominates in industrialised nations only; all resolve within days
Drug fever is the commonest cause globally
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Infection predominates in developing nations and non-infectious inflammatory disease in industrialised nations; a large proportion (up to ~half) remain undiagnosed despite full workup
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Infection predominates in developing nations and non-infectious inflammatory disease in industrialised nations; up to ~half in some series remain undiagnosed despite full workup, with many resolving spontaneously.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the classic 'don't-miss' trio in PUO?
options: TB, lymphoma, and giant cell arteritis
Renal cell carcinoma, leukaemia, atrial myxoma
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: TB, lymphoma, and giant cell arteritis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The classic don't-miss trio is TB, lymphoma and giant cell arteritis (GCA especially in the elderly — treatable and sight-threatening).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is described as the highest-yield step in assessing a patient with PUO?
options: A detailed history (fever pattern, travel, exposures, sexual and drug history, TB risk, B symptoms, joint/skin/eye symptoms, family history, recent surgery/lines)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A detailed history (fever pattern, travel, exposures, sexual and drug history, TB risk, B symptoms, joint/skin/eye symptoms, family history, recent surgery/lines)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: History is the highest-yield step, covering fever pattern/duration, travel, animal/occupational exposure, sexual and drug history, TB risk, weight loss/night sweats, joint/skin/eye symptoms, family history and recent surgery/lines.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is repeated, thorough examination emphasised in PUO?
options: Because the first examination is always wrong
Because new signs (a murmur, lymphadenopathy, a rash, temporal artery tenderness, splenomegaly) often emerge over time and provide the diagnostic lead
Because it is required for notification
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because new signs (a murmur, lymphadenopathy, a rash, temporal artery tenderness, splenomegaly) often emerge over time and provide the diagnostic lead
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A meticulous, repeated examination is essential because new signs such as a murmur, lymphadenopathy, a rash, temporal artery tenderness or splenomegaly often emerge over time and provide the diagnostic lead.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a red flag in PUO?
options: Weight loss + night sweats (malignancy/TB) or a new murmur (endocarditis)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Weight loss + night sweats (malignancy/TB) or a new murmur (endocarditis)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Red flags include weight loss + night sweats (malignancy/TB), a new murmur (endocarditis), localising signs, and immunocompromise/neutropenia (urgent).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How should blood cultures be taken as part of the first-line PUO workup?
options: A single culture after starting antibiotics
Only if the patient is neutropenic
Once daily for a week regardless of antibiotics
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: First-line investigation includes blood cultures ×3 from 3 different sites, taken before antibiotics, alongside FBC + film, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, urinalysis + culture, CXR, HIV test, autoantibodies, TFTs, LDH and a malaria film if travel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which investigation belongs to the second-line (directed) tier in PUO, used to look for occult abscess or lymphadenopathy and to assess for endocarditis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Second-line directed investigations include CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, malignancy), echocardiography (endocarditis — TTE → TOE), viral serology, TB workup and tumour markers.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which third-line (specialist) investigation is increasingly useful for occult malignancy, inflammation or infection in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Third-line specialist investigations include PET-CT (increasingly useful for occult malignancy/inflammation/infection), biopsy (lymph node, bone marrow, temporal artery, liver) and invasive imaging.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the governing principle of investigating PUO?
options: Order every available test simultaneously at presentation
Investigate logically and in a directed way — let history and examination steer the next test — and avoid empirical 'blind' antibiotics/steroids unless the patient is unstable
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics in all patients first
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Investigate logically and in a directed way — let history and examination steer the next test — and avoid empirical 'blind' antibiotics/steroids unless the patient is unstable
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The governing principle is to investigate logically and in a directed way, letting history and examination steer the next test rather than ordering everything at once, and avoiding empirical blind antibiotics/steroids unless the patient is unstable, as they obscure the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the fundamental management principle of PUO?
options: Treat the fever symptomatically and discharge
Treat the underlying cause once found — PUO itself isn't treated, the diagnosis is
Never investigate further once PUO is labelled
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Treat the underlying cause once found — PUO itself isn't treated, the diagnosis is
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Management is to treat the underlying cause once found — PUO itself isn't treated, the diagnosis is.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An elderly patient with PUO has a strong clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis. What is the appropriate exception to the 'avoid blind empirical treatment' rule?
options: Continue to withhold all treatment until biopsy
Give urgent steroids to prevent blindness
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Give urgent steroids to prevent blindness
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: While blind empirical treatment is avoided in the stable patient, strong suspicion of GCA is an exception — urgent steroids are given to prevent blindness; other exceptions are neutropenic/immunocompromised patients (urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics) and clinical instability/sepsis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A stable, improving patient with PUO remains undiagnosed after a full workup. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Ever-more-invasive testing until a cause is found
Careful follow-up, since a significant proportion resolve spontaneously undiagnosed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Careful follow-up, since a significant proportion resolve spontaneously undiagnosed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In the stable, improving patient, a significant proportion of PUO resolve spontaneously undiagnosed, so careful follow-up is more appropriate than ever-more-invasive testing.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The ABCD framework organises malaria prophylaxis. What does each letter stand for?
options: Awareness of risk, Bite prevention, Chemoprophylaxis, Diagnose promptly
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Awareness of risk, Bite prevention, Chemoprophylaxis, Diagnose promptly
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: ABCD = Awareness of risk, Bite prevention, Chemoprophylaxis, and Diagnose promptly (treat any fever after travel as malaria until proven otherwise).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the single most important safety message in malaria prophylaxis?
options: Prophylaxis is 100% effective if taken correctly
No prophylaxis is 100% effective — any fever during or after travel to an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and bite avoidance matters as much as the drugs
Bite avoidance is unnecessary if drugs are taken
Only falciparum needs to be considered after travel
Fever beyond 2 weeks of travel cannot be malaria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: No prophylaxis is 100% effective — any fever during or after travel to an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and bite avoidance matters as much as the drugs
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: No prophylaxis is 100% effective; any fever during or after travel to an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and bite avoidance matters as much as the drugs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is identified as the commonest cause of traveller death in the general pre-travel advice?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Accident/road-traffic risk is highlighted as the commonest cause of traveller death within the general advice section.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which malaria species is the deadly one, and what is its hallmark severe manifestation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: P. falciparum is the deadly species, causing cerebral malaria and the bulk of travel deaths.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A traveller develops malaria months after returning, despite having taken correct prophylaxis. Which species and mechanism explain this?
options: P. vivax / P. ovale; dormant liver hypnozoites that relapse later
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: P. vivax / P. ovale; dormant liver hypnozoites that relapse later
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: P. vivax and P. ovale have a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites) and can relapse months later even after correct prophylaxis — the key to understanding primaquine.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why must most prophylactic antimalarials be continued for 4 weeks after leaving an endemic area?
options: Because they act on the liver hypnozoites
Because they are 'suppressive' — acting on the blood stage, not initial infection or liver hypnozoites — so 4 weeks covers parasites emerging from the liver
Because they prevent mosquito bites for 4 weeks
Because they need 4 weeks to reach therapeutic levels
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because they are 'suppressive' — acting on the blood stage, not initial infection or liver hypnozoites — so 4 weeks covers parasites emerging from the liver
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Standard prophylactic drugs are suppressive, acting on the blood stage rather than initial infection or liver hypnozoites, so they must be continued 4 weeks after leaving to cover parasites emerging from the liver.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which antimalarial only needs to be continued for 1 week after leaving the endemic area, and why?
options: Doxycycline, because it is taken daily
Atovaquone-proguanil, because it acts on the liver stage too
Mefloquine, because it is taken weekly
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Atovaquone-proguanil, because it acts on the liver stage too
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Only atovaquone-proguanil stops at 1 week because it hits the liver stage; the suppressive agents (doxycycline, mefloquine, chloroquine) need 4 weeks to cover emerging blood-stage parasites.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient wants the best-tolerated antimalarial with the shortest post-travel course for a short trip and doesn't mind cost. Which agent fits, and what is its dosing?
options: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone); daily, 1-2 days before and 1 week after
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone); daily, 1-2 days before and 1 week after
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Atovaquone-proguanil is best tolerated overall, taken daily (1-2 days before, 1 week after), has the shortest post-travel course as it acts on the liver stage too, and is good for short trips though expensive.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A budget-conscious traveller is offered doxycycline. Which side effect/advice combination is correct?
options: Neuropsychiatric effects; take at bedtime lying down
Photosensitivity and pill oesophagitis; take with food and stay upright
No side effects; safe in pregnancy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Photosensitivity and pill oesophagitis; take with food and stay upright
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Doxycycline is the cheapest option; side effects include GI upset, pill oesophagitis, photosensitivity and Candida vaginitis. It should be taken with food, staying upright, and is contraindicated in pregnancy and children <12.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with a history of depression is considering malaria prophylaxis. Which agent should be avoided, and why?
options: Mefloquine, due to its neuropsychiatric profile (contraindicated in epilepsy and depression/psychiatric history)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Mefloquine, due to its neuropsychiatric profile (contraindicated in epilepsy and depression/psychiatric history)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mefloquine has neuropsychiatric side effects (vivid dreams, anxiety, depression, psychosis) and is contraindicated in epilepsy and depression/psychiatric history; it should be avoided in such patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the dosing schedule of mefloquine, and what is one practical advantage?
options: Weekly, started 2-3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after; the weekly dose aids adherence and starting early helps detect side effects
Single dose before travel; no monitoring needed
Daily, 1 week after; best for short trips
Weekly, 1 week after; safe in epilepsy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Weekly, started 2-3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after; the weekly dose aids adherence and starting early helps detect side effects
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mefloquine is weekly, started 2-3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after; the weekly dose aids adherence and starting early helps detect side effects, making it suitable for long trips.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pregnant traveller needs malaria prophylaxis. Which statement is correct?
options: Doxycycline is contraindicated; mefloquine can be used and chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate; malaria is more severe in pregnancy
No prophylaxis is needed in pregnancy
Atovaquone-proguanil is the first choice in pregnancy
Primaquine is given routinely in pregnancy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Doxycycline is contraindicated; mefloquine can be used and chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate; malaria is more severe in pregnancy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Malaria is more severe in pregnancy; mefloquine can be used and chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate; doxycycline is contraindicated and atovaquone-proguanil is generally avoided (verify against current UK guidance).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: After significant exposure to P. vivax, primaquine is considered for relapse prevention. What must be checked first, and why?
options: G6PD status, because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: G6PD status, because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Primaquine is the only drug acting on liver hypnozoites and is used for presumptive anti-relapse therapy; G6PD must be checked first because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient presents with a fever 8 months after returning from an endemic area. How should this be approached?
options: Malaria is excluded because it is more than 3 months
Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded
Only investigate if there is a rash
Malaria only presents within 2 weeks of travel
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The 'D' (diagnose promptly) rule: any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is malaria diagnosed on blood films, and what is required to exclude it?
options: A single thin film; one negative excludes it
Thick and thin blood films (thick = detect parasites, thin = speciate + quantify); three negative films over 48 h to exclude, with rapid antigen tests as an adjunct
Blood cultures; two negatives exclude it
Serology alone; one test excludes it
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Thick and thin blood films (thick = detect parasites, thin = speciate + quantify); three negative films over 48 h to exclude, with rapid antigen tests as an adjunct
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Diagnosis uses thick and thin blood films (thick to detect parasites, thin to speciate and quantify); three negative films over 48 h are needed to exclude malaria, with rapid antigen tests as an adjunct.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statements about falciparum malaria and the public-health status of malaria are correct?
options: Falciparum is mild; malaria is not notifiable
Falciparum is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment; malaria is a notifiable disease
Falciparum is self-limiting; malaria is confidentially surveilled
Falciparum requires no urgent treatment; malaria is non-notifiable
Falciparum is the relapsing form; malaria is notifiable only in pregnancy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Falciparum is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment; malaria is a notifiable disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Falciparum malaria is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment, and malaria is a notifiable disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is described as the single most-tested rule (highest-yield fork) in infective diarrhoea?
options: Always give antibiotics for bloody diarrhoea
Never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible, because they increase HUS risk
Always give loperamide to slow the diarrhoea
Antibiotics are mandatory for all travellers' diarrhoea
Stool culture must precede rehydration in every case
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible, because they increase HUS risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fork 2 (the highest-yield rule) is to never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible, as antibiotics increase the risk of HUS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops profuse vomiting 3 hours after eating reheated, handled food. Which organism is most likely?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A very fast onset (1-6 h) of rapid vomiting after reheated/handled food points to Staph aureus, which acts via a preformed enterotoxin. The other very fast cause is Bacillus cereus (reheated rice).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops vomiting a few hours after eating reheated fried rice. Which organism is the classic cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Bacillus cereus from reheated rice has an emetic incubation of 1-5 h and is the classic 'fried rice' vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has bloody diarrhoea and severe abdominal pain that mimics appendicitis after eating undercooked poultry. Which is the most likely organism, and which sequelae are recognised?
options: Campylobacter; Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Campylobacter; Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Campylobacter (commonest bacterial cause) comes from undercooked poultry, causes bloody diarrhoea with severe abdo pain mimicking appendicitis, and has Guillain-Barré and reactive arthritis as high-yield sequelae.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: If antibiotics are indicated for severe or high-risk Campylobacter, what is the first-line agent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: For severe or high-risk Campylobacter (immunocompromised, HIV, heart failure), clarithromycin is first-line, with azithromycin or ciprofloxacin as alternatives — and only after isolating the organism.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A child develops bloody diarrhoea after visiting a petting farm and eating an undercooked beefburger. Why must antibiotics be avoided?
options: Because this suggests E. coli O157, and antibiotics increase the risk of HUS
Because antibiotics cause toxic megacolon directly
Because antibiotics are simply unnecessary in all diarrhoea
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because this suggests E. coli O157, and antibiotics increase the risk of HUS
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Undercooked beef and petting-farm exposure suggest E. coli O157 (STEC); its Shiga toxin can cause HUS, and antibiotics increase that risk — the single most-tested fact in this topic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the triad of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)?
options: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The HUS triad is AKI + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia; it is commonest in children and occurs in ~6% of O157 infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Besides E. coli O157, which other organism in this note also produces Shiga toxin and can cause HUS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Shigella also produces Shiga toxin and can lead to HUS; it spreads faecal-oral or via contaminated water and causes bloody diarrhoea.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops diarrhoea, cramps, fever and vomiting after eating undercooked eggs. Which complication is specifically associated with this organism?
